capabilities.name: acknowledge_platform_alert
capabilities.summary: Mark one platform alert record as seen, clearing it from the unacknowledged list.
capabilities.description:
Says "a human has this". It changes nothing in the cluster and fixes nothing — the workload is exactly as broken afterwards. What it does change is the platform's own behaviour: acknowledging an escalation gives the actor a fresh start on that component, so remediation attempts made before the acknowledgement stop counting against it.

Do not acknowledge to tidy up a list. Acknowledge when the underlying problem has been dealt with, or when the person who owns it has decided what to do.

Get the id from list_platform_alerts. An id belonging to another instance is not found rather than acknowledged.

params.name: alert_id
params.description: UUID of the alert record, from list_platform_alerts.

capabilities.name: add_console_domain
capabilities.summary: Serve this Inframan console on an additional hostname, via the control-plane VM's Caddy.
capabilities.description:
Adds an address the CONSOLE answers on. This is not how a deployed service gets a domain — that is add_domain, which attaches a hostname to a service inside a cluster. Confusing the two points a product's public domain at the Inframan console instead of at the product.

What happens: the central backend records the domain, regenerates this instance's Caddyfile, and the backend hot-reloads Caddy on the control-plane VM. Caddy then obtains a certificate on demand from Let's Encrypt at the VM, so the hostname's A record must ALREADY resolve to `static_ip` from list_console_domains or the certificate cannot be issued and the address serves nothing.

It rewrites live edge routing for the machine serving this API. A failed Caddy reload is reported explicitly and means the domain is recorded centrally but not being served — remove it and add it again.

params.name: domain
params.description: Fully-qualified hostname for the CONSOLE, e.g. "inframan.example.com". No scheme, no path, no wildcard. Its A record must already point at the instance's static IP.

capabilities.name: add_domain
capabilities.summary: Attach a custom domain to an infrastructure and start its HTTPS certificate.
capabilities.description:
DNS FIRST. Call list_domains for the infrastructure's `load_balancer_ip` (or, for an l7 domain, its `application_address`), have the USER create a record for the domain pointing at it, and wait for it to resolve. This call verifies DNS before it writes anything and refuses the domain outright if the record is missing or points somewhere else — that refusal is not a platform fault, it is the work the user still has to do at their registrar. You cannot do it for them.

On success a free, auto-renewing Let's Encrypt certificate is requested through an ACME HTTP-01 challenge served by the cluster's ingress. The domain comes back `pending`; issuance takes a minute or two. Poll get_domain_status until it reads `active`.

Do NOT write the domain into inframan.yaml or deploy until it is active. A service that deploys against a pending domain comes up without that domain's route, silently — reachable only at its automatic address, if it has one — and has to be deployed again afterwards.

If it ends up `failed`, fix the DNS record and call retry_domain — do not add the domain a second time; it is already registered.

The infrastructure must be READY and must have its gateway installed, because the load-balancer IP is what the certificate challenge is answered on.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to attach the domain to, from list_infrastructures. Its load-balancer IP is the one the A record must point at.

params.name: domain
params.description: The fully-qualified domain, e.g. "api.example.com". No scheme, no path, no wildcard. It must already resolve to this infrastructure's load-balancer IP.

params.name: type
params.description: The load balancer the domain is served on: `l4` (default) — the network load balancer, TLS ending at Istio; its record points at `load_balancer_ip` — or `l7` — the application load balancer, which IAP needs. An l7 domain is refused until the user has turned the infrastructure's application load balancer on and it is ready (list_domains then gives `application_address`), and its record must point at that address alone: an A record, or on AWS a CNAME at the load balancer's host name. It is served there from the first, its certificate issued through it.

capabilities.name: apply_node_class_finding
capabilities.summary: Make one of the node class's findings now.
capabilities.description: Makes one finding of the node class, by its `key` as get_node_class lists it, whatever the class's mode. A pass starts now and plans again, so the finding is made as it stands, if it is still one: the new nodes it needs are brought up first, then each workload is moved in turn and waited for on its new pool — down for the time its forecast says where it restarts — and a node emptied is let go. Returns as the pass starts; read get_node_class for the outcome. One pass at a time on an infrastructure: while one runs this is refused.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: key
params.description: The finding's key, as get_node_class lists it.

capabilities.name: apply_node_class_findings
capabilities.summary: Make every finding of the node class now.
capabilities.description: Runs a pass of the node class now that makes everything it finds, whatever the class's mode: the findings get_node_class lists, planned again. Each workload moved is down for the time its forecast says where it restarts. Returns as the pass starts; read get_node_class for the outcome. One pass at a time on an infrastructure.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: apply_optimization
capabilities.summary: Apply one of the optimizer's findings now.
capabilities.description: Applies one finding of the optimizer — one resource of one platform workload, as get_maintenance_pass lists them (a service's is made by open_optimization_pr). A pass runs now and plans again, so the finding is applied as it stands, if it is still one to lower or raise: a lowered request is sent to its component's actor, which lowers it on the running pods in place, and where they will not take it live declares it for the component's next rollout (a workload is never restarted for a saving); a raise is reported to the actor, which raises it to what the container uses now, rolling the workload out where the pods will not take it live. The rest of the plan is recorded and left as it is. One pass at a time on an infrastructure.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: workload_id
params.description: The finding's workload, as get_maintenance_pass names it.

params.name: resource
params.description: cpu or memory.

capabilities.name: apply_platform_update
capabilities.summary: Roll this Inframan instance onto a pending platform release. Restarts the instance.
capabilities.description:
Console and CLI only, deliberately. Applying an update restarts the instance's OWN containers — the backend serving this request, the console, Caddy and the workers on the control-plane VM. Whoever called it loses the connection mid-flight and cannot observe the outcome, so this is a decision a human takes with their hand on the console, not something an agent schedules on their behalf.

Deployed applications keep serving: they run in the user's GKE clusters, which this does not touch. What stops for the length of the rollout is the platform's own control plane — the API, the console, and any workflow that needs a worker during the restart.

The id comes from get_update_notification. The rollout is driven by the central backend, so this returns as soon as it has been accepted, not when it is done.

params.name: update_id
params.description: Id of the pending update, from get_update_notification.

capabilities.name: approve_chart_application
capabilities.summary: Approve what an operator chart's waiting release asks for across the cluster, so it installs.
capabilities.description: People only, an admin of the instance. An operator chart (Strimzi, a database operator) asks for powers across the whole cluster: its own resource types, roles beyond its namespace, admission webhooks. Its release waits at awaiting_approval, its summary's `powers` saying each in words with what to read twice (`risks`), until an admin approves them; the approval covers exactly those grants, what runs with them (`runs`: every pod of the chart, its images, commands and environment, the data of the ConfigMaps and Secrets it reads but what the chart generated, and as whom), the objects its operator acts on (`objects`, each whole) and every risk said, so a later version asking for the same or less installs without asking, and one asking for more, or running other code with them, waits again. A chart that holds nothing across the cluster waits too when its objects are of a resource type another chart application brings: `objects` names that application, whose operator acts on them with its powers. Once an application has been approved, every later version waits for an admin unless an approval covers it — what it runs and keeps (`config`), its objects — one holding nothing across the cluster too (`approved_before`: this application has been approved before: every version of it is approved); the first approval approves what earlier, unapproved versions left in its namespace as it stands (`kept`, the runs marked `kept` and `kept_disks`, by name, never a value), so the upgrade after it asks once more; and approving one over what such a version left running (`quiesce`) stops it — its KEDA autoscalers paused first — and replaces the namespace's service accounts, before anything of the approved version is applied, starting again once it is installed what that version makes; what another operator makes there from its own objects (a CloudNativePG Cluster, a Prometheus) is left running, and refused where it runs as an account the chart empowers. A version of an approved application making nothing else is approved as a whole (`whole`), so the same version rendered again is covered. `fingerprint` is the powers' the admin read: a release waiting with others is refused, to be read again.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The chart application.

params.name: release_id
params.description: The release waiting for the approval, from get_chart_release.

params.name: fingerprint
params.description: The release's summary.powers.fingerprint, as read.

capabilities.name: cancel_config_pr
capabilities.summary: Close an application's open config pull request without merging it.
capabilities.description:
Closes the PR on GitHub and releases the block, so config edits are possible again. The proposed change is discarded — it never reached the servers, because a config PR only takes effect on merge.

Read get_config_pr first and tell the user what is in it. This throws away work somebody may be waiting to review, and an unmerged config PR is often the CORRECTION for a failing release rather than the cause of it: cancelling the PR CI opened to fix immutable-field drift leaves the release failing exactly as before.

To APPLY the change instead, a human merges the PR in GitHub; there is no way to merge it from here, deliberately.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose open config PR to close. From list_applications.

capabilities.name: cancel_resource_deletion
capabilities.summary: Cancel a deletion that is pending or approved, and close its pull request: nothing it names is deleted.
capabilities.description:
Cancels the deletion with every deletion of the same pull request (one for each application of its group), and closes that pull request on GitHub where it is open, best effort. Nothing it names is deleted.

A deletion cancelled after its pull request merged leaves a file that no longer declares those resources: the next release then refuses (RELEASE_WOULD_DELETE) until they are back in inframan.yaml, or deleted again with delete_application_resources. Refused (NOT_CANCELLABLE) once a deletion is applied or cancelled.

params.name: deletion_id
params.description: The deletion. From get_resource_deletions or preview_resource_deletion.

capabilities.name: check_github_app_permissions
capabilities.summary: Compare one connected GitHub App's live permissions and events against what the platform requires.
capabilities.description:
The diagnostic for "the App is connected but nothing deploys". `status` is one of:

- `up_to_date` — the App and its installation both satisfy the requirements.
- `app_outdated` — the App was created from an older manifest and is missing permissions or webhook events. The OWNER must update it, at the update link in the response.
- `installation_pending` — the App is correct but the new permissions are waiting on the installer's approval, at the approve link in the response.
- `not_installed` — the App exists but is installed on no account. The install link in the response is where to reinstall it.
- `disconnected` — the App itself was deleted or revoked on GitHub. It has to be reconnected from the console.
- `unknown` — GitHub could not be reached. This establishes nothing; do not report it as a fault.

Every remedy here is a page a human opens on GitHub. Give the user the URL — none of it can be done from this surface.

params.name: github_app_id
params.description: The connected App to check — the `id` from get_github_app_status, not `app_id`.

capabilities.name: continue_addon_install
capabilities.summary: Start an install that was held waiting for its cloud identity.
capabilities.description:
The second half of an install that came back `awaiting_setup` — a Redis or Postgres tier's, or Grafana's. It takes only the installed_app_id: the name, tier, memory and persistence the customer chose are already on the row, and this cannot change any of them. A resume that accepted options would be a second create, and the instance name is immutable, so the two would eventually disagree about which database this is.

Call it AFTER verify_cloud_identity reports the identity verified. It re-checks the identity itself rather than trusting that you did — the reason the install stopped is that provisioning without an identity forecloses it permanently, and a resume that took the caller's word for it would be a gate with a bypass. If the identity is still unverified this refuses and the install stays held; nothing is lost.

Only `awaiting_setup` installs. A ready one has nothing to continue; a pending one already has a workflow running and re-kicking it would race two reconciles against the same node pool state.

Takes MINUTES once it starts, and returns as soon as the workflow does — poll get_installed_app until status is ready.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The held install, as returned by install_addon or list_platform_apps. Not a catalog app id and not an instance name.

capabilities.name: convert_pipeline
capabilities.summary: Convert a pipeline document between Inframan YAML, GitHub Actions YAML and the console's JSON, saving nothing.
capabilities.description:
Reads a pipeline written in one format and writes it in another, the same conversion the console's pipeline editor makes when its tabs switch. Use it to bring a repository's .github/workflows/*.yml onto Inframan: convert it from github to inframan, read the report, then create_pipeline with the result (or with the workflow itself and format: github).

A pipeline is written in any of three formats, all the same pipeline: `inframan` (Inframan YAML, the default: the shape export_pipeline_yaml returns), `github` (GitHub Actions workflow syntax: a step is a job, its commands the job's run: steps, the phases where jobs sit around two fixed jobs `build` and `deploy` — `uses: inframan/build@v1` and `uses: inframan/deploy@v1` — and what GitHub has no word for under an `inframan:` key; any workflow written for GitHub's runners converts too: checkout, caches, docker build/push, cloud sign-ins and deploys are Inframan's own and replaced, setup-node/python/go/java choose the step's image, a matrix is expanded, a notify step or stage is a job of one `uses: inframan/notify@v1` step with its settings under `with:` (a stage's job carries `inframan: {stage: true}`), a job's `${{ secrets.X }}` becomes the step's secret X (an infrastructure secret of that name) and its `services:` the pre-build step's sidecars, and what a pipeline cannot hold — environment:, unknown actions, a second trigger — is reported unsupported, never dropped unsaid) and `json` (the console's Visual form, the API's field names). A step's `secrets:` maps a variable to the NAME of an infrastructure secret (list_infra_secrets), never a value: the step gets it as that variable, masked in its log. A pre-build step's `sidecars:` ({name, image, env, command, ready}) are containers beside it — a database for its tests — reached at their name or localhost, `ready` a command run in one until it succeeds. list_repository_workflows reads a repository's .github/workflows to import, and convert_pipeline shows what a document becomes before anything is saved.

Returns `document` (the pipeline in `to`), `pipeline` (its fields under the API's names), `report` (for a GitHub workflow: what each job, step and key became — kept, replaced, changed, dropped or unsupported, with its line) and `problems` (what a save would refuse: a pre-build step with no image, a secret the infrastructure does not have, an alert group or a channel a notify step names that the instance does not have).

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the pipeline is for: its secrets and its cloud are checked. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: from
params.description: The document's format.

params.name: to
params.description: The format to write it in.

params.name: document
params.description: The pipeline, as text in `from`.

capabilities.name: count_unacknowledged_platform_alerts
capabilities.summary: Count the platform alert records still waiting on a human.
capabilities.description:
The number the console renders as a badge. Cheap enough to call for a health check before deciding whether list_platform_alerts is worth reading.

Counts DATABASE RECORDS raised by the platform's self-healing, not cluster alerts — list_firing_cluster_alerts is what Prometheus is firing.

capabilities.name: create_agent_deployment
capabilities.summary: Deploy one agent on its own — a deployment of its own, with no repository — and release it.
capabilities.description:
For an agent that needs no repository: one that answers questions from text you give it, or runs on a schedule, a webhook or the platform's events. An agent that works in a repository — reading its code, opening pull requests, running on its pushes — belongs in that repository's inframan.yaml instead, as a service of `type: agent`.

Give `agent`: the agent's block exactly as inframan.yaml writes it under `agent:` — `prompt` (its instructions, written inline: there is no repository to read a file from), `run` (`always`: kept running, answering at an address; `on_demand`, the default: started by a schedule, a webhook or an event), `model` (`<connection>/<model>`, or an alias; the default connection's default model where left out), `tools`, `knowledge` (each file inline, as {path, content}, 256 KiB in all), `budget` (`conversation` or `run`, `day`, `month`, written as "$1.25"), `limits`, `inframan`, `egress`, `on`, `outputs`, `timeout_minutes`, `max_turns` — as a JSON object or its text. A key no agent's block has is refused, not dropped. Or give `template`, one list_agent_templates offers an agent deployed on its own (ask it with infrastructure_id), and `options`, its fields by key; preview_agent_template, with infrastructure_id, shows the manifest it keeps. A template whose agent works in a repository is refused (TEMPLATE_NEEDS_REPOSITORY).

Its manifest — `application: <name>`, `services: {<name>: {type: agent, agent: …}}` — is kept as version 1 and released at once on the infrastructure, with no pipeline: the deployment and its agent share the name. Refused before anything is made: what its release would refuse — the Agents app not ready on the infrastructure (AGENTS_NOT_INSTALLED), no model connection (AGENTS_NOT_CONNECTED), a model no connection serves or nothing prices (AGENT_MODEL_CONNECTION, MODEL_PRICE_UNKNOWN) —, a name an application already has (APPLICATION_NAME_TAKEN), and a manifest an application of published images cannot hold (AGENT_DEPLOYMENT_INVALID): a trigger on a push or a merged pull request, `repository: true`, `approve: [open_pull_request]`, instructions or knowledge named as a repository's files.

`auto_domain` gives an always-on agent its automatic HTTPS address; without it, or a domain added to its manifest later, it answers only inside its cluster. Anyone who reaches the address spends its budget: give it one.

Answers `application` — its `kind` agent, and `agent_service_id` its agent's service, the ID get_agent takes — `manifest_version` and `release_started`. Change it later with save_application_manifest, which keeps the next version and releases it; deactivate_application stops it, keeping its record.

params.name: name
params.description: The deployment's name, which its agent's service takes too: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, beginning with a letter, 40 characters at most. Unique in the instance, immutable, and the default namespace.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure it runs on, from list_infrastructures. It needs the Agents app ready there and a model connection (get_agent_connections).

params.name: namespace
params.description: Kubernetes namespace. Defaults to the name; immutable.

params.name: agent
params.description: The agent's block as inframan.yaml writes it under `agent:`, as a JSON object or its text (YAML or JSON), e.g. {"run": "always", "prompt": "…", "model": "opus", "budget": {"conversation": "$0.40", "day": "$10", "month": "$150"}}. Give this or template.

params.name: template
params.description: A template an agent deployed on its own takes (list_agent_templates with infrastructure_id), such as docs_qa. Give this or agent.

params.name: options
params.description: The template's fields by key, as a JSON object, e.g. {"knowledge_content": "# FAQ …", "model": "anthropic/haiku"}; a field left out takes its default.

params.name: auto_domain
params.description: Give an always-on agent its automatic HTTPS address (auto_domain: true on its service in the manifest); refused for an on-demand agent, which has no address. For a template, its own auto_domain option says the same where the options do not.

capabilities.name: create_alert_group
capabilities.summary: Add an alert group: a name an inframan.yaml's notify: names, and the channels it sends to.
capabilities.description: An alert group is the instance's: a `name` (1 to 40 lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, never `none`; fixed once made, since files name it), a `description`, its `channels` (1 to 10 of the instance's notification channels, in order: it sends to every one that is on), `send_resolved` (whether a message also goes when an alert resolves) and `enabled` (a group that is off sends nothing: how one is silenced). A file names it: an alert's `notify: <group>` (or `notify: none` for no one), and an application's `notify: <group>` beside `services:`, which is the default group of its services' alerts — every alert of it that names none — and nothing else; a pipeline's notify step or stage names one too, for a release's outcome. A group named nowhere is no one. A release whose file names a group the instance does not have is refused (ALERT_GROUP_NOT_FOUND); a chart application, which has no alerts, names none (CHART_APPLICATION_NOTIFY). Make the channels first (create_notification_channel). The group sends nothing until a file names it — an application's alerts or one alert's go to it from the application's next release — or a pipeline's notify step does. Refused: a name another group has (409), a 51st group (409), a channel the instance does not have. Admins only.

params.name: name
params.description: The name files write after notify:, as shop-oncall: 1 to 40 lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. Fixed once made.

params.name: description
params.description: What the group is for, at most 300 characters.

params.name: channel_ids
params.description: The channels it sends to, by their IDs from list_notification_channels: 1 to 10, in order, as a JSON array.

params.name: send_resolved
params.description: Whether a message also goes when an alert resolves; true for a new group.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether it sends at all; true for a new group.

capabilities.name: create_application
capabilities.summary: Create an application from a Git repository and attach it to pipelines.
capabilities.description:
Services are NOT listed by you — they are read from the repository's inframan.yaml, whose services: map is authoritative. CI resolves every service name against that map on each push, so a name invented here could never deploy.

A repo with no inframan.yaml falls back to monorepo detection, then to a single service. An INVALID inframan.yaml is refused outright — fix it and push first.

pipeline_ids is required and there is no infrastructure argument: the pipelines ARE the binding, because each belongs to one infrastructure. Passing pipelines from two infrastructures creates one application on EACH, linked as a group. Get ids from list_pipelines.

github_app_id is required too, even when only one App is connected — call get_github_app_status first and use its `id`. Without it the application is created but no push ever deploys it.

`branch` is where the application LIVES — use the repository's main branch, because every push to it deploys from then on. If you are writing inframan.yaml on a different branch and it is not on main yet, put that one in `branch_for_first_deploy`: the first release for every pipeline builds from there, and the config is read from there too. Omit it when the two are the same. Getting this backwards leaves the application permanently tracking a working branch.

`name` is REQUIRED and must match inframan.yaml's `application:` field exactly — or, when the manifest declares an `applications:` map, one of its SECTION KEYS. A name that is not a section is refused with the list of sections, because the services would otherwise be read from whichever section happened to be first. It used to default to the repository name, which is the same string often enough to pass in testing and different often enough to break a real deployment: a repo called drum-monorepo whose yaml says `application: drum` would have been created as drum-monorepo, and every push would then fail immutable-field validation with nothing on the platform side to correct. Take it from detect_repository. `namespace` still defaults, to the name. The name must be UNIQUE within the instance and is immutable once created; it doubles as the Kubernetes namespace and the application: field in inframan.yaml, which CI validates byte-for-byte on every push, so a mismatch fails deploys until the repo is corrected. An inactive application still holds its name until it is deleted permanently.

params.name: name
params.description: Application name, lowercase. REQUIRED, and it must equal the `application:` field in the repository's inframan.yaml exactly — CI compares the two byte-for-byte on every push and fails the release while they differ. Read it from detect_repository's `application`, not from the repository name: they are equal often enough to look like a rule and differ often enough to break a deployment silently. Immutable once created, used as the K8s namespace, and unique within the instance.

params.name: repo_url
params.description: GitHub repository. Any form works — "org/repo", "github.com/org/repo", or the full https URL, with or without ".git" — it is stored as one canonical clone URL. Its inframan.yaml decides the services.

params.name: pipeline_ids
params.description: Comma-separated pipeline ids from list_pipelines. These decide which infrastructure(s) the application deploys to.

params.name: branch
params.description: The branch this application tracks from now on — the repository's MAIN branch, not whichever one you happen to be working on. Every push to it deploys.

params.name: branch_for_first_deploy
params.description: Only when inframan.yaml is not on `branch` yet: the branch you are writing it on. The first release builds from here; everything after comes from `branch`. Omit when they are the same.

params.name: namespace
params.description: Kubernetes namespace. Defaults to the application name, immutable, and services only reach each other within one namespace. Applications may share one, but not a service name: a service named as another application's service in the namespace is refused (SERVICE_NAME_TAKEN), the first to have the name keeping it.

params.name: github_app_id
params.description: Which connected GitHub App's webhooks deploy this repository. Get it from get_github_app_status — use the `id` field, NOT `app_id`. Required even when only one App is connected: an application without one never deploys on push, and this is not inferred.

capabilities.name: create_application_revision
capabilities.summary: Build and deploy an application again as a new revision.
capabilities.description:
Runs the full release for every service in the application: CI builds each image from the tracked branch, and the resulting revision takes traffic.

To change configuration WITHOUT rebuilding, edit inframan.yaml and push instead: the build is skipped when the commit already has an image, so the same image is redeployed under the new configuration.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to build and deploy. From list_applications.

capabilities.name: create_chart_application
capabilities.summary: Install a self-contained app from its public Helm chart, pinned to one version.
capabilities.description:
For server software published as a Helm chart (NATS, Qdrant, a database, a queue): Inframan installs the chart, and the person never runs Helm. Call preview_chart_application first, with the same manifest, and show the person what it would make and what it refuses.

`manifest` is inframan.yaml's schema for this one application with a `chart:` section in place of `services:`:
  version: v1
  application: nats
  chart:
    repository: https://nats-io.github.io/k8s/helm/charts   # https://… or oci://…, public
    name: nats
    version: 1.3.7          # exact; never a range or latest
    timeout_minutes: 10     # optional, 2–30: how long it may take to be ready
    node_pool: application-pool   # only where the infrastructure has several
    values: {...}           # the chart's own values, as its README documents them
    exposes:                # what services connect to
      NATS_URL: {service: nats, port: 4222, url: "nats://app:{password}@{host}:{port}",
                 password_from: {secret: nats-auth, key: password}}
    secrets:                # infrastructure secrets, by NAME
      NATS_PASSWORD: nats-admin-password
    objects:                # an operator chart's: what the operator runs
      - {apiVersion: kafka.strimzi.io/v1beta2, kind: Kafka, metadata: {name: events}, spec: {...}}
It names no alert group: a chart application has no alerts to send one, so a `notify:` is refused (CHART_APPLICATION_NOTIFY); its installs' outcomes are get_chart_release's and its activity feed's.

`exposes` names a Service and a port the chart makes — or, on an operator chart, one its operator makes from objects: (Strimzi's <cluster>-kafka-bootstrap), which then needs `protocol` or `url` and is checked once the application is ready; the value is host:port (protocol tcp), http://host:port (http), https://host:port (https) — unset, what the Service port says: its appProtocol, else its name alone or before a dash, http for http, http2 and h2c, https for https, tcp otherwise — or `url` with {host}, {port} and {password} (read from a Secret the chart keeps, password_from). A service of any application on the infrastructure connects with `NATS_URL: chart/nats/NATS_URL` in its connections: block; the value reaches its pod by secretKeyRef and never leaves the cluster. `secrets` name infrastructure secrets, never values: they are written into the Secret inframan-secrets in its namespace, which a chart's own existingSecret options read (point them at that name), and ${secret:NAME} in the values puts one in where a chart has no such option. A version's secrets reach that Secret only as its install starts; an upgrade that fails gives back what it held. Never write a password into the values.

An operator chart — one that asks for powers across the cluster (preview_chart_application's `powers`) — waits at awaiting_approval until an admin of the instance approves them in the console; tell the person, and do not save it again. `objects` are namespaced documents of the application's namespace (the cluster the operator runs), installed with the chart and waited for. Inframan places the pods of the chart's own templates on the node pool as it renders them, and the pods an operator makes from `objects` as no node takes them: each is given the node pool's toleration (every node pool is tainted), and nothing else of it changes; nothing need be written into an object's pod template for it. An admission webhook the operator registers as it runs is kept off the platform's namespaces as the chart's own are. A pod the cluster refuses the toleration fails the install at once, saying which and what to give its object's pod template.

It is kept as version 1 and installed: the application reads installing, then ready once every workload it made, every pod of its namespace and every object of `objects` that reports a Ready condition is ready (and none reports NotReady, Stalled or Reconciling), or failed with the reason (the pod that crashed and its log, the pod no node took, the image that would not pull). Follow it with get_chart_release. Its pods run on the application node pool's nodes; it sleeps and wakes with the infrastructure; get_logs reads its logs by the application's name; its images are scanned as it installs and listed under it (get_infrastructure_vulnerabilities with application_id); the ServiceMonitors and PodMonitors the chart ships are scraped (query_metrics).

It has no public address. Change it later with save_application_manifest (each save is a version, and a failed change leaves the last good version running).

params.name: name
params.description: Application name, lowercase letters, digits and '-', at most 53 characters. Must equal the manifest's `application:`. Immutable; the Helm release's name and the default namespace.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to install it on. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: manifest
params.description: The manifest, as preview_chart_application checked it.

params.name: namespace
params.description: Kubernetes namespace, the application's alone. Defaults to the name; immutable. Refused, saying whose it is: the platform's (monitoring, istio-ingress, grafana, keda, …), Kubernetes' (kube-*, default), an add-on's, and another application's.

capabilities.name: create_config_pr
capabilities.summary: Open a pull request bringing a service's inframan.yaml back in line with the platform.
capabilities.description:
Regenerates the application's inframan.yaml from the platform's current configuration for this service and opens a PR with it. Applies nothing on its own — a human merges it, and the merge deploys.

Refused while another config PR is open for the same application, and, before GitHub is asked anything, when the service's name is another application's service in the namespace (SERVICE_NAME_TAKEN), as the merge's release would refuse it.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service whose configuration to write out. From list_services.

params.name: base_branch
params.description: Branch the PR merges into. Defaults to the service's, then the application's, tracked branch.

capabilities.name: create_env_group
capabilities.summary: Create an empty environment group on an infrastructure.
capabilities.description:
A group belongs to the INFRASTRUCTURE, not to a service — inframan.yaml only references one by name, so the group has to exist before a service can attach it. That is what this does.

Creates the BUNDLE, not its contents: the group comes back empty and nothing is deployed. Two steps follow, and neither is done here — put variables in it, then attach it. Putting VALUES in is a console operation and deliberately not available here — a value passed as a tool argument lands in the conversation and the client's logs before it reaches the platform. Attaching is a yaml edit: name the group in the service's envGroups: block and push.

So the sequence is: create it here, ask the user to fill it in the console, then reference it from inframan.yaml. Say that plainly rather than reporting the group as ready — an empty group attached to a service contributes nothing.

`group_type` is fixed at creation and cannot be changed afterwards:
• `env` — plain values, stored by the platform. This is the default.
• `secret` — values kept in the customer's GCP Secret Manager and also passed to the Docker build as build args. Filling a secret group in means sending values, which is a console operation. It needs the infrastructure's Secret Manager on (get_infrastructure_features, secret_manager): while it is off, creating one is refused with code secret_manager_off. An `env` group needs none of it.

Creating the group is safe on any surface because no value passes through it — only a name.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to create the group on, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: name
params.description: Name for the group, e.g. "shared-config". How humans will refer to it.

params.name: group_type
params.description: "env" for plain values (default), or "secret" for Secret Manager-backed values that are also build args. Cannot be changed later.

capabilities.name: create_image_application
capabilities.summary: Create an application of published container images, with no repository, and release it.
capabilities.description:
For running images someone else publishes (metabase, redis, an image your own CI pushes elsewhere) with no repository in Inframan. To add ONE published image to an application that has a repository, do not use this: give the service `image: {repository, tag}` in that repository's inframan.yaml instead (a commit, or add the service from the console, which opens a config PR).

`manifest` is inframan.yaml's schema for this one application — `version: v1`, `application: <name>`, `services:` — with every service an `image:` block instead of `path`/`build`. Everything else a service supports is the same: type, port, scaling, domains, connections, env, envGroups, secrets, rollout, environments. It is kept as version 1 and released at once; there is no CI — nothing is built, and pre-build steps never run — but pre-deploy and post-deploy steps of the pipeline run as for any release.

Images must be PUBLIC: the release resolves each tag anonymously to its digest and runs that digest, and refuses an image it cannot read that way before anything deploys. `latest` is refused unless a digest is given with it.

`infrastructure_id` makes it on that one infrastructure, as a chart application is made, and it needs no pipeline: a release with none linked runs none of a pipeline's steps. pipeline_ids given with it must be that infrastructure's, and are linked, their pre-deploy and post-deploy steps run. Without infrastructure_id, pipeline_ids attach the application to infrastructures exactly as create_application's do, one application each; each infrastructure's application keeps its own copy of the manifest, so a later change is made to each. Change it later with save_application_manifest or deploy_service_image; never by writing service rows, which the next release rewrites from the manifest. For one agent deployed on its own, create_agent_deployment writes the manifest from the agent's block.

params.name: name
params.description: Application name, lowercase letters, digits and '-'. Must equal the manifest's `application:`. Immutable, unique in the instance, and the default namespace.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure it is made on, from list_infrastructures: one application, with no pipeline needed. Give this or pipeline_ids.

params.name: pipeline_ids
params.description: Comma-separated pipeline ids from list_pipelines. Without infrastructure_id, which infrastructures it deploys to, one application each; with it, that infrastructure's pipelines to link.

params.name: manifest
params.description: The application's manifest, inframan.yaml's schema, every service an `image:` with `repository` and `tag` (or `digest`).

params.name: namespace
params.description: Kubernetes namespace. Defaults to the name; immutable. Shared with another application, none of its services may be named as one of that application's (SERVICE_NAME_TAKEN).

capabilities.name: create_infra_secret
capabilities.summary: Store a secret value on an infrastructure under a name services can reference.
capabilities.description:
The value is written to the customer's GCP Secret Manager and the platform keeps only a reference; the service that needs it names the secret in its inframan.yaml `secrets:` block and receives it at deploy time.

CONSOLE ONLY, deliberately. The secret value would be an argument to this call, and an argument is written into the conversation and the host client's logs before it reaches the platform — which is exactly the exposure the Secret Manager path exists to avoid. Nothing about doing it from an agent is faster, and the credential would be burned. Ask the user to add it in the console, then confirm with list_infra_secrets that the name is there.

Sending an existing name replaces its value rather than creating a second secret.

Needs the infrastructure's Secret Manager: refused with code `secret_manager_off` while it is off, and with `cloud_account_not_ready`, naming the grants, while the cloud account is not yet verified for them.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to store it on, from list_infrastructures. It decides which cloud project the value is written into.

params.name: name
params.description: The name services will reference from inframan.yaml, e.g. "DATABASE_URL".

params.name: value
params.description: The secret value. Console only — it goes straight to GCP Secret Manager.

capabilities.name: create_initial_config_pr
capabilities.summary: Open a pull request that adds an application's inframan.yaml to its repository.
capabilities.description:
Registers a git-backed application in its own repo: the platform renders the root inframan.yaml from what it knows about the application and opens a PR adding it. Merging that PR is what triggers the first deploy — this call deploys nothing.

For an application whose repository has NO inframan.yaml yet. If the file is already committed, do not call this: it proposes the platform's rendering as the whole file, and the repository's version is the source of truth. Check with get_service_inframan_yaml, which shows what would be proposed, and edit the committed file directly instead.

Refused while another config PR is open — get_config_pr says whether one is, and the console clears it — and, before GitHub is asked anything, when a service it would declare is named as another application's service in the namespace (SERVICE_NAME_TAKEN), as the merge's release would refuse it.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to register in its repository. From list_applications.

params.name: base_branch
params.description: Branch the PR merges into. Defaults to the application's tracked branch, which is almost always right.

capabilities.name: create_notification_channel
capabilities.summary: Add a notification channel: an SMTP sender, Slack, Google Chat, Microsoft Teams, or a signed webhook.
capabilities.description: A channel is `email` (an SMTP sender of the admin's choosing, TLS required — for Gmail, smtp.gmail.com, 587, the account and an app password), `slack` (an incoming webhook), `google_chat` (a space's webhook), `teams` (a Workflows webhook) or `webhook` (an https:// address of a public host, each body signed with HMAC-SHA256 in X-Inframan-Signature). Its secret — the SMTP password, the chat webhook's address, the signing secret — is kept by the instance, encrypted, and never read back: a read says `secret_set`. A channel is just a channel: it has no rules, and is sent what the alert groups it is in are sent. A chat channel's address must be its vendor's own webhook host, and a webhook's a public host; each is checked again as it is sent, and dialled at public addresses only, TLS verified, no redirect followed. A new channel is sent nothing until an alert group sends to it (create_alert_group, update_alert_group). `rules` are refused: channels have none. Refused too: a name another channel has (409), a 26th channel (409). Admins only.

params.name: type
params.description: What the channel is.

params.name: name
params.description: What the channel is called, one line of at most 60 characters.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether it gets messages.

params.name: smtp_host
params.description: Email: the SMTP server's host, a public name.

params.name: smtp_port
params.description: Email: its port, 587 by default (465 for TLS).

params.name: smtp_security
params.description: Email: starttls, or tls (implicit, usually 465); by the port where not given.

params.name: smtp_username
params.description: Email: the user name it signs in with; empty for a server that takes mail without one.

params.name: from_address
params.description: Email: the address messages come from.

params.name: from_name
params.description: Email: the name they come from, Inframan where not given.

params.name: recipients
params.description: Email: the addresses it writes to, comma-separated, at most 50.

params.name: webhook_url
params.description: Webhook: its https:// address, on a public host.

params.name: secret
params.description: The channel's secret: the SMTP password, the Slack, Google Chat or Teams webhook's address, or the webhook's signing secret (16 to 256 characters). Empty keeps the one kept.

params.name: rules
params.description: Not taken: a channel has no rules. A request that sends rules is refused; what a channel is sent is its alert groups' (create_alert_group).

capabilities.name: create_pipeline
capabilities.summary: Create a CI/CD pipeline on an infrastructure from a YAML definition.
capabilities.description:
Pipelines are stored by the platform, not committed to the repo, so this is how one comes into existence.

Pass the definition as YAML — the same shape export_pipeline_yaml exports, so the way to learn the format is to read an existing pipeline first.

Required: `name` and `trigger_event` (push, pull_request or pull_request_merged). `trigger_branch` is a glob and defaults to `*`.

Creating a pipeline does not run it, and does not attach it to anything — use link_pipeline to bind it to an application.

A pipeline is written in any of three formats, all the same pipeline: `inframan` (Inframan YAML, the default: the shape export_pipeline_yaml returns), `github` (GitHub Actions workflow syntax: a step is a job, its commands the job's run: steps, the phases where jobs sit around two fixed jobs `build` and `deploy` — `uses: inframan/build@v1` and `uses: inframan/deploy@v1` — and what GitHub has no word for under an `inframan:` key; any workflow written for GitHub's runners converts too: checkout, caches, docker build/push, cloud sign-ins and deploys are Inframan's own and replaced, setup-node/python/go/java choose the step's image, a matrix is expanded, a notify step or stage is a job of one `uses: inframan/notify@v1` step with its settings under `with:` (a stage's job carries `inframan: {stage: true}`), a job's `${{ secrets.X }}` becomes the step's secret X (an infrastructure secret of that name) and its `services:` the pre-build step's sidecars, and what a pipeline cannot hold — environment:, unknown actions, a second trigger — is reported unsupported, never dropped unsaid) and `json` (the console's Visual form, the API's field names). A step's `secrets:` maps a variable to the NAME of an infrastructure secret (list_infra_secrets), never a value: the step gets it as that variable, masked in its log. A pre-build step's `sidecars:` ({name, image, env, command, ready}) are containers beside it — a database for its tests — reached at their name or localhost, `ready` a command run in one until it succeeds. list_repository_workflows reads a repository's .github/workflows to import, and convert_pipeline shows what a document becomes before anything is saved.

Webhooks (`webhooks:` list) are notifications. Each: `name` (unique in the pipeline), `url` (https:// only; the certificate is verified and redirects are not followed), `method` (POST default; PUT, PATCH, GET), `headers` (map), `events` — `deploy_success` (per service, once its version is ready) and/or `release_success` (once per release, after its traffic has moved; POST only; body {event, delivery_id, application, infrastructure_id, revision, images: {service: image}}), `vulnerabilities_found` (per service, when its release's image scan finds anything at or above the service's security.fail_on — high where it has no policy) and/or `scan_blocked` (per service, when its security policy refuses the release); both carry {event, delivery_id, application, infrastructure_id, service, deployment_id, image, digest, critical, high, medium, low, fixable, secrets, blocked, code, message, findings: [IDs]}. Optional: `secret` — the NAME of an infrastructure secret (list_infra_secrets), never a value; it is read at send time and sent in `secret_header` (default Authorization) after `secret_prefix` (default "Bearer " in Authorization, otherwise none); `retries` (0-10, default 3, attempts after the first, from 10s doubling to 5m; 5xx, 408, 429 and network errors are retried); `success_codes` (default any 2xx); `timeout_seconds` (1-60, default 10); `exclude_services` (left out of release_success's images). There is no copy_images_to: copying images is a promote_images release stage. Deliveries are on the application's activity feed as webhook_delivered / webhook_failed; a webhook never fails a release.

Release stages (`release_stages:` list) run in order once per release, after its traffic has moved (never for a superseded, failed or fixed-traffic release), and never fail the release. Each: `id` ([a-z][a-z0-9_], at most 32, unique), `name`, `type`, `continue_on_failure` (default false: a failed stage skips the ones after it). Types: `promote_images` — `registry` (a path such as asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/project/repo; GCP infrastructures only), optional `services` and `exclude_services`; copies each image to <registry>/<last repository segment>:<tag> as the infrastructure's cloud account (it needs roles/artifactregistry.writer there), digest kept; outputs `images` {service: copy}. `webhook` — the webhook keys above but `events`, plus optional `body`, a Go text/template over .release {application, infrastructure_id, revision, images, delivery_id} and .stages.<earlier id> {status, outputs}, with functions `json` and `default` (empty body = that data as JSON; a JSON body that does not render valid JSON fails the stage); sent with X-Inframan-Event: release_success and X-Inframan-Delivery equal to .release.delivery_id; outputs `status_code`, `response`. Example body: {"images": {{ json .stages.promote.outputs.images }}, "revision": {{ .release.revision }}}. `notify` — a message through the instance's notifications (below). `wait` — `duration_seconds` (1-86400). `manual_judgment` — `prompt`, `timeout_minutes` (1-10080, default 1440); a person approves or rejects it in the console (an agent cannot); reject or timeout fails it. `publish_files` — `service` (the service whose image holds the files: one built FROM scratch with them, never run — scaling off, min_replicas 0), `bucket` (a Cloud Storage bucket name, no gs://; GCP infrastructures only), optional `prefix` (where the files go; `{version}` in it is replaced by the content of `version_file`, a file in the image, which it then requires) and `overwrite` (default false: a file the bucket already has is left as it is, so a published version never changes); uploads every regular file of the release's image of the service as the infrastructure's cloud account (it needs roles/storage.objectCreator on the bucket, objectAdmin to overwrite); outputs `version`, `bucket`, `prefix`, `files`, `published`, `already_there`. list_release_stages reads how a release's stages ran.

A notify step sends a message through the instance's notifications (list_alert_groups, list_notification_channels). In any phase's steps it is a step with `name` and `notify: {group | channels, when, message}` in place of image and commands; as a release stage it is `type: notify` with `group` or `channels`, `when` and `message`. Exactly one of `group` (an alert group's name) and `channels` (1-10 channel names) — a save refuses a group the instance does not have (ALERT_GROUP_NOT_FOUND) or a channel (CHANNEL_NOT_FOUND). `when`: `success` (the default: the run, or the release, got this far), `failure` (it failed before this step, or the release failed) or `always`. A failed run still sends its later failure and always steps, and a failed release its failure and always stages; a stopped one sends nothing. `message` is optional, a Go text/template of at most 2000 characters over .application, .infrastructure, .revision, .commit, .commit_message, .branch, .started_by, .service, .build, .phase, .step, .status, .reason, .link (a stage also .stages.<earlier id> {status, outputs}), built-in functions only; one that fails to render sends the default with a note. A notify step takes no image, commands, env, secrets, sidecars, shell, working_directory, watch_paths or force, and never fails a release: what it sent, or why nothing, is on the step's record. A notify step or stage is the only way a release's outcome reaches a channel: a failed release is on the bell and the feed, and no alert group is sent it by itself, so a release stage with `when: failure` or `always` is how people hear of one. An alert group or a channel a pipeline names cannot be deleted.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure to create the pipeline on. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: yaml
params.description: The pipeline definition, in `format` (Inframan YAML unless it says otherwise). Inframan YAML is exactly the shape export_pipeline_yaml returns — read one first rather than composing from memory. Top level: name, optional description, a NESTED trigger: {event, branch}, and the step arrays pre_build / pre_deploy / post_deploy (NOT pre_build_steps — those are the JSON API's names and are not read here). Each step is {name, image, commands, optional timeout, optional services: [names] to scope it to particular services}. Optional `webhooks:` and `release_stages:` lists — see the tool description for their keys. Unknown keys are REJECTED rather than ignored, so a typo fails loudly instead of storing a pipeline missing the part you meant.

params.name: format
params.description: The document's format: inframan (default), github (a GitHub Actions workflow) or json.

params.name: drop_unsupported
params.description: Save a GitHub workflow without the parts the pipeline cannot hold. Without it such a workflow is refused, each part named, so it can be taken out of the document first.

capabilities.name: deactivate_application
capabilities.summary: Deactivate an application: remove its services from the cluster and mark it inactive, keeping its record.
capabilities.description:
Reversible. The application's services are removed from the cluster, so it stops serving and stops costing, and it is marked inactive — but the record survives, with its deployment history, revisions and snapshots intact, and reactivate_application brings it back.

The data on its disks is kept: a chart application, and one whose services keep a disk (storage:), are deactivated with keep_data true, which keeps every disk so reactivating it finds the data again. keep_data false is refused here: what is on a disk nothing brings back, so deleting it is the person's choice, made in the console.

This is almost always the one to use, and it is the only removal you can perform. Erasing the record outright is a console operation.

An application that is already inactive is reported as such rather than deactivated again.

If the user named a repository rather than an application, resolve it first with list_applications(repo_url=...). A repository can back several applications — across infrastructures, or more than one within a single infrastructure — so it never identifies one on its own. On more than one match, ask which; do not guess.

THIS RETURNS BEFORE THE APPLICATION IS INACTIVE. It starts a workflow that removes the services one at a time and marks the application inactive only once every one is gone, so a successful reply means the deactivation STARTED. Until then the application still reads active, and that is correct. Confirm with get_application or list_applications; if the workflow has failed it stays active, and the reply you already have cannot tell you that.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to deactivate. From list_applications — resolve it there and confirm with the user when a repository matches several.

params.name: keep_data
params.description: Required, and true, for a chart application and for one whose services keep a disk (storage:): the disks are kept, so reactivating it finds its data again (Helm deletes no claim a chart made; an operator chart's operator is stopped first, and its disks let go of the objects that own them, so deleting its `objects` takes none with it). false is refused here — deleting the data is the person's choice, in the console. Ignored for an application with no disk.

capabilities.name: deactivate_application_deleting_data
capabilities.summary: Deactivate an application and delete the data on its disks. Cannot be undone: a person's choice, made in the console.
capabilities.description:
deactivate_application, with the data on the application's disks deleted rather than kept: a chart application's disks — the claims of its own namespace, none where another application uses it — and each disk a service keeps (storage:). The record survives, marked inactive, and reactivate_application brings the application back — on new, empty disks. THE DATA CANNOT BE UNDELETED, which is why this is never an agent's: deactivate_application keeps the disks.

Returns when the deactivation STARTS, as deactivate_application does.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to deactivate, its disks deleted.

capabilities.name: decide_agent_approval
capabilities.summary: Approve or deny a tool call of an agent's run that waits for a person.
capabilities.description: An agent whose file names tools under `approve:` stops before each call of one and waits, thirty minutes at most, for a person: get_agent_run lists the run's `approvals` with the tool and its input. `decision` is `approve`, and the call goes ahead as the agent wrote it, or `deny`, with an optional `reason` the agent is told; a denial is final for that call. One already answered or expired is refused with how it stands (409, `already_decided`).

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the agent: the ID of its service, from list_agents.

params.name: run_id
params.description: The run's ID.

params.name: approval_id
params.description: The approval's ID, from the run's `approvals`.

params.name: decision
params.description: approve or deny.

params.name: reason
params.description: Why, in a sentence the agent is told with a denial. At most 500 characters.

capabilities.name: decide_release_stage
capabilities.summary: Approve or reject a manual judgment stage that is waiting.
capabilities.description: A manual judgment holds the stages after it until a person decides. Approving runs them; rejecting fails the stage and skips the rest unless it continues on failure. Refused with 409 when the stage is not waiting.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application.

params.name: revision_id
params.description: The revision whose stage to decide.

params.name: stage_id
params.description: The stage: its run row's `id` or its `stage_id`.

params.name: decision
params.description: approve or reject.

params.name: comment
params.description: Why, recorded with the decision.

capabilities.name: delete_alert_group
capabilities.summary: Delete an alert group nothing names.
capabilities.description: Refused while an application's notify: or an applied alert's own notify: names it, or a pipeline's notify step or stage does (409 `alert_group_in_use`, naming each in `used_by`): change their notify: in inframan.yaml and release them, and change the pipelines (update_pipeline), first, or turn the group off (update_alert_group) to silence it. Its channels stay. Admins only.

params.name: group_id
params.description: The group's ID, from list_alert_groups.

capabilities.name: delete_application_permanently
capabilities.summary: Erase an application and all of its history. Cannot be undone.
capabilities.description:
DESTRUCTIVE AND FINAL. The application record is erased, taking its deployment history, revisions and snapshots with it. There is nothing left to reactivate and nothing left to roll back to.

Use deactivate_application instead unless the record itself must be removed — that stops the application serving and costing while keeping everything needed to bring it back.

Cluster resources are cleaned up first if the application is still active.

Do not call this to "clean up" or "remove" an application unless the person asking has said the history is not wanted.

Never resolve the target from a repository alone. A repository can back several applications — prod and nonprod, a group_id fan-out across infrastructures, or more than one application inside a single infrastructure — so call list_applications(repo_url=...) first and, on more than one match, name each with its infrastructure and ask which. Erasing the wrong one cannot be undone.

THIS RETURNS BEFORE THE ERASE HAS HAPPENED. On an application that is still active it starts a workflow that removes the cluster resources and then the record, and returns once that workflow is accepted, so a successful reply means the erase STARTED and not that it finished. Confirm with list_applications: the application is gone when it no longer appears. If it is still listed a minute or two later the workflow is FAILING rather than slow, and the reply you already have cannot tell you that.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to erase permanently. From list_applications — resolve it there and confirm with the user when a repository matches several.

capabilities.name: delete_application_resources
capabilities.summary: Delete some of a deployment's services, agents, Postgres and Redis: a pull request that removes them from inframan.yaml, whose merge releases and deletes them.
capabilities.description:
A deletion is how a deployment's services and agents, and the Postgres and Redis its appstore: declares, are deleted: a release never deletes what a deployment runs because its file stopped declaring it, and a release whose file no longer declares something with no approved deletion naming it fails before anything happens (RELEASE_WOULD_DELETE).

Call preview_resource_deletion first, and confirm with the user what goes. For a repository's deployment this opens one pull request on base_branch (inframan/config-delete-<application>-<time>) removing the resources from the application's section of inframan.yaml (a Postgres or a Redis from its appstore:), line by line, every other line and comment kept; it blocks other config edits while open, as every config pull request does. Merging it releases the deployment on every infrastructure of its group, and that release deletes exactly them; closing it without merging deletes nothing. A file that already declares none of them (a release refused for them) needs no pull request: the deletion is approved at once, and released where a push to base_branch releases. For an images deployment there is no pull request: its manifest's next version without them is kept and released at once.

Every resource that holds data must be asked with keep_data true here: a kept disk stays in its namespace, listed by list_kept_data, and a service declared again under its name gets it back. A Postgres asked with keep_data true is uninstalled with its database, its backups and password kept and listed by list_kept_data; a Redis that keeps a volume cannot keep it, so only a person deletes it. Deleting the data is a person's choice, made in the console (DELETING_DATA_IS_HUMAN_ONLY). An agent's records — its runs, conversations and usage — go with it.

Refused: CONNECTED_FROM_OUTSIDE (something not deleted connects to one), DELETION_PENDING (a deletion names one already), LAST_RESOURCE (every service the deployment runs: delete the deployment instead), CONFIG_PR_OPEN (a config pull request is open: merge or cancel it first), NOT_DECLARED (a name the deployment does not run), NOT_DELETABLE_HERE (a chart or an agent deployment), FILE_NOT_EDITABLE (a file the line edit cannot keep: it is never written whole). Follow it with get_resource_deletions; cancel_resource_deletion withdraws it.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The deployment. From list_applications.

params.name: resources
params.description: What to delete, a JSON array: [{"name":"backend-worker","keep_data":true}], each by its name in the file, from preview_resource_deletion; "kind": "service" or "appstore" only where a service and a Postgres or Redis share the name.

params.name: base_branch
params.description: The branch whose inframan.yaml the pull request edits and merges into: required for a repository's deployment (offer its last release's branch, then its default branch), ignored for an images one.

capabilities.name: delete_application_resources_deleting_data
capabilities.summary: Delete some of a deployment's services, agents, Postgres and Redis, deleting the data they hold. Cannot be undone: a person's choice, made in the console.
capabilities.description: delete_application_resources, with keep_data false allowed: a resource asked with keep_data false has its disk — a Postgres its database, backups and password — deleted with it when the release applies the deletion, and a Redis that keeps a volume may be deleted. THE DATA CANNOT BE BROUGHT BACK, which is why this is never an agent's: delete_application_resources keeps every disk and every Postgres's backups. The same body and answer.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The deployment. From list_applications.

params.name: resources
params.description: What to delete, a JSON array: [{"name":"backend-worker","keep_data":true}], each by its name in the file, from preview_resource_deletion; "kind": "service" or "appstore" only where a service and a Postgres or Redis share the name.

params.name: base_branch
params.description: The branch whose inframan.yaml the pull request edits and merges into: required for a repository's deployment (offer its last release's branch, then its default branch), ignored for an images one.

capabilities.name: delete_cloud_account
capabilities.summary: Unlink a GCP project from this instance, removing the platform's record of it.
capabilities.description:
The dangerous one, and not for the reason it looks. Nothing in GCP is touched: the service accounts, their grants, the clusters, the registries and the buckets all survive and keep costing money. What is destroyed is the platform's only pointer to them.

Every infrastructure provisioned through this link carries its id, and this is not blocked when they still do — they are simply left referencing a row that no longer exists. Re-registering the same project afterwards mints a NEW id and does not reattach them, so this is not reversible by repeating the setup. Call list_infrastructures and confirm nothing is using it before removing it.

Use this to remove a link that was created in error or whose project is genuinely finished with. To stop using a project while keeping its infrastructure working, leave the link alone.

params.name: cloud_account_id
params.description: UUID of the cloud account to unlink, from list_cloud_accounts. Verify with list_infrastructures that nothing provisions through it first.

capabilities.name: delete_domain
capabilities.summary: Detach a custom domain, removing its gateway and TLS certificate.
capabilities.description:
Takes the domain off the cluster: its Istio Gateway and its Let's Encrypt certificate are removed. Everything served on that hostname stops being reachable over it IMMEDIATELY — this is a live traffic change, not a cleanup of an unused record.

Any service whose inframan.yaml routes on this domain keeps claiming it and will have no public route until the domain is added back and the service redeployed. Check list_applications for services using the hostname before removing it.

Coming back is not free: re-adding means DNS must still point at the load balancer and a fresh certificate must be issued through ACME again, which is rate-limited by Let's Encrypt per domain. Do not remove a domain to "reset" a failed one — retry_domain does that without spending an issuance.

Deletion is asynchronous; the record disappears when the workflow finishes.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the domain belongs to, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: domain_id
params.description: UUID of the domain to detach, from list_domains.

capabilities.name: delete_env_group
capabilities.summary: Delete an environment group and every variable in it.
capabilities.description:
Deletes the whole BUNDLE. Every service the group is attached to loses all of its variables at once on the next deploy, and the group record does not say which services those are — the attachments live on the services. Check each service's groups before removing one.

Not recoverable by repeating it. For an `env` group, the encrypted rows being deleted are the only copy of those values the platform holds. For a `secret` group, the references being deleted are the platform's only handles on values in Secret Manager that nothing can display, so rebuilding the group means someone typing every value in again.

To remove ONE variable, use the console. To stop one service using the group while others keep it, use the envGroups: block in inframan.yaml.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the group belongs to, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: group_id
params.description: UUID of the group to delete, from list_env_groups.

capabilities.name: delete_env_group_var
capabilities.summary: Remove one variable from an environment group by key.
capabilities.description:
Removes a single KEY from the bundle, leaving the group and its other variables in place. Every service attached to the group stops receiving it on the next deploy.

Works for a secret group's key too: what is removed there is the platform's reference, not the value, which stays in GCP Secret Manager. Removing a pointer reveals nothing.

To empty a group entirely, remove its keys one at a time. Deleting the GROUP is a console operation and is not available to you — it removes the group itself and detaches it from every service, which is a much larger change than emptying it.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the group belongs to, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: group_id
params.description: UUID of the group to remove it from, from list_env_groups.

params.name: key
params.description: The variable name to remove, from list_env_group_vars.

capabilities.name: delete_env_var
capabilities.summary: Remove an environment variable from a service by key.
capabilities.description:
Works for any type, including a secret's reference — removing a pointer reveals nothing, and refusing it would leave a service permanently carrying a secret nothing could detach.

Deleting a secret's reference does NOT delete the secret from Secret Manager; it stops this service receiving it.

Takes effect on the next deploy.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service to remove it from. From list_services.

params.name: key
params.description: The variable name to remove. From get_service_env_vars.

capabilities.name: delete_infra_secret
capabilities.summary: Remove an infrastructure secret, by id, from the platform's records.
capabilities.description:
Deletes the platform's POINTER. The value stays in GCP Secret Manager, but the platform loses its only handle on it, and every service whose inframan.yaml names this secret stops resolving it — those deploys fail until the name is created again.

Console only, mirroring create_infra_secret. Recreating it means someone typing the value in again, and nobody can read the old one back out of the platform to do that — not through an agent, and not in the console. A person removing a credential knows whether they still have it; nothing in the record says so.

Check list_infra_secrets and the services referencing the name first.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the secret belongs to, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: secret_id
params.description: UUID of the secret to remove, from list_infra_secrets.

capabilities.name: delete_installed_app
capabilities.summary: Destroy one installed Redis or Postgres instance and its data. Cannot be undone.
capabilities.description:
DESTRUCTIVE AND FINAL. The instance is torn down and its persistent disk is deleted with it — there is no snapshot, no tombstone and nothing to restore from. Anything the application kept in it is gone.

This BLOCKS while it works: three to five minutes when it is the last install of its size and the node pool has to be destroyed too. A failure leaves the install in `uninstalling` so it can be retried.

Only named installs (Redis, Postgres) can be deleted this way. The platform's own apps are refused here — uninstall_platform_app is theirs.

Services still pointing at this instance will fail to connect afterwards; there is no check for that.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: UUID of the install to destroy, from list_platform_apps or get_installed_app. Confirm the instance name with the user first.

capabilities.name: delete_kept_data
capabilities.summary: Delete kept data for good: a kept disk, or a Postgres's kept backups and password. Cannot be undone: a person's choice.
capabilities.description: Deletes what a deletion kept: a disk's claim in its namespace with the cloud's disk behind it, or a Postgres's backup bucket and password, as the infrastructure's cloud account. THE DATA CANNOT BE BROUGHT BACK, which is why this is never an agent's. Answers deleted, or deleting where the bucket is still being emptied (list_kept_data drops it once gone). Refused while a disk is in use again (KEPT_DATA_IN_USE: a service declared again under its name took it back; for backups, a Postgres of that name is installed).

params.name: kept_data_id
params.description: The kept data, from list_kept_data.

capabilities.name: delete_notification_channel
capabilities.summary: Delete a notification channel and its record of what it was sent.
capabilities.description: Refused while an alert group sends to it or a pipeline's notify step or stage names it (409 `channel_in_use`, naming the `groups` and the `pipelines`): take it out of each group (update_alert_group) or delete the group, and change the pipelines (update_pipeline), first. Admins only.

params.name: channel_id
params.description: The channel's ID, from list_notification_channels.

capabilities.name: delete_pipeline
capabilities.summary: Delete a pipeline definition permanently.
capabilities.description:
The pipeline is removed outright — there is no undo, and no confirmation beyond the one your client asks you for.

Applications linked to it are NOT unlinked first; the links are simply orphaned, which is what the console does too. If the intent is only to stop a pipeline running for one application, use unlink_pipeline instead and leave the definition alone.

params.name: pipeline_id
params.description: The pipeline to delete. From list_pipelines.

capabilities.name: deploy_service_image
capabilities.summary: Move a service pulled from a published image to a new tag or digest.
capabilities.description:
The change goes where the service's configuration lives:
• In a repository's application it opens a config PR changing `tag:` under the service's `image:` in inframan.yaml — one line. Nothing deploys until the PR is merged; the merge is a push and releases. The file stays the truth, so a rollback to an earlier commit runs the image that commit named. Refused while another config PR is open (get_config_pr).
• In an image application it keeps the next manifest version and releases it now.

Either way the release resolves the tag to its digest, pins that digest, and builds nothing. A service built from its repository is refused: its new version is a push.

Give `tag`, or `digest` to pin one exactly (the tag is then kept for people to read). A new tag drops a digest the file had, so the new tag decides.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The pulled service. From list_services; `image_repository` is set on it.

params.name: tag
params.description: The image tag to run, e.g. "v0.51.0". Not "latest" without a digest.

params.name: digest
params.description: A sha256:… digest to pin instead of, or with, the tag.

params.name: base_branch
params.description: Repository applications only: the branch the PR targets. Defaults to the application's.

capabilities.name: destroy_infrastructure
capabilities.summary: Tear an infrastructure down — every cloud resource it owns, then its record. Destructive and not reversible.
capabilities.description:
DESTRUCTIVE AND FINAL.

Starts DestroyInfrastructureWorkflow, which is provisioning run backwards: every application on the cluster is deleted, the installed apps are uninstalled (Postgres and Redis pools, then the platform's own gateway, monitoring and CI/CD in reverse install order), then Terraform destroys the GKE cluster and its node pools, then the VPC, Cloud NAT, firewall rules and, for a zero-trust infrastructure, its NCC spoke — and the instance's hub with it when no other spoke is left — and finally the state bucket.
