Console only. Agents use get_app_metric for the series, or get_installed_app_metrics for every metric's current value at once.

params.name: app
params.description: Which app: "redis" or "postgres".

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The install's instance name, e.g. "cache-prod".

params.name: metric
params.description: Metric name for that app, e.g. "cache_hit_rate".

params.name: infra_id
params.description: Infrastructure the app is installed on. Omit for the latest one.

params.name: start
params.description: Window start in unix seconds. Omit with `end` for the last hour.

params.name: end
params.description: Window end in unix seconds. Omit with `start` for the last hour.

params.name: step
params.description: Resolution step in seconds. Default 60.

capabilities.name: get_named_metric_series
capabilities.summary: Run a catalog metric for an application and return Prometheus's series verbatim.
capabilities.description:
The console's chart path for a named metric: the PromQL comes from the metric catalog, and the full matrix response is returned so the chart can draw every series. `group_label` names the label the query grouped by, so a caller does not re-derive the per-metric mapping the catalog already owns; `split_label` names the label a metric is always split by (status_codes' status_class).

Console only. Agents use get_metric, which runs the same resolver and returns points with a summary; list_metrics enumerates the names both accept.

params.name: metric
params.description: Metric name from the catalog, e.g. "cpu" or "memory".

params.name: application
params.description: Application name, or several comma-separated for an environment view.

params.name: service
params.description: Optional service name. Omit to cover the whole application.

params.name: group_by
params.description: Split into series: "service" or "app". Omit for one aggregate line.

params.name: infra_id
params.description: The infrastructure the page shows: the applications of the names on it. Omit only where each name is an application on one infrastructure.

params.name: start
params.description: Window start in unix seconds. Omit with `end` for the last hour.

params.name: end
params.description: Window end in unix seconds. Omit with `start` for the last hour.

params.name: step
params.description: Resolution step in seconds. Default 60.

capabilities.name: get_node_class
capabilities.summary: Read the node class's findings on an infrastructure: which nodes it would free, at what price and downtime.
capabilities.description: Returns the node class (Inframan's Karpenter, nonprod GKE only) on an infrastructure: its `mode`, its last pass (`last_pass`), whether a pass is `running`, the `findings` still to make — not made yet, or a try that failed — the largest saving first, and apart from them the findings made within the last day (`applied`, each also on the feed as the class's). A finding is one move the class would make: `kind` place (onto the class), move-back (onto the system pool), consolidate (empty one of its pools), drain (a system node let go) or outgrown (a pool whose pods wait, moved whatever it costs); `title` and `why`; the `pool` it moves onto, the nodes it adds (`nodes_added`, `added_machine_type`) and frees (`freed`); `monthly_usd`, the cloud bill it saves a month at Google's list prices for Spot in the cluster's region (`priced` false and `price_note` when the price list could not be read); and per workload (`workloads`) a `forecast`: its `path` (live, surge — new pods before old stop, restart, evict), `downtime` with `seconds` and its `basis`, and what `fails` while it is down and what `holds`. `downtime_seconds` on the finding is the longest of them, and `down` the workloads that go down. `outcome` (applied or failed, `outcome_detail`, per workload `outcomes` with the downtime measured) is set once a pass tried it. The class passes each time the watcher sees something it places by move — a pod waiting, a node come or gone, a request changed — so the findings are current within a minute or two. `monthly_usd` at the top is what the findings not yet applied save together.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: get_node_pool_defaults
capabilities.summary: Read the platform node pools a new infrastructure is created with.
capabilities.description:
These are the PLATFORM's pools, not your applications'. The system pool hosts istiod and the ingress gateway, and on a nonprod infrastructure the Monitoring stack too; it carries a taint those components tolerate and nothing else does, which is what keeps a user deployment from starving the mesh or the metrics stack.

Built from code at every read, for the tag asked for, and never stored or edited: every infrastructure is created with exactly these. The pools a running cluster actually has are on the infrastructure record — read them with get_infrastructure.

Application pools are not here. They are passed per-environment to provision_infrastructure.

params.name: tag
params.description: The tag of the infrastructure to be made: "prod" or "nonprod". Omitted, nonprod.

capabilities.name: get_notification_channel
capabilities.summary: Read one notification channel and the newest messages it was sent, with what it answered.
capabilities.description: The `channel` as list_notification_channels reads it, and its newest 20 `deliveries`: each message's kind, severity, title, issue key and the alert `group` that sent it, whether it was `sent`, is still `sending` (tried again for about an hour), `failed` or `skipped`, how many tries it took, and what the channel last `answer`ed — cut short, never its address or secret. Messages are kept thirty days.

params.name: channel_id
params.description: The channel's ID, from list_notification_channels.

capabilities.name: get_optimizations
capabilities.summary: Read an infrastructure's incidents and what the actor, Karpenter and the optimizer did about them.
capabilities.description: Returns an infrastructure's incidents and actions (the infrastructure's Incidents & actions tab in the console): the optimizer (`optimizer`: its `mode` and its last pass), the findings of its last pass (`findings`, as get_maintenance_pass lists them), and a timeline over the last `hours` (24 by default, 720 at most), newest first, each event with its `source` (actor, karpenter, optimizer): each `incident` the actor recorded as its watcher found it (`type` its failure, `status` open or resolved), each `remediation` the actor made by itself (`type` its action: a raise, a pod restarted, a component applied again, a person asked; `detail` what changed; `incident_id` the incident it answered and `cause` what that was — tell them together), each `optimization` (what became of a request a pass lowered: `type` its outcome, `from` and `to`, `effect`), each `class` change Karpenter (the node class) made or failed to make (`type` its finding's kind, `status` success or failure, `title` what it did to the nodes, `pool` the pool it moved onto, `workloads` every workload it moved, `effect` what it gave back or saves, `headlines` what each workload went through; never a GKE setting, the platform's migration), and each `pass` asked for or that changed something (`type` its trigger, `status`, its summary in `detail`). Karpenter's findings still to apply are get_node_class's. The optimizer passes each time the watcher sees a recommendation or a request move, so the findings are current within a minute or two. `automatic` marks what the platform did by itself: every remediation, a change from the optimizer's own pass in act mode, and Karpenter's own.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: hours
params.description: How far back the timeline reaches, in hours. Default 24, up to 720.

capabilities.name: get_pipeline
capabilities.summary: Get one pipeline definition: its trigger and its build and deploy steps.
capabilities.description:
The stored definition — trigger event, branch glob and the pre-build, pre-deploy and post-deploy step arrays.

pre_build_steps, pre_deploy_steps, post_deploy_steps and webhooks are JSON arrays of objects, ready to read — not strings needing a second parse. Same shape here as in list_pipelines. An empty stage is [], never null.

To EDIT a pipeline, read it as YAML with export_pipeline_yaml instead: update_pipeline takes YAML back, so that round-trips and this does not.

This is the definition, not a run. get_deployment_pipeline shows what one execution of it did.

params.name: pipeline_id
params.description: The pipeline to fetch. From list_pipelines or list_linked_pipelines.

capabilities.name: get_platform_app_config
capabilities.summary: Read the editable component configuration of an installed platform app.
capabilities.description:
Only the platform's own component-based apps answer this: gateway (Istio), monitoring (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo) and CI/CD. Each entry is one component with its current `values_json` — the Helm values or custom-resource spec actually applied — plus the settings schema the console renders and how the self-healing actor sizes each workload (`scaling_config`).

Read this when diagnosing why a platform component is unhealthy: it is the difference between the defaults and what is really running. Changing a setting is a CONSOLE operation and is not available to you — report what needs changing and let the user make the edit there. No one changes a platform workload's CPU or memory by hand: the actor raises what fails, sized from what it measured.

CREDENTIAL VALUES ARE REDACTED. Any field whose name reads like a secret — credentials, password, token, api_key, private_key, bearer, authorization — comes back as "***REDACTED***" at every depth, in `values_json` and in `default_settings`. Monitoring's document carries the live bearer token the platform's own alert webhook authenticates with, and a value read out here would land in the conversation and the client's logs, which is the one place a credential must never be. Everything else is exactly what is applied. The sentinel is a placeholder, not the stored value: whoever writes this document back leaves it untouched and the real value is preserved.

Components with no user-facing configuration are omitted.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure the app is installed on. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: app_id
params.description: Catalog app id (NOT the installed_app_id), from list_platform_apps.

capabilities.name: get_preferences
capabilities.summary: Get the instance's timezone and its current UTC offset.
capabilities.description:
Instance-wide display settings. Every timestamp the platform returns — deployment times, incident times, log lines — is rendered against this zone, so read it before interpreting or repeating a time back to the user, rather than assuming UTC or the machine's own zone.

Returns the IANA name, the offset from UTC in seconds AS OF NOW (so DST is already accounted for), the current local time, and the zone abbreviation.

A fresh instance that has never set one answers with the default rather than an error.

capabilities.name: get_provisioning_setup
capabilities.summary: Provisioning's one setup after GKE: what the infrastructure's apps need granted by the person, as one script, and whether it is verified.
capabilities.description:
Right after the GKE cluster is created, and before anything is installed on it, provisioning asks every app the infrastructure installs which grants it needs that Inframan will not make (no IAM in your project, ever): the CI/CD app's builder account — its roles and, for in-cluster builds, the Workload Identity binding for ci-builder, which names the pool Google creates with the cluster. All of it is ONE script (`setup.script`, re-runnable) and ONE verify. `sections` names each app's part.

`status`: not_required (no app needs anything — provisioning does not stop), not_reached (the cluster does not exist yet), pending (provisioning is paused here), verifying, failed (`last_error` names the first missing grant), verified.

WHAT TO DO WITH IT. You cannot run the script yourself. Show it to the user, wait for them to say they have run it, then call verify_provisioning_setup — a pass resumes provisioning.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure. From list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: get_resource_deletions
capabilities.summary: List a deployment's deletions, newest first, each with what it deletes, what it keeps and its pull request.
capabilities.description:
A deletion is how a deployment's services and agents, and the Postgres and Redis its appstore: declares, are deleted: a release never deletes what a deployment runs because its file stopped declaring it, and a release whose file no longer declares something with no approved deletion naming it fails before anything happens (RELEASE_WOULD_DELETE).

A deletion is pending while its pull request is open, approved once it merges (an images deployment's at once), applied once a release has deleted everything it names, and cancelled when its pull request closes without merging or someone cancels it. Each item says whether its data is kept and, once applied, what the release said of it.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The deployment. From list_applications.

params.name: status
params.description: Only these statuses, comma-separated: pending, approved, applied, cancelled. Every status when unset.

capabilities.name: get_service
capabilities.summary: Get one service in detail: type, port, image, scaling, domain and WIF status.
capabilities.description:
A service is one deployable unit — a web service, a worker or a job — and it belongs to exactly one application.

`auto_domain` is whether the file asks for the service's automatic HTTPS address (`auto_domain: true`; off by default), and `auto_domain_host` is that address — public, under the hosting's domain, given at the first release that asks for it once the infrastructure's wildcard certificate is ready. Empty while it has none, and always for a worker or job. A web service with neither it nor `domain` is reachable only inside the cluster.

A worker that declares a `port` is a TCP server — a database, a queue, a cache — and `address` is where it is reached inside the cluster, host:port (`<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:<port>`), the same across releases: what a connection to it is valued with. It is health-checked on that port (a TCP connect unless the file declares its checks), and a release reads it ready only once its port answers. Empty for every other service. A worker's `port` column on its own says nothing: workers never given one read the default, 80, and a worker on 80 or 8080 — defaults the platform once wrote itself — is a TCP server only with `network.protocol: tcp`.

`effective_rollout_strategy` is how the NEXT release replaces what is running: "blue-green" (the new version starts beside the old one and takes traffic when ready) or "recreate" (the old one is stopped first — for a worker that must not run twice, or a cluster with no room for both). `rollout_strategy` is what the file declares, and empty there means blue-green. It is changed in inframan.yaml, or from the application's Releases tab in the console, which stages it into the service's config PR; an edit changes nothing until that PR is merged and a release runs.

Services are NOT created or deleted through the platform. They are read from the repository's inframan.yaml, whose `services:` map decides which ones exist, so adding or removing one is a commit to that file. The only action offered against a running service is restart_application, which bounces every service in its application together.

Config-sync timing: port, domain, scaling and resource fields are written from inframan.yaml only after a SUCCESSFUL deploy. Empty values on a service that has never deployed cleanly are expected rather than a fault — check list_service_deployments before treating them as one.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

capabilities.name: get_service_alerts
capabilities.summary: List a service's own alerts — each as its release declared it, the expression Prometheus or Loki evaluates, and whether it is firing.
capabilities.description:
A service's own alerts are written under the service in its inframan.yaml (`alerts:`): each names a metric of the platform's catalogue (`metric:`, read exactly as the service's chart reads it, in its own unit), a PromQL query over the service's own metrics (`query:`), or a LogQL filter over the service's own log lines (`logs:`, such as `|= "panic"` or `| json | level="error"`, counted over `window:`, 1m to 1h, 5m by default), and one threshold, `above:` or `below:` (a log alert's is a count of lines), held `for:` a while (1m to 24h, 5m by default; a log alert's 0 to 24h, 0 by default: it fires at once), with a `severity` (critical, warning, info). Inframan renders a metric or query alert as a Prometheus alerting rule of the infrastructure's own Prometheus, and a log alert as a rule of its Loki's ruler counting the lines the console's logs view shows for the service, and applies them once a release serves, so a push that changes only alerts changes nothing else. A firing alert is shown on the infrastructure's Observability tab, under Alerts, with Start investigation (start_investigation with an instance's `subject_key`), and is sent to the alert group it names (`notify: <group>`), else its application's (`notify:` beside `services:`), `notify: none` sending it to no one; a group named nowhere is no one (list_alert_groups lists the instance's).

This reads them for one service: each alert as the serving release declared it (`metric`, `query` or `logs` and `window`, `comparison` above or below, `threshold`, `for`, `severity`, `summary`), its `expression` — what is evaluated: the catalogue's query for the service, the query with every selector held to the application's namespace, or the count of the service's lines that pass the filter, compared with the threshold — and its `state`: inactive, pending (the condition holds, not yet for `for`), firing, or unknown (the state could not be read, or the rule is not loaded yet: a rule is evaluated a minute or two after a release applies it). `instances` are the series it is pending or firing for, each with its `value`, `active_at` and `subject_key`; `health` and `last_error` are Prometheus' or Loki's own of the rule (an expression that errors when it is evaluated says so there). Each alert's `state_from` says where its state was read: `rules` or `alerts` (Prometheus'; `alerts` on an infrastructure whose monitoring gateway predates the rules read), `loki_rules` (Loki's ruler's), or `loki_query` — its count evaluated now, where the gateway predates Loki's ruler reads: an alert that fires at once reads firing or inactive from it, one that waits reads unknown with its count — until the Monitoring app's next reconcile. An empty list means the release that serves declares no alert for the service.

Each alert also says `subject_key` (its issue's key, every series it fires for has it), `own_summary` (whether `summary` is its file's own or one written for it), `last_fired_at` / `last_resolved_at`, when its newest firing began and its newest resolve ended it, as the infrastructure's AlertManager told the backend, and who hears it: `notify` (the alert group it is sent to, empty for no one), `notify_from` (`alert`, its own notify:; `application`, its application's; `none`), `notify_exists` (whether the instance has that group now) and `own_notify` (what its file wrote: a group, `none`, or empty for the application's). The service's application's own group is `notify` / `notify_exists` at the top: the default group of its alerts, and nothing else (a release's outcome reaches people only through its pipeline's notify steps). An alert applied before alert groups notifies no one until its application's next release. What an alert of the service may read is said too: `kind` (web or worker; `cannot_alert` says why a job or an on-demand agent has none), `runtime`, `metrics` (the catalogue metrics it can alert on, each with its `title` and `unit`, `requests` for one counted from the requests the service is sent), `requests_not_collected` (why the infrastructure collects no request metrics, where it does not), `max_alerts`, and `source` — `repository`, where a change is a config PR of its inframan.yaml, or `image`, where it is the image application's next manifest version. For every service's alerts on an infrastructure at once, by application and service, read list_service_alerts. The console's Alerts tab stages a change into the service's config PR; an agent makes it in the file — a change of the repository's inframan.yaml, or save_application_manifest for an image application.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

capabilities.name: get_service_disk
capabilities.summary: A worker's disk: its size and path, and how much of it is used.
capabilities.description:
A worker that declares `storage: {size, path}` keeps a disk of its own: one lasting workload, a StatefulSet named for the service, its one pod replaced in place on the same disk at each release. This reads the disk as the service last released (`size`, `path`, its claim) and what its kubelet says of it — `used_bytes` and `capacity_bytes` — from the infrastructure's Prometheus; `read` is false, with `reason`, where they could not be read. `has_disk` is false for a service without one.

A disk grows by a release that asks a larger `size`; a smaller one, or none, is refused. It is deleted only by deactivating the application with its data deleted, the person's choice in the console: deactivate_application keeps it.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

capabilities.name: get_service_env_groups
capabilities.summary: List the environment groups attached to a service, as ids.
capabilities.description:
An environment group is a named set of variables shared by several services, so one change reaches all of them. This returns which groups a service is attached to, not what is inside them.

Read this BEFORE the envGroups: block in inframan.yaml: that call REPLACES the set, so it needs the current ids sent back alongside the change or the groups you left out are silently detached.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

capabilities.name: get_service_env_vars
capabilities.summary: List a service's environment variables: names, types and non-secret values.
capabilities.description:
Three kinds of row come back, and the `env_type` tells them apart:
• `variable` — a plain value, returned in full.
• `secret` — stored in GCP Secret Manager. The VALUE IS NEVER RETURNED, to any caller, on any surface; the console does not show it either. You get the name and `is_secret: true`, which is enough to know it is wired up.
• `connection` — a link to a sibling service or an installed database, resolved to an address at deploy time. There is no stored value to return.

A `connection` that carries `chart` is one to a chart application — `chart/<application>/<NAME>` in the connections: block — which has no row of its own: it is listed after the rows as the release that serves the service declared it, with the application (`application`, and `application_id` where it is on the service's infrastructure), the `expose` it names, its `slug` as the file writes it and the `namespace` its binding is read in. It changes only in inframan.yaml (an image application's manifest), and a service that has not served since the connection was added does not list it yet.

So a blank `value` on a secret or a connection is correct, not a failure, and there is no other call that would reveal it.

The list is whole or the call fails: a variable whose value cannot be decrypted, or a part that cannot be read, fails it (naming the variable, never its value), so a set written back from it never drops or garbles what was not read.

To CHANGE any of this, edit inframan.yaml in the repository and push: the env:, connections: and envGroups: blocks are authoritative, and every successful deploy rewrites these rows from the file — so a change made any other way is undone by the next release. A secret's VALUE can only be set in the console, which writes it straight to Secret Manager without it passing through a tool call.

Variables listed here are what the service receives on its NEXT deploy, which is not necessarily what the running pods hold.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

capabilities.name: get_service_inframan_yaml
capabilities.summary: Render the inframan.yaml the platform believes an application should have.
capabilities.description:
Generated from the DATABASE, not read from the repository. It is one SIDE of a drift comparison, not the answer to it: where the two disagree, the repository is what CI builds from and this is what the platform last recorded.

DO NOT rewrite a repository to match this. Build fields especially — `build.dockerfile` and a service's `path` — are written back only by a SUCCESSFUL deploy, so a service that changed its Dockerfile path and has not deployed since will show the OLD value here. That gap is the drift you are looking for, not a correction to apply. Editing the repo to match would point the build at a path that does not exist.

Absences are meaningful and are not omissions: `namespace` is left out when it equals the application name, because that is its default, and a service's `path` is left out when the build context is the repository root. Neither missing key means the value was lost.

A service's disk is its record's, and its files, connections to chart applications, metrics, traces and a worker's `peers: true` are the ones its serving release rendered — none for a release from before they were kept. A connection to a Storage bucket (`storage/<instance>`) is shown as the variable holding the bucket's name once the service has released since it was made: the same value at runtime, not drift. Comments and environments' blocks are never rendered.

One root inframan.yaml describes a whole application, so the service id only selects which application to render; the answer covers all of its services.

`application` and `namespace` are immutable. If the repository's file disagrees with these, that is the drift CI refuses a release for, and the fix is a config PR — edit inframan.yaml in the repository and push — not an edit to the platform.

params.name: service_id
params.description: Any service of the application to render. From list_services.

capabilities.name: get_service_vulnerabilities
capabilities.summary: List the known vulnerabilities and baked-in secrets of a service's released image.
capabilities.description:
Every release scans the image it deploys, beside the release and never stopping it: the infrastructure's own Trivy server matches the image's OS and language packages against its vulnerability database, and lists any secret baked into the image's layers or config. This reads the scan of the serving release, or of the release named by deployment_id.

`status` is scanned, scanning (the release's Scan step has not finished) or not_scanned, with `reason` saying why (an image built on builder machines before scanning, the infrastructure's Trivy server not ready, a release from before scanning). `counts` are of the whole scan; `vulnerabilities` are the findings matching the filters, the most severe first, then those with a fix, then the highest CVSS score; `total` is how many match, and `next_offset` pages on. `database_updated_at` is when the vulnerability database the scan matched against was built: a finding published after it shows at a later scan.

`signature` says whether the release signed the image, by digest, with the infrastructure's own KMS key (status signed, signing or not_signed with `reason`; an image that could not be signed fails nothing, and `enforced` is true only on a release from before the Image policy app was removed). Inframan signs only what it builds into the infrastructure's registry; the signature is cosign's, beside the image.

`repository` is the release's repository — the service's build context at the commit its image was built from — scanned beside the image: its dependencies' vulnerabilities (`target` is the lockfile that pins each), secrets committed to git (file and line), and `misconfigurations` of its Dockerfile, Kubernetes, Terraform and Helm files (check, file, line and `resolution`, how to fix it). It is null for a published image and a release from before repositories were scanned; its `status` and `reason` say why one was not scanned. Under the service's `security.repository: enforce` its findings can refuse a release as the image's do.

How to fix each kind:
• A language package (pkg_type npm, gomod, pip, …): move it to `fixed_version` or later in the manifest that declares it (package.json, go.mod, requirements.txt), then release.
• An OS package (pkg_type alpine, debian, ubuntu, …): use a newer tag of the Dockerfile's base image, or upgrade the package in the Dockerfile, then release.
• A finding with no `fixed_version` has no fix yet: there is nothing to bump.
• A misconfiguration: follow its `resolution` in the file and line it names.
open_vulnerability_fix_pr proposes the fix of a finding, or of a whole manifest, as a pull request; each finding of the repository says its `ecosystem`, its `manifest` and whether it is `direct`, and `fixes` lists the pull requests asked for.
• A secret: rotate it first — it is in every copy of the image already pushed — then build without it, passing build secrets through the service's `secrets:` in inframan.yaml. Only the secret's rule, file and lines are kept, never its value.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

params.name: deployment_id
params.description: A release of the service, from list_service_deployments. Omit for the serving release.

params.name: min_severity
params.description: The least severe finding to list: critical, high, medium or low. Omit for every severity.

params.name: fixable
params.description: List only findings that have a fixed version. Default false.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many findings per page. Default 100, maximum 500.

params.name: offset
params.description: How many findings to skip: the next_offset of the previous page.

params.name: repository_limit
params.description: How many of each of the repository's lists — dependencies, secrets, misconfigurations — per page. Default 25, maximum 500.

params.name: repository_offset
params.description: How many of each repository list to skip: the repository's next_offset of the previous page.

capabilities.name: get_service_wif_info
capabilities.summary: Get a service's Workload Identity Federation state and the identities it binds.
capabilities.description:
Workload Identity Federation binds this service's Kubernetes service account to a Google service account, so its pods authenticate to Google APIs as that identity and NO KEY FILE EXISTS anywhere — nothing to leak, nothing to rotate.

`wif_status` is the whole answer:
• empty — never set up. Google API calls from this service fail on credentials.
• `PENDING_BINDING` — enable_wif reserved the names, and the human's cloud step has not been run yet. Still no working identity.
• `BOUND` — live.

This is the call to poll after enable_wif: the platform cannot create the Google service account itself, so the status only moves once the user runs the returned command.

A Google API failing inside a service that reads anything but BOUND is almost always this and not the code.

On an AWS infrastructure `cloud` is "aws" and the identity is the IAM role in `aws_role_arn`, which the pods take through EKS Pod Identity; the same three states apply.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

capabilities.name: get_sleep_run
capabilities.summary: Read an infrastructure's latest sleep or wake, step by step.
capabilities.description:
Returns the most recent sleep or wake of one infrastructure as the steps it went through — checking the infrastructure, the node pool minimums, stopping or starting the platform apps, the services and the databases, releasing or bringing back nodes, taking down or bringing back the network's billed parts (the NAT gateways on AWS, a hub spoke on GCP), reconciling each app — the gateway first on a wake — waiting for the services — each with its status (pending, running, completed, partial, failed, skipped), a one-line summary, and lines naming what it touched. While a transition runs this is live: read it again to follow it. The console shows the same steps under the infrastructure's sleep banner.

READ THIS WHEN A CLUSTER IS PARTLY IDLE OR PARTLY AWAKE, or a sleep or wake failed: the partial or failed step says what was left running or not brought back, and why. Returns null when the infrastructure has never slept.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: get_storage_access_setup
capabilities.summary: Get the gcloud commands that let a service write to a Storage bucket, and whether it is done.
capabilities.description:
A Storage instance is a bucket in the user's own project. For a service to write to it, its Google service account has to be granted on the bucket, and Inframan CANNOT make that grant: granting to service accounts is outside the roles the platform holds, deliberately. So the platform generates two commands, the user runs them with their own gcloud, and a probe verifies the result.

This returns `setup.script` (one re-runnable bash block), `setup.steps` (each command with its reason) and the current `status`: identity_required, pending, verifying, verified or failed.

ORDER. The service needs a verified Workload Identity FIRST — that is the account the bucket is granted to. `identity_required: true` means there is no account yet: do enable_wif → the user runs its commands → verify_wif, then come back here.

WHAT TO DO WITH IT. You cannot run these commands yourself. Show the user the script, wait for them to say they have run it, then call verify_storage_access. Then connect the service to the bucket: `UPLOADS_BUCKET: storage/<instance>` in its inframan.yaml connections (the console can do the same). A connection is refused, and a release refuses, until the grant is verified.

PER SERVICE, PER BUCKET. Each service has its own account and each bucket its own grant; two services on one bucket are two ceremonies.

ON AWS (`cloud` is "aws") the bucket is S3 and the service's identity is its IAM role (service_account_email holds the role's ARN): the grant is one `aws iam put-role-policy` naming the bucket, run in AWS CloudShell, and the same order applies — the role must be verified (enable_wif → verify_wif) before the bucket can be granted.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The Storage instance, from list_platform_apps (an instance under the storage app).

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service that will write to the bucket. From list_services.

capabilities.name: get_trace
capabilities.summary: Get one distributed trace: every span, which service ran it and how long it took.
capabilities.description:
The answer to "where did the time go". Spans are returned parent-first, each with its service, operation, duration and the handful of attributes worth reading (HTTP status and route, database system, error and exception detail); the rest of the OTLP attribute set is dropped because it is mostly infrastructure labels.

Get the id from search_traces. `error_spans` is the shortcut — spans that recorded an error or a 4xx/5xx — and is usually where to start rather than reading the tree top to bottom.

Traces expire from Tempo's retention window, so an id from an old incident may legitimately return nothing.

params.name: trace_id
params.description: Trace id in hex, from search_traces or from a log line's trace field.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure the trace is on, from list_infrastructures. Omit for the instance's most recent one.

capabilities.name: get_update_notification
capabilities.summary: Check whether a platform update is waiting for this instance.
capabilities.description:
Reports the pending release the control plane has offered this instance: its id, version and changelog, or has_update=false when there is nothing waiting.

This is about the INFRAMAN INSTANCE ITSELF — the backend, console and workers on the control-plane VM — not about the user's applications or clusters. Read it before applying it. Applying is a CONSOLE operation and is not available to you: report the pending version and let the user run it, because it restarts the instance you are talking to.

capabilities.name: get_workload_domain
capabilities.summary: Show the domain the hosting makes hostnames under, if it has one.
capabilities.description:
The hostnames Inframan makes are under the HOSTING's domain: the automatic HTTPS address a web service asks for with `auto_domain: true`, <service>-<app>.<infrastructure>.<domain>, and a Redis or PostgreSQL install opened for external access, <instance>-<engine>.<infrastructure>.<domain>. Whoever runs the deployment sets it, with the DNS provider it is at, and Inframan writes the records there. An instance cannot change it.

Returns `configured`; when true, `domain` and `provider`. When false, services get no automatic address and external access cannot be opened on this hosting, and `message` says so.

capabilities.name: get_workload_recommendations
capabilities.summary: What the optimizer's recommender would have each platform workload request, and how far it has got.
capabilities.description:
Reads the optimizer app's recommender on one infrastructure: VPA's recommender, watching every platform workload the actor sizes. It recommends only: nothing in the cluster acts on a recommendation, and the maintenance pass is what will lower a request, through the actor.

Each workload has a `state`: `settled` (a recommendation from a day or more of watching), `learning` (a recommendation from less), `pending` (none yet for its primary container), `blocked` (the recommender refuses its object; `why` says why) or `missing` (no object: the optimizer is not installed or synced on the infrastructure, or its cluster does not run the workload). Per container, the request VPA would set (`target_cpu_milli`, `target_memory_bytes`), its lower and upper bounds, and `observed_hours`: how long the recommender has watched it, the days Prometheus kept when it was installed included (its history is seeded from them, so a workload settles on the day of the install); a young one's upper bound is far above its target.

`coverage.ready` is the gate: the recommender running, and at least 80% of the workloads it can watch settled. Platform workloads only — never a customer's services (their inframan.yaml sizes them) and never a Redis or PostgreSQL instance (its tier does).

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to read. From list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: import_environment
capabilities.summary: Put an exported environment file back: its env groups, secret groups and secrets, onto an infrastructure.
capabilities.description:
Reads the file export_environment downloads, exactly as downloaded, onto this infrastructure or another one. It creates the groups and secrets that are missing and overwrites the values of those that exist — a group's variables by key, a secret by name — and deletes nothing, so importing a file twice is importing it once. A group whose type differs from the file's refuses the whole import, since a group's type is fixed. With dry_run it only says what it would do.

CONSOLE ONLY and instance admins only, like the export: the file carries every value in plain text. Each import is recorded in the activity feed.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to import into.

params.name: file
params.description: The exported file: its JSON object, or its text as pasted.

params.name: dry_run
params.description: Say what the import would do, and write nothing.

capabilities.name: install_addon
capabilities.summary: Install a named Redis or Postgres onto an infrastructure.
capabilities.description:
REAL INFRASTRUCTURE, REAL MONEY. This provisions a GKE node pool through Terraform and applies the operator's resources inside the cluster. It takes MINUTES, not seconds. On a nonprod AWS infrastructure the install runs on the system pool instead of a pool of its own, and a prod AWS one refuses it.

MAY COME BACK HELD RATHER THAN STARTED. If this app tier has no verified cloud identity on the infrastructure, the call SUCCEEDS with status `awaiting_setup`: the install is recorded with everything the customer chose, and nothing is provisioned or billing. It is not an error and the request is not lost — do not retry it and do not create a second one.

The identity has to exist before the pod does. It is attached to the pod at creation and cannot be added to a running database without rebuilding it, which on a datastore means downtime and a data move.

When you get `awaiting_setup`, the sequence is: get_cloud_identity_setup for this infrastructure, app and tier — show the customer the commands and ask them to run them, since Inframan cannot (creating a service account needs a permission it is deliberately not granted) — then verify_cloud_identity, then continue_addon_install with the installed_app_id you already have. One-time per app tier per infrastructure; later installs of the same tier start immediately.

The call returns as soon as the workflow starts. It is NOT done when it returns: poll get_installed_app until `status` is ready before telling anyone the database is up or wiring a service to it. A failed install reports its reason there too.

Ask the user before calling. Confirm the infrastructure, the instance name and the size — this provisions billable capacity that runs until someone removes it, and removing it is not something you can do.

`instance_name` is required and PERMANENT: several named installs of one app can live on one infrastructure, and the name is how they are told apart and how services address them. It becomes part of the Kubernetes namespace and cannot be changed afterwards, so ask rather than inventing one.

`memory` is optional and applies to BOTH apps, but it does not mean the same thing in each, so do not carry a number across from one to the other.

For Redis it is the usable DATASET size: the pod is sized 25% above it for background-save headroom. For Postgres it is the POD's memory, and roughly a quarter becomes shared_buffers while max_connections is derived from what is left — so asking for the same figure buys a smaller working set on Postgres than on Redis, and quietly changes how many clients it will accept.

In both cases the NODE is then sized to fit the pod, so a larger memory means a larger, costlier machine. Choose with the user, because changing it later is refused when the new size needs a different machine.

COST CHANGES AT MACHINE BOUNDARIES, NOT AT MEMORY VALUES, and this is the single most useful thing you can tell someone sizing an instance. Each install gets its own node, so the bill is the node's — every size that lands on the same machine costs the same. On a nonprod infrastructure:
• Postgres — 256mb, 512mb, 1gb and 2gb ALL land on one e2-medium. Recommending 256mb over 2gb saves the user nothing and costs them working set and connections (a 256mb Postgres gets 20 connections, a 2gb one 120). The next machine starts just above 2gb.
• Redis — 256mb, 512mb and 1gb land on e2-medium; 2gb crosses to the next machine, because the pod is sized 25% above the dataset for fork headroom and that is what the node must hold.
So the same "2gb" is one machine class on Postgres and the next one up on Redis. Do not carry a size across engines and assume the price follows.

What that means in practice: when a user asks for the cheapest option, do not reach for the smallest number. Find the LARGEST size that stays on the same machine as the smallest one — it is the same bill with more database. Only recommend crossing a boundary when they actually need what is on the other side, and say plainly that it is where the cost step happens. Prod is sized differently and starts a machine class higher, so these boundaries are nonprod ones.

`persistence` decides whether the instance's data sits on a durable volume that outlives its pod, and it is PERMANENT — there is no path to flip a running install, because turning persistence off would delete the volume the data is on. LEAVE IT UNSET unless the user has actually expressed a preference: unset means the app's own default, which is on.

Postgres is persistent whatever you send, and an explicit false is refused rather than quietly upgraded. It is a database of record; an ephemeral one loses every committed transaction the next time its pod moves, and on a single Spot node that is measured in hours.

Postgres is BACKED UP by default, and you should still be careful how you say so. Every install archives WAL continuously to its own bucket and takes a base backup daily at 03:00 UTC, which is what makes point-in-time recovery possible. Use `backup_hour_utc` to move that hour; there is no switch here to turn it off, and a database of record should not have one.

What that does NOT yet mean is a restore anybody has performed. The mechanism is complete and untested end to end, so answer "backups are running and recoverable in principle" rather than "your data is safe" — those are different claims and only the first is currently evidenced.

Redis is where the choice is real. Off is a legitimate, cheaper configuration for a pure read-through cache: no disk to pay for, and nothing in it that cannot be recomputed from the origin. What it costs is the RESTART. An add-on pool is a single Spot node, so a preemption brings the instance back EMPTY — and every request that would have been a cache hit goes to the database behind it at once, a cold-start stampede onto the origin at the moment the origin is the only thing left. Choose off only when the user has told you what is behind the cache and that it can absorb that; otherwise say nothing and take the default.

`tier` is "basic", the only one that exists today. The rule behind it, for when there are more: a tier promising replication or failover needs a REGIONAL cluster, which is what a prod-tagged infrastructure gets. Nonprod is zonal by deliberate cost choice, so an HA tier there would place every replica in the primary's zone — costing more and surviving nothing — and is refused. Do not invent a tier name: list_platform_apps with an infrastructure_id reports `allowed_tiers` per add-on for that specific cluster, and that is the set this accepts.

Both keep their passwords in the cloud account's secret manager, so both need the infrastructure's Secret Manager: refused with code `secret_manager_off` while it is off, and with `cloud_account_not_ready`, naming the grants, while the account is not yet verified for them — get_infrastructure_features says which (`secret_manager`). Turning it on, and re-running the account's setup, are the user's.

Add-ons only. The platform's own apps — gateway, monitoring, cicd — cannot be installed here or anywhere else by an agent; list_platform_apps and get_platform_app_config are how you read their state.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure to install onto. From list_infrastructures. It must be READY — there is no cluster to install into before that.

params.name: app_id
params.description: Catalog app id for Redis or Postgres, from list_platform_apps. Not a name, and not an installed_app_id.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The name this install is known by, e.g. "sessions" or "cache-prod". Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, 53 characters or fewer, unique per app on the infrastructure. Permanent — ask the user.

params.name: tier
params.description: Only "basic" exists today. The accepted set is per-cluster, not global: list_platform_apps with an infrastructure_id reports `allowed_tiers` for each add-on on that infrastructure. A tier promising replication or failover needs a regional (prod) cluster and is refused on a zonal one.

params.name: memory
params.description: Optional, both apps, e.g. "512mb", "1gb", "4gb" — but read as the usable DATASET on Redis and as the POD's memory on Postgres, where shared_buffers and max_connections are derived from it. Cost steps at machine boundaries, not at these values: on nonprod, Postgres is one machine from 256mb through 2gb and Redis from 256mb through 1gb. See the tool description before advising a smaller size to save money.

params.name: backup_hour_utc
params.description: Postgres only, optional: the hour of day base backups run, 0-23, in UTC — NOT the customer's local time, and worth saying out loud when you report it. Omit unless the user asked for a particular time; the default is 03:00 UTC. Backups are ON for every Postgres and this only moves them. There is no cron here on purpose: pick an hour, and the platform builds the schedule.

params.name: postgres_version
params.description: Postgres only, optional: the major version, "16", "17" or "18" (default 18, the newest). Match the database the data will come from: a dump or copy from Postgres N must land on N or newer, never older. It can be raised later in place (with downtime), never lowered.

params.name: persistence
params.description: Whether this install's data sits on a durable volume. OMIT unless the user has asked for one or the other: omitted takes the app's default, which is on for every add-on, and a false you supplied on your own initiative is a request for a datastore that comes back empty after any pod restart. Postgres refuses false — it is a database of record. Redis accepts it: cheaper for a pure cache, at the price of a cold-start stampede onto the origin when the Spot node it runs on is preempted. PERMANENT — it cannot be changed after the install.

capabilities.name: install_platform_app
capabilities.summary: Install an app from the store (Knative, KEDA, Grafana, LikeC4, pgweb, Redis, Postgres) onto an infrastructure.
capabilities.description:
REAL INFRASTRUCTURE, REAL MONEY. This runs Helm inside the cluster as an in-cluster job, and for Redis-style apps it may create a GKE node pool through Terraform first. It takes MINUTES, not seconds.

The call returns as soon as the workflow has started. It is NOT done when it returns: poll get_installed_app until `status` is ready before telling anyone the app is up or wiring a service to it. A failed install reports its reason there too.

Ask the user before calling. Confirm which infrastructure, and for Redis-style apps the instance name and size — this provisions billable capacity.

Redis and Postgres (category `opensource`) REQUIRE `instance_name` and `tier`: several named installs of one app can live on one infrastructure, and the name is how they are told apart and how services address them. Only `basic` tier is available today; a future tier promising replication or failover will be accepted only on a prod (regional) infrastructure, because a zonal cluster cannot honour it. `memory` is optional and Redis-only. `persistence` is optional for every add-on — omitted takes the app's default (on), Postgres refuses an explicit false, and the choice cannot be changed after the install.

The platform's own apps (gateway, monitoring, cicd) are one-per-infrastructure and take none of those: pass the app id alone. Installing one that is already installed is refused; a FAILED install is retried in place.

Grafana is one per infrastructure and REQUIRES `address` — {"mode":"auto"} for the hosting's automatic HTTPS address (grafana.<infra>.<hosting domain>, available once the infrastructure's certificate is served), or {"mode":"domain","domain":"grafana.example.com"} for one of the infrastructure's ACTIVE domains that no service routes on; an install with neither is refused. `auth` is optional: {"mode":"login"} (the default, Grafana's own login as admin — the password is shown with reveal_addon_password) or {"mode":"oauth","provider":"google|github|gitlab|azuread|okta|generic","client_id":…,"client_secret":"<NAME of an infrastructure secret holding it>", …}. Never put a client secret's value here. Like a database tier, Grafana may come back `awaiting_setup` for its cloud identity: get_cloud_identity_setup, verify_cloud_identity, then continue_addon_install.

LikeC4 — the architecture site of the infrastructure's applications, built from the models they list under `likec4:` in inframan.yaml — is one per infrastructure and REQUIRES `address`, exactly as Grafana's. `auth` is optional: {"mode":"password"} (the default, user `likec4` — the password is shown with reveal_addon_password) or {"mode":"oauth","provider":"google|github|gitlab|azuread|okta|generic","client_id":…,"client_secret":"<NAME of an infrastructure secret>", …} with "issuer_url" for generic. It has no cloud identity and never waits for one.

pgweb — the infrastructure's database client, a web client for its PostgreSQL databases that runs DbGate — is one per infrastructure and takes `address` and `auth` exactly as LikeC4 (user `pgweb` for the password). It connects only to the databases whose client switch is on (set_postgres_client), which can also install it.

Get both ids from list_platform_apps.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure to install onto. From list_infrastructures. It must be READY — there is no cluster to install into before that.

params.name: app_id
params.description: Catalog app id from list_platform_apps. Not a name, and not an installed_app_id.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: Required for Redis/Postgres: the name this install is known by, e.g. "sessions" or "cache-prod". Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, 53 characters or fewer, unique per app on the infrastructure. Ask the user rather than inventing one — it becomes part of the Kubernetes namespace and cannot be changed later.

params.name: tier
params.description: Required for Redis/Postgres. Only "basic" is available today. The accepted set is per-infrastructure — list_platform_apps with an infrastructure_id reports it as `allowed_tiers` — because a tier promising replication or failover is refused on a zonal (nonprod) cluster.

params.name: memory
params.description: Optional, Redis only: the instance's memory, e.g. "512mb" or "2gb". Omit to take the tier default. Sets both the pod's limit and Redis's own maxmemory.

params.name: persistence
params.description: Optional, opensource apps only: whether the install's data sits on a durable volume. Omit to take the app's default (on). Postgres refuses an explicit false. Permanent — it cannot be changed afterwards.

params.name: address
params.description: Grafana, LikeC4 and pgweb only, required: a JSON object, {"mode":"auto"} or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}.

params.name: auth
params.description: Grafana only: a JSON object. {"mode":"login"} (default) or {"mode":"oauth", "provider", "client_id", "client_secret" (the NAME of an infrastructure secret), and as the provider needs: "tenant_id" (azuread), "okta_domain" (okta), "auth_url"/"token_url"/"api_url" (generic); optional "scopes", "allowed_domains", "allowed_organizations", "allowed_groups", "admin_groups", "editor_groups", "role_attribute_path", "keep_login_form"}. For LikeC4 and pgweb: {"mode":"password"} (default) or {"mode":"oauth", "provider", "client_id", "client_secret", and "tenant_id" (azuread), "okta_domain" (okta), "issuer_url" (generic); optional "scopes", "allowed_domains", "allowed_organizations" (github, one), "allowed_groups"}.

capabilities.name: link_pipeline
capabilities.summary: Attach a pipeline to an application so pushes run it.
capabilities.description:
This is the step that makes a pipeline fire. Creating one does nothing on its own — an agent that calls create_pipeline and stops has built something that will never run.

Linking the same pipeline twice is reported rather than duplicated.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to attach it to. From list_applications.

params.name: pipeline_id
params.description: The pipeline to attach. From list_pipelines.

capabilities.name: list_activity
capabilities.summary: Read the instance's activity feed: every application's events, and each infrastructure's own, newest first.
capabilities.description:
The instance's history in one feed, newest first: every application's events, as list_application_activity gives them, and what each infrastructure recorded of its own — domains, env groups and secrets, Karpenter's node changes (node_class), the optimizer's (maintenance). Each event carries its application's name (application_name) where it has one. It is the console's Activity tab of the instance, and its Overview's recent releases (revision_deploy_succeeded, revision_deploy_failed).

Use it for "what happened across the instance" or "what changed on this infrastructure"; for one application, narrow it with application_id or read list_application_activity. Same event shape, categories, statuses and cursor as there: a failure, or a warning (vulnerabilities_found, new_vulnerabilities_found, traffic_route_unconfirmed), is an issue start_investigation takes as `event:<id>`.

Narrowed to an infrastructure, it lists what it recorded and its applications' events. Dismissed events are hidden unless asked for. Paginated by an opaque cursor: pass the next_cursor of the previous page, and stop when it comes back empty.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Optional: an infrastructure's UUID, from list_infrastructures. Its own events and its applications'.

params.name: application_id
params.description: Optional: an application's UUID, from list_applications.

params.name: categories
params.description: Optional comma-separated categories, e.g. "deploy,node_class". Omit for everything.

params.name: status
params.description: Optional status filter: in_progress, success, failure or info.

params.name: include_dismissed
params.description: Include events somebody dismissed from the feed. Default false.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many events per page. Default 25, maximum 100.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The next_cursor from a previous call, to read the following page. Omit for the first page.

capabilities.name: list_agent_conversations
capabilities.summary: List an always-on agent's conversations, the one last spoken in first.
capabilities.description: Each conversation with when it started and was last spoken in, its `messages`, its `cost_micros` (micro-dollars at list prices), a short `visitor` hash (the same visitor on the same day has the same one; the address itself is never kept) and the `error` code its last answer ended with, if any (`budget_reached`: the conversation, the day or the month reached the agent's budget). Paged: pass the answer's `next_cursor` as `cursor` for the next page. Conversations are kept thirty days.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the agent: the ID of its service, from list_agents.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many to return, 25 by default and 100 at most.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The `next_cursor` of the page before.

capabilities.name: list_agent_runs
capabilities.summary: List an on-demand agent's runs, newest first.
capabilities.description: Each run with its `trigger` (`type`: manual, schedule, webhook or event; `detail`: the event's name, the schedule, or who started it), its `status` — `queued`, `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `timed_out`, `budget_reached`, `cancelled`, or `skipped` (a trigger that started nothing: the infrastructure was asleep, or ten runs already waited) — with `status_detail`, a sentence, where it did not succeed; when it was queued, started and ended; its `turns`, `cost_micros` and token `usage` once it has ended; its `summary`, the agent's last message; `awaiting_approval`, how many of its tool calls wait for a person now (a running run with any is waiting, not working); and `pull_request`, the pull request it opened from what it changed (number, url, branch, title and `state`: open, merged or closed), null for none. Paged: pass the answer's `next_cursor` as `cursor`. Runs are kept ninety days.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the agent: the ID of its service, from list_agents.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many to return, 25 by default and 100 at most.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The `next_cursor` of the page before.

capabilities.name: list_agent_templates
capabilities.summary: List the agents Inframan can write for you: Docs Q&A, an incident analyser, issue to pull request.
capabilities.description:
Each template is a whole agent, written as a service of inframan.yaml: its `id`, `title`, `summary`, `mode` (`always` or `on_demand`), a `default_name` for the service, what the agent is given (`gives`), what must exist for it to work (`needs`), the few `fields` that differ from one repository to the next (each with its `key`, `kind` — `text`, `toggle` or `model` — `default` and whether it is `required`), and `yaml`, the service its defaults write. Every template asks its `model` (`<connection>/<model>`, such as openai/gpt-5 or gemini/gemini-3.8-flash; empty for the default connection's default model). `docs_qa` answers questions from a folder of the repository at an address; `incident_analyser` runs when a release fails or the platform escalates a failure, reads the instance and the code, and opens a pull request for a small fix; `issue_to_pr` runs on a webhook from an issue tracker and opens a pull request, every shell command waiting for a person. With `application_id`: `ready`, whether that application's infrastructure has a ready Agents app and a model connection (`not_ready_reason` says which is missing; an agent can be added either way, and its release is refused until then), and `addable`, whether the console's Add service can write one there, and `models`: each of the infrastructure's connections, the default first, with models suggested for it as a file writes them, and `default_model`, what an agent that names none is given. A suggestion is no limit: any model the connection's provider has can be named. To add one yourself: preview_agent_template for the service's YAML, then put it under `services:` of the application's inframan.yaml as any change to the file.

With `infrastructure_id` and no application: what an agent deployed on its own (create_agent_deployment) can take there — `standalone` true, each template with its form for that (its knowledge given inline: `docs_qa` asks `knowledge_content`, of kind `textarea`, the text it answers from) and `agent`, its agent's block with every default, as create_agent_deployment's `agent` takes it; `unavailable`, the templates whose agent works in a repository, each with why; `ready` and `addable`, whether an agent deployment can be made there now; and the same `models`.

params.name: application_id
params.description: UUID of the application the agent would be added to, from list_applications.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: With no application_id: the infrastructure an agent deployed on its own would run on, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: list_agents
capabilities.summary: List the instance's agents: services of type agent, with their model, address, status and spend.
capabilities.description: An agent is a service of an application whose inframan.yaml gives it `type: agent`: a model with its own instructions and knowledge, answering at an address, spending against budgets through its infrastructure's model connection. Each entry has its `mode` (`always`: kept running, with an address; `on_demand`: it runs when something starts it — a person, a schedule, a webhook or an event — and holds no pod between runs), `model`, `status` — `ready`, `not_released` (no release of it has served yet), `not_connected` (its infrastructure has no ready Agents app or no model connection; `status_detail` says which), `stopped` (no pod, or the infrastructure sleeps), `failing`, and for an on-demand agent `running` (a run runs or waits) or `last_run_failed` — its `address` ("" where it has none), its `budget` and what it `spent` today and this month, in micro-dollars (1,000,000 to the dollar; 0 is no cap), its conversations this month, and for an on-demand agent its `triggers` (each with its `type`; an event's `event`, the `branch` glob it is held to, and its `phrase`: where it has one, a push or a merged pull request starts the agent only when its head commit message, or the pull request's title or merge commit message, carries that text, as `[skip ci]` is read), its `last_run` and `runs_month`. `mcp` lists the MCP servers of the user's services its file names (agent.mcp): each `name` (its tools are `<name>_<tool>`), `target`, `path`, the `tools` it is given (null for every tool the server lists), those that wait for a person (`approve`), the `secret` named for its credential, and its `address`, where the agent's gateway calls it now, or its `problem`, why it cannot be called now. `standalone` is true for an agent deployed on its own (create_agent_deployment): its application holds it and nothing else, and is changed through its manifest (save_application_manifest). Narrow with `infrastructure_id` or `application_id`.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Only the agents of this infrastructure.

params.name: application_id
params.description: Only the agents of this application.

capabilities.name: list_alert_groups
capabilities.summary: List the instance's alert groups: who hears each service alert and each pipeline's notify step.
capabilities.description:
An alert group is the instance's: a `name` (1 to 40 lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, never `none`; fixed once made, since files name it), a `description`, its `channels` (1 to 10 of the instance's notification channels, in order: it sends to every one that is on), `send_resolved` (whether a message also goes when an alert resolves) and `enabled` (a group that is off sends nothing: how one is silenced). A file names it: an alert's `notify: <group>` (or `notify: none` for no one), and an application's `notify: <group>` beside `services:`, which is the default group of its services' alerts — every alert of it that names none — and nothing else; a pipeline's notify step or stage names one too, for a release's outcome. A group named nowhere is no one. A release whose file names a group the instance does not have is refused (ALERT_GROUP_NOT_FOUND); a chart application, which has no alerts, names none (CHART_APPLICATION_NOTIFY).

Each group with its `channels` (each channel's name, type and whether it is on), `send_resolved`, `enabled`, its `last_test`, and `used_by`: the `applications` whose notify: names it, the `alerts` whose own notify: does, as their serving releases applied them, and the `pipelines` whose notify steps or stages name it (each with `where`, such as post_deploy.<step> or release_stages.<id>). `limits` say how many groups and channels there may be. What is sent, and to whom: a service's own alert (inframan.yaml `alerts:`) when it fires, and when it resolves where the group sends resolves, to the alert group the alert names (`notify: <group>`), else its application's (`notify:` beside `services:`), `notify: none` sending it to no one; and a pipeline's notify step or stage (create_pipeline), to the group or the channels it names, as its run or release reaches it. An application's `notify:` is the default group of its services' alerts and nothing else: a release that fails, a chart application's install that fails and new vulnerabilities in its images are on the bell, the feed and the console, and reach a channel only through a pipeline's notify step (a release stage with `when: failure` or `always` for a failed release). Nothing else is sent: not the platform's or Kubernetes' default alert rules, not an agent's tool call waiting for approval, not an investigation's end — the console shows them. A group named nowhere is no one. To make a group or change one, an admin uses the console's Settings, Notifications, Alert groups; to send an application's or an alert's messages to one, write its name with notify: in inframan.yaml.

capabilities.name: list_app_components
capabilities.summary: List the components of an installed app and where each one stands: ready, failed, blocked, skipped.
capabilities.description:
An installed app is a set of components — Helm releases, custom resources, manifests, Terraform, configuration — applied as a graph: each one the moment the components it needs are in, so one that fails holds up only what needs it. This lists every component the app has on the install's infrastructure, in install order, with where the last reconcile to reach it left it:
• `ready` — applied and ready.
• `failed` — its apply failed; `reason` is the error.
• `blocked` — not attempted, because `blocked_by` ("<app>/<component>", possibly another app's) did not get there. Deal with that one and the blocked ones follow on the next reconcile.
• `skipped` — deliberately not applied on this infrastructure.
• `waiting` / `applying` — a reconcile is working on it now.
• `unknown` — no reconcile has recorded it. The platform apps (gateway, monitoring, CI/CD) are reconciled as a graph and record every component; the add-ons from the app store are not yet, and read unknown throughout.

Read this when get_installed_app reports an app failed or degraded: the app fails for a component, and this names which one, why, and what it held up. `updated_at` is when the component's record last changed.

Read-only. The id is the installed_app_id from list_platform_apps (`installs[].id`), not the catalog app id.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: UUID of the install, from list_platform_apps (`installs[].id`) or the install response's installed_app_id.

capabilities.name: list_application_activity
capabilities.summary: Read an application's activity feed: builds, deploys, config changes, traffic shifts and auto-remediations.
capabilities.description:
The history of what HAPPENED to an application, newest first — one entry per logical event, each with who did it (a person, a git push, or the platform itself) and how it ended.

This is the first thing to read when asked "what changed?" or "why did this break?": it puts a deploy, a config change and the platform's own remediation on one timeline, which none of list_deployments, get_logs or get_metric can do alone.

Categories are build, deploy, pre_deploy, post_deploy, config_change, traffic, domain, incident, auto_remediation, lifecycle and security. Statuses are in_progress, success, failure and info — filter on failure to go straight to what went wrong. A failure, or a warning (vulnerabilities_found, new_vulnerabilities_found, traffic_route_unconfirmed), is an issue start_investigation takes as `event:<id>`; an investigation's end is investigation_finished (category agent).

security is a release's image scan that found anything critical or high, or a secret baked into the image (vulnerabilities_found, the counts in metadata), or a release the service's security policy refused (scan_blocked, status failure, with the refusal in metadata.message and the finding IDs in metadata.findings), or the daily rescan finding new critical or high advisories against an image a service runs (new_vulnerabilities_found, the IDs in metadata.findings); get_service_vulnerabilities lists the findings.

lifecycle is a deactivation, reactivation or erase: one entry per attempt (application_deactivation, application_reactivation, application_erase), in_progress until its workflow ends and then success, or failure with the reason in metadata.error.

IT IS ALSO HOW YOU LEARN WHETHER SOMETHING FINISHED. The mutating tools return as soon as work is accepted, not when the cluster has caught up, so this feed — not a second call to the tool — is where the outcome appears. A traffic change writes `traffic_shift_requested` (in_progress) when accepted and `traffic_settled` (success) when the cluster matches; a release writes revision_deploy_succeeded or revision_deploy_failed. Poll here rather than re-issuing the change, which would start a second run of the same work.

Paginated by an opaque cursor: pass the next_cursor from the previous page to continue, and stop when it comes back empty. Dismissed events are hidden unless you ask for them.

params.name: application_id
params.description: UUID of the application whose feed to read, from list_applications.

params.name: categories
params.description: Optional comma-separated categories, e.g. "deploy,auto_remediation". Omit for everything.

params.name: status
params.description: Optional status filter: in_progress, success, failure or info.

params.name: include_dismissed
params.description: Include events somebody dismissed from the feed. Default false.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many events per page. Default 25, maximum 100.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The next_cursor from a previous call, to read the following page. Omit for the first page.

capabilities.name: list_application_deployments
capabilities.summary: List the CI/CD runs for one application, across all of its services, newest first.
capabilities.description:
One row per SERVICE per release, carrying status, commit and image — so a release of a three-service application appears as three rows.

This is the first thing to read when a deploy did not work. Take the `id` of the failing row into get_deployment_pipeline to see which step failed, and get_deployment_logs for its output. Once the cause is fixed, a push releases again — there is no re-run of a failed release, because the same code fails the same way.

list_deployments answers the same question across the whole instance; use this one when the application is already known.

Paginated by an opaque cursor, exactly as list_deployments and list_application_activity are. The reply is an object — {count, deployments, next_cursor} — and next_cursor is how you tell a complete answer from a truncated one: non-empty means there ARE older runs, so pass it back as cursor and keep going `count` is the size of THIS PAGE, not the number of runs that exist — there is no total. Follow next_cursor until it comes back empty if you need them all.

until it comes back empty. An empty next_cursor is the only proof you have seen every run this application has. How many rows came back tells you nothing on its own — one release of a five-service application is five rows, so a page of 20 is four releases.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose runs to list. From list_applications.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many runs per page, newest first. Default 20; anything above 100 is clamped to 100. Asking for a large number is not how you read the whole history — follow next_cursor for that.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The next_cursor from a previous call, to read the following page. Omit for the first page.

capabilities.name: list_application_revisions
capabilities.summary: List an application's deployed revisions, newest first, with their traffic weights.
capabilities.description:
A revision is an APP-WIDE immutable version: every service in the application, at the versions that shipped together. Revisions are what traffic is split across — there is no per-service weighting anywhere in this platform, so a question about "which version is live" is answered here.

THIS IS THE FIRST STEP OF A ROLLBACK. Going back to an earlier release means pointing traffic at its revision, so read this list, find the last one that was good, and pass its `id` to update_revision_setting with mode="fixed". Every revision that ever deployed is still listed — nothing is pruned — so the target is always here even when its Knative services have already been removed for carrying no traffic.

`revision_number` is the human-readable ordering, `id` is what update_revision_setting wants, and `traffic_weight` is the percentage the revision serves right now. A revision with status `failed` never deployed and cannot take traffic; `retired` means it is not serving but can be brought back.

Not the same as this application's deployments, which are per-service CI/CD runs — one release of a three-service application is one revision and three deployments.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose revisions to list. From list_applications.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many revisions to return, newest first. Default 20, maximum 100.

capabilities.name: list_applications
capabilities.summary: List the applications in this instance, with their services. Filter by repo_url to find which applications a repository backs.
capabilities.description:
An application groups the services deployed from one repository.

A REPOSITORY DOES NOT IDENTIFY AN APPLICATION. One repository can back several applications, and that is normal rather than a mistake to correct:
  - the same repository deployed to prod and to nonprod is two applications;
  - one create_application can fan an application across infrastructures in a single call — those share a group_id and a repo_url;
  - a repository can back more than one application within a SINGLE infrastructure, so narrowing to one cluster does not make the answer unique either.
An application is identified by the triple (repository, infrastructure, name), and only application_id is truly unique. Never infer one from a repository.

SO: when the user names a repository rather than an application, call this with repo_url. If it returns more than one, you do not know which one they mean — list the matches back with their name, infrastructure name/tag, namespace and status, and ask which. Do not guess, do not pick the newest, and do not act on all of them. This matters most before anything destructive: deactivate_application takes the id resolved here, and erasing an application outright is a console operation rather than one of yours.

Inactive applications are included by default. A deactivated application keeps its record and history and can be reactivated, so it is not deleted and hiding it would misrepresent the instance — but it also has nothing running, so check status before treating a match as live. Pass status to narrow.

This returns a SUMMARY per application — identity, infrastructure, and one line per service — because a list answers "which one". For scaling, resources, env, probes, the rendered manifest or build logs, call get_application on the id you picked.

Each service line carries last_deploy_status, which is the outcome of its LAST deploy and not a statement about what is running now.
