A deactivated application still reads DEPLOYED there, because its services were removed from the cluster while the record kept the last result. The application's own status field is the live signal; read that one to know whether anything is serving.

Config-sync timing: service fields (domain, port, scaling, resources, env) sync from inframan.yaml to the database only after a SUCCESSFUL deploy. Empty values on a service that has never deployed cleanly are expected, not a fault — check its deployment status before treating them as one.

Each carries last_release_branch: the branch its newest release was built from — the one its push named, or its own branch where none did — and "" before any release recorded one. It is where people release from now: offer it first as the base branch of a pull request for the application, before its own branch.

Each application says what it is as a deployment — the console calls an application a deployment, and the API keeps the word application — in `kind`: `repository` (services built from a repository's inframan.yaml), `images` (published images working together, with no repository; `image_count` is how many services of its newest manifest run a published image), `chart` (one Helm chart) or `agent` (one agent on Inframan's runtime and nothing else, as create_agent_deployment makes one; `agent_service_id` is its agent's service, the ID get_agent takes, once its row is made). The kind is computed as it is read, never stored: an images application whose manifest comes to hold one agent alone is an agent deployment, and the reverse.

params.name: repo_url
params.description: Only applications deployed from this repository. Any form works: "org/repo", "github.com/org/repo", or a full https/SSH URL, with or without ".git". Expect more than one match and disambiguate with the user.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Only applications on this infrastructure, from list_infrastructures. Narrows the answer but does not guarantee a single match.

params.name: status
params.description: "active" or "inactive". Omit for both, which is the default.

params.name: kind
params.description: Only applications of these kinds, one or several separated by commas: repository, images, chart or agent. Omit for every kind.

capabilities.name: list_cloud_accounts
capabilities.summary: List the linked GCP cloud accounts — the projects infrastructure can be provisioned into.
capabilities.description:
Returns account ids, project ids and service-account emails. Provisioning infrastructure needs a cloud account id from here.

Each account's effective_status says whether it can be used: verified, or needs_update (its setup must be rerun and verified before anything new acts in it; missing names what it lacks), pending, verifying or failed.

`secret_manager` says whether the account's setup carries Secret Manager's grants. It follows the account's infrastructures: one created with Secret Manager, or turning it on, puts the grants in — and the account reads needs_update until its setup is re-run and verified; once none of its live infrastructures has Secret Manager on (the last turning it off, or the first created without it), they come out. An account with no infrastructure yet has them.

capabilities.name: list_connectable_services
capabilities.summary: List the services this service may point a connection variable at.
capabilities.description:
Call this BEFORE the connections: block in inframan.yaml. It is the only way to know which targets are legal, and a connection to an illegal one is accepted nowhere — the platform refuses it rather than deploying something that cannot resolve.

Each entry carries a `scope`:
• `application` — a sibling in the same application. Siblings deploy together as one revision, so the caller is wired to the exact version that shipped with it, deliberately bypassing any weighted traffic split at the edge.
• `namespace` — a web service or TCP server of ANOTHER application sharing this namespace, reached at its stable internal address.

A TCP server — a worker that declares a port, such as a database or a queue run from its image — carries `address`, host:port: the connection's value, in either scope, never pinned to a version.

Nothing outside the namespace ever appears: the platform does not route between namespaces, and applications that need to talk are co-deployed into one. An empty list means this service has nothing it is allowed to call, not that the lookup failed.

A sibling worker or job with no `address` has no port, so it cannot be a connection target — pick a web service or a TCP server.

`chart_apps` lists the infrastructure's chart applications that are ready, from any namespace, each with what it offers: connect to one with its `slug`, `chart/<application>/<NAME>`, in the connections: block; `value` is how the value reads, its password as <password>.

To connect to a Redis or Postgres rather than to a service, this list is not where you look — pass an installed app to the connections: block in inframan.yaml instead.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service that would hold the connection — the CALLER, not the target. From list_services.

capabilities.name: list_console_domains
capabilities.summary: List the hostnames this Inframan console itself is served on, and the IP they point at.
capabilities.description:
THE CONSOLE'S OWN ADDRESSES — not the domains of anything deployed. These are served by Caddy on the control-plane VM, which terminates TLS there with on-demand Let's Encrypt certificates. A domain attached to a deployed service is a different subsystem with its own tools (add_domain, get_domain_status); it lives on an infrastructure's cluster ingress and never appears here.

Returns each hostname with `is_default` — true for the auto-generated `*.console.inframan.cloud` address the instance was provisioned with, which is the one that keeps working if a custom domain's DNS breaks — plus `static_ip`, the control-plane VM's address that any custom console domain's A record must point at.

Needs a connection to the central backend, which owns the Caddyfile for every instance; without one this reports that rather than an empty list.

capabilities.name: list_declared_appstore_items
capabilities.summary: List the Postgres and Redis an application's inframan.yaml (or images manifest) declares under appstore:, each with its install and status.
capabilities.description:
An application's file may declare the Postgres and Redis it runs with, in its `appstore:` section, each under the name its services connect to it by:

```yaml
appstore:
  main:
    app: postgres
    version: "18"
    instance_type: basic-256mb
    storage_gi: 10
  sessions:
    app: redis
    memory: 256Mi
services:
  api:
    connections:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres/main
      REDIS_URL: redis/sessions
```

A Postgres takes `version` (16, 17 or 18; 18 unset), `instance_type` (basic-256mb, basic-1gb, basic-4gb), `storage_gi` and `backup_hour_utc`; a Redis `memory` and `persistence`; both are the basic tier. Every other app of the store is installed once per infrastructure, from the app store in the console, never in a file. A release installs what the section declares and the application lacks, before it builds: the install is the application's, and its services' connections find it at that release. An install of the same app and name made in the app store refuses the release (APPSTORE_NOT_DECLARED_HERE: connect to it with connections: instead), as does one another application's file declares (APPSTORE_NAME_TAKEN). A declared item is made by its file and never changed by it: a file that asks something else of one that runs refuses the release (APPSTORE_DIFFERS), and the change is made on the item's page. On Google Cloud each tier needs its cloud identity first: until it is set up (get_cloud_identity_setup, then verify_cloud_identity) the release is refused with APPSTORE_NEEDS_SETUP, the install held with its choices, and the next release continues it. The app store refuses to uninstall a declared item (DECLARED_BY_APPLICATION): it is deleted from its deployment.

This lists one application's declared items: each `name`, its `app` (postgres or redis), its `installed_app_id` (get_installed_app reads it whole), its install's `status` (pending, installing, ready, awaiting_setup, failed, updating, uninstalling) and `state` (that status resolved for display, with what to do where a person is waited on), `declared` — the entry its file declares it with, as the newest release read it — and its `infrastructure_id`. An empty list means the file declares none, or no release has reached them yet.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose declared items to list. From list_applications.

capabilities.name: list_deployments
capabilities.summary: The CI/CD run feed: recent deployments across the instance, newest first.
capabilities.description:
Each row carries its service, application and infrastructure, plus status, trigger reason, and — on runs that got that far — commit and image. This is the fastest way to answer "what happened to my last deploy": read it before asking the user for details they have already got.

WHAT THE STATUSES MEAN. PENDING, BUILDING, QUEUED and DEPLOYING are in flight. READY means the service is built, applied and its pods are up — and NOT released: the release has not promoted it yet, so do not report a READY run as shipped. DEPLOYED means released, traffic has moved. SKIPPED means the service is fine and takes no traffic, because the release it belonged to failed or because nothing it watches changed. FAILED is the run itself.

A RELEASE'S VERDICT IS ITS REVISION'S, not its rows'. Rows of one release can read READY while the release is still deciding; if you need to know whether a release shipped, read the revision.

commit_hash and image_url are written on SUCCESS. A FAILED run usually has both empty even when its build resolved a commit and pushed an image — that is recorded in list_application_activity, not here. Empty means the run did not reach that step, never that no such commit exists.

commit_hash is the commit the IMAGE was built from, which is not always the push that cut the release. For a service with a monorepo path it is the newest commit touching THAT PATH, so a commit changing only inframan.yaml at the repo root releases the service without touching its directory: the build is skipped, the previous image is reused, and commit_hash names the older commit that image came from. The commit that triggered the release is in trigger_reason.

So: to answer "is my change live", read trigger_reason. To answer "what code is in this image", read commit_hash. Quoting one for the other is how a config change looks like it never deployed.

Paginated by an opaque cursor, exactly as list_application_activity is. The reply `count` is the size of THIS PAGE, not the number of runs that exist — there is no total. Follow next_cursor until it comes back empty if you need them all.

is an object — {count, deployments, next_cursor} — and next_cursor is how you tell a complete answer from a truncated one: non-empty means there ARE more runs, so pass it back as cursor and keep going until it comes back empty. An empty next_cursor is the only proof you have seen every run matching the filter. How many rows came back tells you nothing on its own.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Optional: only runs belonging to this infrastructure.

params.name: status
params.description: Optional exact status filter, e.g. FAILED, DEPLOYED, BUILDING.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many runs per page. Default 50; anything above 200 is clamped to 200. Asking for a large number is not how you read the whole feed — follow next_cursor for that.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The next_cursor from a previous call, to read the following page. Omit for the first page.

capabilities.name: list_domains
capabilities.summary: List custom domains and the load-balancer IP their DNS must point at.
capabilities.description:
The starting point for anything domain-related, and the only place the load-balancer IP comes from — the user must create an A record pointing their domain at that IP BEFORE add_domain will accept it.

With infrastructure_id: that infrastructure's domains plus its `load_balancer_ip`. Without it: every domain in the instance, grouped by infrastructure, each group carrying its own IP. The IPs differ per infrastructure — a domain pointed at the wrong one fails verification. On an AWS infrastructure the value is several comma-separated addresses, one per zone: the user creates an A record for each (any one verifies; all of them keep the domain up through a zone outage). Those are the network load balancer's, for an `l4` domain; `application_address`, present while the infrastructure's application load balancer is on and ready, is where an `l7` domain points instead.

Each domain carries a status: `pending` while the certificate is being issued, `active` once it is serving HTTPS, `failed` when issuance gave up. Only `active` means traffic works.

A domain with `served_by` is where Grafana, LikeC4 or pgweb is served: it holds every path of the domain, and a release that routes a service on it is refused (DOMAIN_HELD_BY_APP).

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Optional: only this infrastructure's domains, from list_infrastructures. Omit for every domain in the instance, grouped by infrastructure.

capabilities.name: list_env_group_vars
capabilities.summary: List the variable KEYS in an environment group, without their values.
capabilities.description:
Keys, and whether each one is a secret and a build arg. VALUES ARE NOT RETURNED, by design and on every surface this reaches — a value read out here would land in the conversation and the client's logs, which is the one place a credential must never be. A person who needs to see or change a value does it in the console, where it does not pass through anything else.

That is enough to answer what a group PROVIDES: which names a service gets by attaching it, and whether they reach the Docker build. Use it before the envGroups: block in inframan.yaml to check a group carries what a service needs, and before assuming a variable is missing — it may be arriving from a group rather than being set on the service.

A `secret` group's values are in GCP Secret Manager and are not shown to anyone, in the console either.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the group belongs to, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: group_id
params.description: UUID of the group whose keys to list, from list_env_groups.

capabilities.name: list_env_groups
capabilities.summary: List an infrastructure's environment groups, with how many variables each holds.
capabilities.description:
An env group is a named bundle of environment variables defined on an infrastructure and attached to services — one bundle shared by many services, rather than the same variables copied into each one.

Two types, fixed when the group is created. A `env` group holds plain values the platform stores itself. A `secret` group holds values kept in the customer's GCP Secret Manager, and every variable in it is also passed to the Docker build as a build arg.

This returns names, types and variable COUNTS — not the variables themselves. Use list_env_group_vars for the keys, and the envGroups: block in inframan.yaml to attach a group to a service. Attaching is done by naming it in the service's envGroups: block in inframan.yaml and pushing — the deploy resolves the names.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure whose groups to list, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: list_firing_cluster_alerts
capabilities.summary: List the alerts Prometheus and Loki are firing right now in an infrastructure's cluster.
capabilities.description:
LIVE STATE read from the cluster's own Prometheus, and its Loki's ruler, which evaluates services' log alerts — the same alerts AlertManager routes to the platform. An alert here is a condition that is true at this moment; it disappears on its own when the condition clears, and there is nothing to acknowledge.

NOT the same as list_platform_alerts, which returns database records the platform raised when its self-healing gave up. Ask here for "what is wrong in the cluster right now"; ask there for "what has been escalated to me". A workload can be firing here while the platform is still remediating it, with no record on the other side yet.

`state` is firing or pending — pending means the condition is true but has not held for long enough yet. Omit infrastructure_id to use the instance's most recent infrastructure.

Each alert carries `subject_key`, its issue's key: what start_investigation takes to have the platform's investigator find its root cause, and get_investigation_status reads.

Requires the monitoring stack to be installed on that infrastructure.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Which cluster to read, from list_infrastructures. Omit for the instance's latest infrastructure.

capabilities.name: list_github_branches
capabilities.summary: List a repository's branches, with the head commit of each.
capabilities.description:
Read this before choosing create_application's `branch`, rather than assuming "main" — a repository whose default is "master" or "trunk" would be tracked on a branch that does not exist, and nothing would ever deploy.

It is also how to check that the branch carrying a freshly pushed inframan.yaml is really there before creating the application against it.

params.name: owner
params.description: GitHub account that owns the repository, e.g. "acme" in acme/api.

params.name: repo
params.description: Repository name on its own, e.g. "api" — not the full path.

params.name: github_app_id
params.description: Optional: which connected App to read through, from get_github_app_status. Omit it and the owner is matched against the connected accounts, which is right whenever the repository belongs to one of them.

capabilities.name: list_github_repositories
capabilities.summary: List the repositories the connected GitHub Apps can reach, each tagged with the App that reaches it.
capabilities.description:
Use this to turn a repository the user names into the exact `full_name` and `default_branch` create_application needs, and to find which App reaches it — each entry carries `github_app_id`, which is the value to pass on as github_app_id.

An empty list with an App connected means the App is installed on the account but was granted no repositories, or was uninstalled. check_github_app_permissions distinguishes those and returns the GitHub page the user has to visit.

A repository the user expects to see and cannot is almost always under a different account than the connected App.

capabilities.name: list_infra_secrets
capabilities.summary: List the secrets defined on an infrastructure, by name.
capabilities.description:
NAMES ONLY, and that is not a restriction of this surface — the platform cannot show a value to anyone, in the console either. The value lives in the customer's GCP Secret Manager and is materialised into the cluster at deploy time; the platform keeps a pointer.

The names are the useful part. A service asks for a secret by NAME from its repo's inframan.yaml `secrets:` block, so this is how you check that a name a service references actually exists before a deploy fails on it, and what the available names are when writing that block.

Unlike an env group, an infrastructure secret is not attached to services — it is pulled by name from the repo's config.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure whose secret names to list, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: list_infrastructures
capabilities.summary: List the provisioned infrastructure environments (GKE clusters) in this instance.
capabilities.description: Call this FIRST when the user mentions environments, clusters, or infrastructure. Almost every other operation needs an infrastructure_id, and this is where it comes from.

capabilities.name: list_investigations
capabilities.summary: List the instance's investigations, newest first.
capabilities.description: Each investigation with its issue (`subject_kind`, `subject_key`, `subject_title`), its application where it is about one, `status`, its `summary` once it has ended, who started it, its cost and when. Filter by `status` (queued, running, succeeded, failed, timed_out, budget_reached, cancelled, skipped; or `open` for queued and running, `failed` for every end but success), `kind` (platform_alert, cluster_alert, event, log), `application_id` or `infrastructure_id`. Paged: pass the answer's `next_cursor` as `cursor`.

params.name: status
params.description: A status, `open`, or `failed`.

params.name: kind
params.description: platform_alert, cluster_alert, event or log.

params.name: application_id
params.description: Only an application's.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Only an infrastructure's.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many to return, 25 by default and 100 at most.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The `next_cursor` of the page before.

capabilities.name: list_kept_data
capabilities.summary: List what deletions kept on an infrastructure — a service's disk, a Postgres's backups and password — newest first, or one deployment's.
capabilities.description: A service deleted keeping its data leaves its disk in its namespace, billing until someone deletes it (kind disk); a Postgres deleted keeping its data leaves its backup bucket and its password, in the cloud account (kind postgres_backups: the bucket and the password's secret, by name; a new Postgres of its name is refused until they are deleted, since it would archive into the same bucket). Each is listed here with its size, the resource and deployment it was kept from (the deployment's name is empty once that deployment is erased), and where it is. Deleting kept data is a person's choice, made in the console; tell the user what is kept and what it costs.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: application_id
params.description: Only what this deployment's resources left.

capabilities.name: list_linked_pipelines
capabilities.summary: List the pipelines attached to an application, each with the infrastructure it deploys to.
capabilities.description:
A pipeline only runs for an application once it is LINKED, so this is how to tell whether a push actually deploys anything. An empty list means nothing deploys on push, however healthy the application looks.

Each entry carries its infrastructure: an application linked to pipelines on two infrastructures deploys to both, and that is visible nowhere else.

list_pipelines shows every pipeline that exists, linked or not. Use link_pipeline and unlink_pipeline to change what is here.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose pipelines to list. From list_applications.

capabilities.name: list_metrics
capabilities.summary: List the metrics that can be read, with what each one measures.
capabilities.description:
Call this before get_metric if you are unsure which metric answers the question. Returns names, units and a description of each.

`runtime` is `knative` for metrics that exist only for services deployed on the Knative runtime (scaling.type: concurrency — Actual Concurrency, Cold Start); it is `any` otherwise. Asking a knative-only metric about a service on the deployment runtime returns no series and a `not_applicable` reason, not zeros.

capabilities.name: list_notification_channels
capabilities.summary: List the instance's notification channels: where its alert groups send.
capabilities.description: Each channel's `type`, `name`, whether it is `enabled`, its settings (an email channel's SMTP host, port, security, user name, from address and `recipients`; a webhook's `webhook_url`), `secret_set` — never the secret — the alert `groups` that send to it, by name, the `pipelines` whose notify steps or stages name it, and its `last_test`. Also `channel_types`. A channel is `email` (an SMTP sender of the admin's choosing, TLS required — for Gmail, smtp.gmail.com, 587, the account and an app password), `slack` (an incoming webhook), `google_chat` (a space's webhook), `teams` (a Workflows webhook) or `webhook` (an https:// address of a public host, each body signed with HMAC-SHA256 in X-Inframan-Signature). Its secret — the SMTP password, the chat webhook's address, the signing secret — is kept by the instance, encrypted, and never read back: a read says `secret_set`. A channel is just a channel: it has no rules, and is sent what the alert groups it is in are sent. What is sent, and to whom: a service's own alert (inframan.yaml `alerts:`) when it fires, and when it resolves where the group sends resolves, to the alert group the alert names (`notify: <group>`), else its application's (`notify:` beside `services:`), `notify: none` sending it to no one; and a pipeline's notify step or stage (create_pipeline), to the group or the channels it names, as its run or release reaches it. An application's `notify:` is the default group of its services' alerts and nothing else: a release that fails, a chart application's install that fails and new vulnerabilities in its images are on the bell, the feed and the console, and reach a channel only through a pipeline's notify step (a release stage with `when: failure` or `always` for a failed release). Nothing else is sent: not the platform's or Kubernetes' default alert rules, not an agent's tool call waiting for approval, not an investigation's end — the console shows them. A group named nowhere is no one. For the groups themselves, read list_alert_groups. Every message says what happened, the group that sent it, links to it in the console and, for an issue, carries Start investigation: a link to the console's /investigate?subject=<key>, which shows the issue's button and starts nothing by itself. Channels are set up by an admin in the console, under Settings, Notifications.

capabilities.name: list_pipelines
capabilities.summary: List CI/CD pipelines, optionally for one infrastructure.
capabilities.description:
Pipelines define the build and deploy steps for a repository and branch. Creating an application needs a pipeline_id from here.

Each row carries its full definition: pre_build_steps, pre_deploy_steps, post_deploy_steps and webhooks are JSON arrays of objects, ready to read — not strings needing a second parse. Same shape get_pipeline returns, so a stage count can be read straight off this list. An empty stage is [], never null.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Optional: only pipelines for this infrastructure. Omit for all.

capabilities.name: list_platform_alerts
capabilities.summary: List the platform's own alert records — the console's bell: a release that failed, and what the platform asks a person to look at.
capabilities.description:
These are ROWS IN THIS INSTANCE'S DATABASE, the console's notification bell: a release that failed (failure_reason `release_failed`, its application as component_name and its revision in the title), and anything else the platform hands a person. What the platform's self-healing cannot settle is escalated to the Inframan team, never written here. An unacknowledged record means "somebody needs to look"; start_investigation with `platform_alert:<id>` has the platform's investigator find its root cause. A record is sent to no notification channel: a pipeline's notify step or stage (create_pipeline) is how people hear of a failed release.

NOT the same as list_firing_cluster_alerts, which is live Prometheus/AlertManager state inside the user's cluster. Use that one for "what is wrong right now"; use this one for "what has been handed to me". A cluster alert can fire and clear without ever producing a record here, and a record here can outlive the condition that caused it, because it survives until acknowledged.

Unacknowledged only by default, newest first. Each row carries the component, the failure reason, severity and the message the actor wrote.

params.name: include_acknowledged
params.description: Include records somebody has already acknowledged. Default false — only the ones still waiting on a human.

params.name: limit
params.description: How many records to return. Default 50, maximum 200.

capabilities.name: list_platform_apps
capabilities.summary: List the installable platform apps and where they are installed.
capabilities.description:
These are the managed apps the platform installs INTO a cluster — Redis, Postgres and the platform's own gateway, monitoring and CI/CD stacks. They are not your applications; use list_applications for those.

With `infrastructure_id`: the catalog annotated with install state for that one infrastructure — `installed`, `status`, `health`, and for Redis-style apps an `instances` array, because several named installs of one app can share an infrastructure. This is the shape to read before installing anything.

That scoped shape also carries the install RULES for each add-on on that specific cluster, which is what makes it worth reading first rather than guessing:
• `allowed_tiers` — the tiers install_addon will accept there. Per-cluster, not per-app: a tier promising replication or failover needs a regional (prod) cluster and is refused on a zonal nonprod one, so the same add-on offers different sets on different infrastructures. Pass a value from this list rather than composing a tier name.
• `persistence_required` — true when the app's data must sit on a durable volume and `persistence` is not yours to set (Postgres). False means the choice is real, and defaults to on.

Without it: the catalog plus every install in this instance, across all infrastructures. Use this to find an install when you do not know which infrastructure it is on.

Each install carries an `id` — that is the installed_app_id the other tools take.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Optional: annotate the catalog with install state for this one infrastructure. From list_infrastructures. Omit to see every install in the instance instead.

capabilities.name: list_release_stages
capabilities.summary: List the release stages of one revision, in order, with each one's status and outputs.
capabilities.description:
Release stages are a pipeline's post-release steps (`release_stages:` in the pipeline YAML): promote_images, webhook, wait, manual_judgment and publish_files, run in order once the release's traffic has moved. This reads how they ran for one release: `status` is pending, running, waiting, succeeded, failed or skipped; `summary` is one line (the failure's reason when failed); `outputs` are what the stage produced (a promote's `images`, a webhook's `status_code` and `response`, a judgment's `decision`, `by` and `comment`, a publish's `version`, `prefix` and `files`); `judgment` is a manual judgment's prompt, timeout_at and decision.

A stage never fails its release. A stage that is `waiting` is a manual judgment holding for a person in the console — an agent cannot decide it. An empty list means the release's pipeline has no stages, or they have not started.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application. From list_applications.

params.name: revision_id
params.description: The revision's `id`, from list_application_revisions.

capabilities.name: list_repository_workflows
capabilities.summary: Read a repository's GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/*.yml), each file whole, to bring one onto Inframan.
capabilities.description:
The first step of moving a repository's CI/CD onto Inframan: read its workflows at a branch, then convert_pipeline the one that builds and deploys (from github to inframan) and read its report, then create_pipeline with it (or with the workflow itself and format: github) and link_pipeline it to the application.

Name the repository by `application_id` (its repository at its branch) or by `owner` and `repo` (`branch` empty for its default). Returns `workflows`: each file's `path`, `name` (its name:), `document` (the file as it is), `url`, and `disable_url` — the workflow's page in the repository's Actions, where a person turns it off (Disable workflow) once Inframan runs it, or every push is built and deployed twice. Nothing is changed in the repository. A file over 256 KiB, or one GitHub would not give, says why in `skipped`; at most 30 files are read (`truncated`).

params.name: application_id
params.description: Read the repository of this application, at its branch. From list_applications.

params.name: owner
params.description: GitHub account that owns the repository, e.g. "acme" in acme/api. With `repo`, in place of application_id.

params.name: repo
params.description: Repository name on its own, e.g. "api".

params.name: branch
params.description: The branch to read, from list_github_branches. Empty: the application's branch, else the repository's default.

params.name: github_app_id
params.description: Optional: which connected App to read through, from get_github_app_status.

capabilities.name: list_service_alerts
capabilities.summary: List every service's own alerts on an infrastructure, by application and service, and whether each is firing.
capabilities.description: Every service's own alerts (inframan.yaml `alerts:`, as get_service_alerts describes them) on one infrastructure, in one read: grouped by application (`applications`, by name; each its `application_id`, `namespace`, `revision_number`, the release whose alerts these are, and `counts`) and then by service (`services`, by name; each its `service_id`, `counts` and `alerts`). Each alert is exactly what get_service_alerts gives of it — its `metric`, `query` or `logs`, `comparison`, `threshold`, `for`, `severity`, `summary`, `expression`, `state` (inactive, pending, firing or unknown) and `state_from`, the `instances` it is pending or firing for with their `value`, its `subject_key` (what start_investigation takes while it fires), `last_fired_at` / `last_resolved_at`, and who hears it (`notify`, `notify_from`, `notify_exists`, `own_notify`); each application also says its own group (`notify`, `notify_exists`), the default group of its alerts and nothing else. The infrastructure's Prometheus' rules and its Loki ruler's rules are each read once for every service listed. `counts` say how many alerts are firing, pending, inactive and unknown, over everything listed and per application and service; `metrics` are the catalogue metrics the alerts read, each with its `title` and `unit`. Only applications whose serving release declares alerts are listed; an empty list says so in `note`. Narrow it with `application_id` (one application) and `service` (the services of that name). This is what an infrastructure's Observability tab lists under Alerts in the console — never the cluster's own default rules, which list_firing_cluster_alerts reads and which notify no one; for one service's alerts with what a form may add, use get_service_alerts.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: application_id
params.description: Only this application's services: its UUID, from list_applications. Refused as not found unless it is on the infrastructure.

params.name: service
params.description: Only the services of this name (of application_id's, where both are given).

capabilities.name: list_service_deployments
capabilities.summary: The build-and-deploy history of one service, newest first.
capabilities.description:
One row per CI/CD run of THIS service: commit, image, status and timings.

Service-scoped, which is the distinction that matters when something did not update. A revision moves every service in an application together, but an image is built per service — so "the api is still serving old code" is answered here, by whether its last run reached DEPLOYED at all.

For the whole instance's run feed use list_deployments; for one run's per-step logs, take a deployment id from here.

Paginated by an opaque cursor, exactly as list_deployments and list_application_deployments are. The reply is an object — {count, deployments, next_cursor} — and next_cursor is the only "you have seen everything" signal: non-empty means there ARE older runs, so pass it back as cursor until it comes back empty. The default page is 10 and a service that deploys on every push passes 10 runs in a day, so a full page here is usually NOT the whole history.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

params.name: limit
params.description:
How many runs per page, newest first. Default 10; anything above 100 `count` is the size of THIS PAGE, not the number of runs that exist — there is no total. Follow next_cursor until it comes back empty if you need them all.

is clamped to 100. Follow next_cursor to read further back rather than asking for a large number.

params.name: cursor
params.description: The next_cursor from a previous call, to read the following page. Omit for the first page.

capabilities.name: list_services
capabilities.summary: List every service in this instance across all applications.
capabilities.description: Each service carries its type and port. A worker that declares a port is a TCP server — a database, a queue, a cache — and carries `address`, host:port, its fixed address inside the cluster, the same across releases: what a connection to it (`service/<app>/<service>`) is valued with. Every other service has none.

capabilities.name: list_storage_access
capabilities.summary: List every service's access to a Storage bucket.
capabilities.description: For one Storage instance, each service that has started the access ceremony, with its status and, while pending, the commands. A service absent from the list has never been granted; start with get_storage_access_setup for it.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The Storage instance, from list_platform_apps.

capabilities.name: open_database_ports
capabilities.summary: Add ports 5432 and 6379 to an infrastructure's ingress load balancer, once.
capabilities.description:
External access to Redis and PostgreSQL arrives on the ingress load balancer's ports 6379 and 5432. Infrastructures created since external access shipped have them; an older one gets them here, once.

On Google Cloud this recreates the load balancer's forwarding rule, so every app on the infrastructure is unreachable for about two minutes. On AWS it adds two listeners and nothing else changes. Nothing is reachable on the new ports until an install's access is opened.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: From list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: open_optimization_pr
capabilities.summary: Make an application's services' optimizer findings by one pull request to its inframan.yaml, and apply them now.
capabilities.description: A service's request changes only by a pull request: the optimizer never changes a customer's service by itself. Given the services a person chose — their findings' workloads (`workload_ids`, service:<service id> each, comma-separated, as get_optimizations lists their findings; `workload_id` for one), all of one application's — or an application (`application_id`: every one of its services), a pass runs now, plans again, and for those services' CPU and memory findings as they stand opens ONE pull request on the application's repository writing them into its inframan.yaml — only the request lines change, in each service's resources or, where its file has environments, this infrastructure's — and applies them at once: on the running pods in place where they take it, else by one release of the application started now (its images and configuration as last served, none of its pipeline). A service with nothing to change is left out. Until the pull request is merged or closed the platform holds the requests over the file. Merging it releases nothing new: the release its merge starts finds what it renders already running, and applies nothing. Closing it lets the change go: the services are released back to what their file asks. Returns the pass, its `pull_requests` (`number`, `url`, `services`) and each finding's outcome. A service is in one open pull request at a time: a named one in another is refused, and an application's are passed over. One pass at a time on an infrastructure.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: workload_ids
params.description: The services' findings' workloads, service:<service id> each, comma-separated: one application's.

params.name: workload_id
params.description: One service's finding's workload, service:<service id>, as get_optimizations names it.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose services' findings to write: every one of them, when no workload is named.

capabilities.name: open_vulnerability_fix_pr
capabilities.summary: Open a pull request that moves a vulnerable package, or the base image, to its fixed version.
capabilities.description:
Fixes what get_service_vulnerabilities found, by a pull request on the service's repository — never by changing anything running. Name one finding (`vulnerability_id`, and `package` where one ID is found in several), or a manifest (`manifest`: a path from that read's repository findings' lockfile, or `Dockerfile`) to fix everything fixable in it.

• A Go module, an npm package or a Poetry package is moved by the ecosystem's own tool (`go get` and `go mod tidy`; `npm install --package-lock-only --ignore-scripts`, a package another pulls in pinned with an override; `poetry add --lock`) in its official image, in a Job of the infrastructure's own cluster that installs nothing and runs no script of the repository's; a pip requirements file has its lines moved. Each version is the lowest fixed one in the installed version's major line. The manifest is the one the repository's scan found the package in: a package only the image has (a tool its base image carries) is not the repository's to fix.
• The image's OS packages are fixed by the Dockerfile's base image: its last stage moves to the newest tag of the same line (same variant, same major — and minor, for a three-number tag). Where the infrastructure builds in its cluster the tag is scanned first, and one that clears none of the findings is not proposed.

Returns the fix at once, `status` running: the pull request opens when its Job is done, a minute or a few, and the fix's `status` (opened, with `pr_url`; nothing, the branch has it already; failed, with `reason`) is in get_service_vulnerabilities' `fixes` and on the application's feed (fix_pr_opened, fix_pr_failed). One fix of a manifest and its packages is open at a time. Merging the pull request releases the service, whose next scan shows what it fixed.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the service, from list_services or get_application.

params.name: vulnerability_id
params.description: The finding to fix: its ID (CVE-…, GHSA-…, GO-…) as get_service_vulnerabilities lists it.

params.name: package
params.description: The finding's package, where one ID is found in several.

params.name: manifest
params.description: Instead of a finding: a lockfile or manifest path from the repository's findings, or Dockerfile, to fix everything fixable in it.

params.name: deployment_id
params.description: The release whose findings to fix, from list_service_deployments. Omit for the serving release.

capabilities.name: preview_agent_template
capabilities.summary: Write an agent from a template: the service's YAML for the name and options you give, and what is wrong with it.
capabilities.description:
Returns `yaml`, the service exactly as it would be written under `services:` of inframan.yaml (its name and its block, two spaces a level), and `problems`, sentences saying why it would be refused as it stands (a required option left empty, a name that cannot be a service's, a name the application or its namespace already has, a model the release would refuse: a connection the infrastructure lacks, or a model nothing prices); empty when it is fine. The options are the template's `fields` (list_agent_templates), each by its key; one you leave out takes its default. The agent's instructions are written into the file (`prompt:`): read them and change them to suit the repository. Nothing is saved or proposed by this.

With `infrastructure_id` and no application: the agent deployed on its own (create_agent_deployment) — `yaml` its service, `manifest` the whole manifest kept as its version 1, and `problems` what would refuse it there (a template whose agent works in a repository, the form, the model, a name an application or the namespace already has). Over a query string a long `knowledge_content` does not fit: give its first lines here, and the whole text to create_agent_deployment.

params.name: template_id
params.description: The template: docs_qa, incident_analyser or issue_to_pr.

params.name: name
params.description: The service's name. The template's default_name where left out.

params.name: application_id
params.description: UUID of the application it would be added to; with it, a name already taken there is a problem.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: With no application_id: the infrastructure an agent deployed on its own would run on.

params.name: knowledge_content
params.description: docs_qa deployed on its own: the text it answers from, kept inline in its manifest.

params.name: knowledge_path
params.description: docs_qa: the folder of the repository the agent answers from. `docs` where left out.

params.name: knowledge_url
params.description: docs_qa: where that folder's pages are published, so the agent links the pages it used.

params.name: auto_domain
params.description: docs_qa: give it an automatic HTTPS address. True where left out.

params.name: slack_secret
params.description: incident_analyser, issue_to_pr: the NAME of an infrastructure secret holding a Slack incoming-webhook URL, where its findings are posted. Never the URL itself.

params.name: open_pull_requests
params.description: incident_analyser: let it open a pull request for a small fix. True where left out; false makes it report only, with no tool that edits.

params.name: model
params.description: Every template: the model the agent calls, as <connection>/<model> (list_agent_templates' `models` suggests them). The default connection's default model where left out.

capabilities.name: preview_chart_application
capabilities.summary: Check a chart application's manifest: render the chart against its cluster and list what it would make and what Inframan refuses, installing nothing.
capabilities.description:
Always call this before create_chart_application, and before saving a changed chart application's manifest. It fetches the chart, renders it as Helm would install it against the infrastructure's cluster (whose API server answers while the infrastructure sleeps), places it on the application node pool, and returns: the objects it would create (hooks marked), the workloads with their replicas, the disks with their sizes, the images, the chart tests left out, `exposes` — each with the value a service connecting to it would be given — and `refusals` — what Inframan refuses and why. Any refusal refuses the whole chart: fix the values (most charts can turn the refused part off) or choose another chart. An expose naming a Service or a port the chart does not make is refused, naming the Services and ports it does make. Secrets are put in as placeholders (<secret NAME>): Check reads no value.

Refused: objects in another namespace, anything past Inframan's edge (a Service of type LoadBalancer or NodePort, an Ingress, Gateway API, Istio or Knative kinds), anything that reaches the node (privileged containers, host namespaces, hostPath, host ports, added capabilities — Pod Security's baseline level), a ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor that reads a file (bearerTokenFile, a TLS file), selects another namespace or writes the labels Prometheus gives a series (honorLabels; a relabeling or targetLabels of namespace, pod, container, node, service, job or instance; a labelmap; a rewrite of __address__), a Secret named inframan-secrets… or chart-<application>-binding, which Inframan keeps, a ServiceAccount's long-lived token Secret, and a resource type of one of Kubernetes' own API groups. Refused too: Inframan's own labels and annotations (`inframan.cloud/…`, `managed-by: inframan`) on the chart's objects, a Service's `externalIPs`, a render too large for Helm to keep its release record, and a namespace or Helm release that is not the application's own.

An operator chart's powers across the whole cluster — its resource types (CRDs), ClusterRoles and their bindings, admission webhooks and policies, any other cluster-wide object — are listed in `powers`, said in words with `risks` to read twice, not refused; with them, where its pods carry them, `runs` (what each of its pods runs, and as whom, with the data of the ConfigMaps and Secrets it reads — the passwords and certificates the chart generates left out), `namespace_roles` and `objects` (each object of `objects` its operator acts on, with the images, accounts and commands it names), which are approved with them. An object of a resource type another chart application brings is in `objects` whoever renders it — that application's operator acts on it — so a chart holding nothing across the cluster needs an approval too when its objects are of such a type. Once the application has been approved (`powers.approved_before`), every version is approved, one holding nothing across the cluster too: its `runs`, the Secrets and ConfigMaps it makes (`config`) and its objects are listed as an operator chart's are; and `kept` names the Secrets, ConfigMaps, Roles and RoleBindings of its namespace a version no admin approved left (and `runs` marks `kept` what it left running, `kept_disks` its disks by name and size), approved as they are now, a Secret's values and a disk's contents never shown; `quiesce` says approving stops what runs in the namespace now, and replaces its service accounts, until the approved version is installed; a pod another operator makes there that runs as an account the chart empowers is in `refusals`. A version making nothing else to approve is approved as a whole (`whole`, `makes`). `approval` is `needed` until an admin of the instance approves them on the application's page (an agent cannot), or `approved` where an earlier approval covers them all. A resource type the cluster has already under another owner — another chart application, the platform — is left as it is (listed in `dropped`, and in `resource_types_left`). `notes` say what Inframan does not do for it, where there is anything: the pods an operator makes from `objects` are not among it, since Inframan gives each that no node takes the node pool's toleration.

Nothing is installed and nothing is kept. Give application_id to check a change to an existing chart application; give infrastructure_id for a new one. The manifest travels in the request's body, as create_chart_application's does, so anything that can be created can be checked first.

It needs the permission creating a chart application needs (application:create), not a read's: it fetches a chart the caller chose and renders it against the infrastructure's cluster. A viewer cannot check one.

params.name: manifest
params.description: The manifest: `version: v1`, `application`, optional `namespace`, and `chart: {repository, name, version, values, node_pool?, timeout_minutes?}`.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Where a new chart application would be installed. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: application_id
params.description: An existing chart application whose change is checked.

capabilities.name: preview_maintenance
capabilities.summary: See what a maintenance pass would lower on an infrastructure, without changing anything.
capabilities.description: Runs a maintenance pass's reads and its decisions and applies nothing: for each platform workload the actor sizes, its primary container's CPU and memory request now (`declared`), the recommender's target for it (`recommended`: VPA's, from its history, which the optimizer seeds from Prometheus when it is installed), and the `decision`: `lower` to `target` (the recommender's), `raise` to `target` (the recommender wants more than it asks, and the actor would raise it: the container used a fifth more than its request over the last 15 minutes, `use_now`; it is raised to that), `keep` or `skip`, with `why`. `use` (the week's CPU 95th percentile and memory peak) and `measured` are the cluster-state monitor's, shown beside it: they set no number. CPU in millicores, memory in MiB. Nothing moves until the recommender's coverage is ready (`plan.coverage`), nor for a workload it has not settled on. Requests only, never a limit; never a first request; never a resource the actor raised in the last 3 hours on nonprod or the last day on prod; nothing under a 5% change. `saving_cpu_milli` and `saving_memory_mi` are what the lowered requests give back, over every replica. Platform workloads only — never a customer's services (their inframan.yaml sizes them) and never a Redis or PostgreSQL instance (its tier does).

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: preview_resource_deletion
capabilities.summary: List what a deployment's deletion could delete: each service, agent, Postgres and Redis, the data it holds, and what refuses it.
capabilities.description:
A deletion is how a deployment's services and agents, and the Postgres and Redis its appstore: declares, are deleted: a release never deletes what a deployment runs because its file stopped declaring it, and a release whose file no longer declares something with no approved deletion naming it fails before anything happens (RELEASE_WOULD_DELETE).

Read this first, and tell the user what goes and what is kept. For each resource: its kind (service, or appstore for a Postgres or a Redis the file declares under appstore:, with its installed_app_id), its type (web, worker, job or agent; postgres or redis), its data (a disk with its size; a Postgres's database, whose backups and password can be kept; a Redis's volume, which cannot; or none) and whether a keep-data choice applies, whether it can be deleted and, when not, why — CONNECTED_FROM_OUTSIDE (a service of another application connects to it), DELETION_PENDING (a deletion names it already), LAST_RESOURCE (it is every service the deployment runs: delete the deployment instead; never a Postgres or a Redis) — and every service connecting to it. A connection from a service of the same application refuses it only unless that service is deleted too. Also: the applications of its group (one per infrastructure; the file is shared, so a deletion covers each), its open config pull request, which blocks a deletion, the deletions pending or approved, its default branch and its last release's branch.

Connections are what each service last released; delete_application_resources checks the file again. A Helm chart and an agent deployment are refused here (NOT_DELETABLE_HERE): a chart's resources are its own, and an agent deployment is deleted whole.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The deployment (an application, a repository's or of images). From list_applications.

capabilities.name: provision_infrastructure
capabilities.summary: Provision a new environment: private GKE cluster, VPC, registry, load balancer and the platform stack.
capabilities.description:
Builds a whole environment inside the customer's own GCP project: a VPC with subnet, Cloud NAT and firewall rules; a PRIVATE GKE cluster with the node pools you pass plus the platform's own system pool; an Artifact Registry; a load balancer; and on top of it a LEAN platform: the Istio ingress/routing engine, cert-manager, CI/CD, and Google-managed observability. Knative (scale-to-zero) and the in-cluster Prometheus/Loki/Tempo stack are platform apps installed afterwards from the infrastructure's Apps tab when wanted, not part of provisioning.

THIS CREATES REAL, BILLABLE CLOUD RESOURCES. A cluster with a couple of always-on nodes costs money every hour it exists, and nothing here is a dry run. It is also LONG-RUNNING — ten to twenty minutes — and this call returns as soon as the workflow starts, not when the cluster is usable.

PAUSES ONCE FOR THE PERSON, right after the GKE cluster is created and before anything is installed on it: the grants the infrastructure's apps need and Inframan will not make (the CI/CD builder account, and for cloud Monitoring its read and write grants), as one script. get_infrastructure_status shows `state.phase` needs_setup; get_provisioning_setup gives the script. Show it to the person, wait for them to say they ran it, then call verify_provisioning_setup — a pass resumes provisioning on its own.

ASK THE USER FIRST. Do not guess any of these; a wrong answer is not a wrong argument, it is a cluster that has to be torn down by hand:
1. `name` — what to call the environment, e.g. "prod" or "platform".
2. `region` — which GCP region, e.g. "asia-south1". This decides latency and price and cannot be changed afterwards.
3. `tag` — "prod" or "nonprod". prod gets a REGIONAL cluster (nodes across three zones) and Knative with scale-to-zero disabled; nonprod gets a zonal cluster and Spot nodes to save cost. This is a cost and availability decision, not a label.
4. `node_pools` — at least one APPLICATION pool, with a machine type and node bounds. This is the bulk of the bill.
5. CIDRs — ask whether they have an existing network these must not overlap. An overlapping range is refused by GCP well into the run and the failure is PERMANENT: retrying cannot fix it, the record has to be reset and provisioned again.

Also call list_cloud_accounts first — `cloud_account_id` names the GCP project this is built in, and there is nothing to infer it from. Its effective_status must be verified: any other account is refused with the step that fixes it (needs_update: the user reruns its setup, then verify_cloud_account).

node_pools is a JSON ARRAY, passed as a string. A complete example:

    node_pools = "[{\"name\":\"application-pool\",\"machine_type\":\"e2-standard-4\",\"min_node_count\":1,\"max_node_count\":3,\"initial_node_count\":1,\"disk_size_gb\":50,\"disk_type\":\"pd-balanced\",\"spot\":false}]"

Only `name`, `machine_type` and `max_node_count` are required per pool; the rest default to 50GB pd-balanced, on-demand (non-Spot), with auto-repair and auto-upgrade on. The field names are exact — `min_node_count` and `max_node_count`, NOT min_nodes/max_nodes, which are silently read as zero.

WHAT YOU DO NOT PASS: the system pool (the platform adds it; istiod and the ingress gateway are pinned to it by taint — the monitoring pool now belongs to the Observability app and appears only when that app is installed), the cluster name (generated), or which platform apps to install (the lean default set is fixed; Serverless and Observability are added later from the infrastructure's Apps tab in the console — a console operation).

`zero_trust` (default false) is the security posture: Network Policy on the cluster, an Istio sidecar in every application pod, and per-service mTLS/authorization policies. It costs about one extra system node plus ~100m CPU per pod, and it is CREATE-TIME ONLY — Network Policy recreates node pools on a running cluster. Ask the user; do not default it on.

`secret_manager` (default true) keeps the infrastructure's secrets — infrastructure secrets, secret env-group variables, the passwords of Redis, PostgreSQL, Grafana, LikeC4 and pgweb — in the cloud account's secret manager. Leave it on unless the user asks: off is only allowed for a zero-trust infrastructure on Google Cloud that the instance reaches across its hub, and is refused anywhere else (code `secret_manager_required`), because there the infrastructure's certificate authority is kept in Secret Manager. On, its grants join the cloud account's setup: an infrastructure read through its gateway is refused until the account holds them (the user reruns the account's setup, then verify_cloud_account); a zero-trust one is created, and what needs Secret Manager on it waits for the account — the answer's message says so. Off, the grants leave the account's setup unless another of its infrastructures has Secret Manager on.

Node counts feed the pod-CIDR budget. GKE pre-allocates two IPs per pod per node, so the pod range has to cover the platform pools plus your pools at their maximum. A pod_cidr too small for the pools you asked for is refused up front with the arithmetic — widen the range or lower max_node_count rather than retrying.

HOW MANY: a managed instance runs ONE infrastructure per cloud; on the central hosting there is no limit (get_infrastructure_limit says which). Call list_infrastructures first: on a managed instance a second on the same cloud is refused, and the answer is not to retry it.

Afterwards, poll get_infrastructure_status until it reads READY. Do not create applications or attach domains before then. On an in-cluster infrastructure, READY may come with `build_identity`: builds need one command the user runs, and the first release waits on it.

params.name: cloud_account_id
params.description: UUID of the linked GCP account to build in, from list_cloud_accounts. This decides which project is billed.

params.name: name
params.description: Name for the environment, lowercase, e.g. "prod". Seeds the VPC, subnet and cluster names and cannot be changed later. ASK THE USER.

params.name: region
params.description: GCP region, e.g. "asia-south1" or "us-central1". Fixed once provisioned. ASK THE USER — do not default to one.

params.name: tag
params.description: "prod" or "nonprod". prod builds a regional (3-zone) cluster on on-demand nodes; anything else is treated as nonprod — zonal, Spot nodes. A cost and availability choice: ASK THE USER.

params.name: zero_trust
params.description: Enable the zero-trust posture (Network Policy + mesh sidecars + per-service mTLS/authz policies). On a managed instance it also makes the GKE control plane private: reachable only across the instance's own network hub, which the first zero-trust infrastructure creates and which is billed while any exists. Without it the control plane is public, allow-listed to Inframan's address alone, and no hub is created. Default false. It cannot be changed after provisioning in this release. ASK THE USER.

params.name: cicd_type
params.description: Where this infrastructure's images are built: "builder-vm" (Inframan's pool of ephemeral build machines) or "in-cluster" (a Job on a dedicated, network-isolated node pool of the infrastructure itself, in the customer's project). Omit for the default, in-cluster. Fixed for the life of the infrastructure. In-cluster builds are Dockerfile builds only. builder-vm is GCP's, and the central hosting does not offer it: there every infrastructure builds in its own cluster (get_infrastructure_limit's `cicd_types`).

params.name: secret_manager
params.description: Keep the infrastructure's secrets in the cloud account's secret manager. Default true. false is only allowed with zero_trust on a Google Cloud account of a managed instance (the one infrastructure that reads its monitoring across the hub) and is refused anywhere else. Leave it out unless the user asks.

params.name: node_pools
params.description: JSON array of APPLICATION node pools, as a string. On a GCP cloud account each is a class of Inframan's Karpenter, which places the services on the cheapest machine of its series that fits them: `name`, `machine_series` (e2 or n2d), `spot`, `cpu_limit` (its vCPU in total, a multiple of 2) and an optional `disk_size_gb` (each node's disk, 20 to 500 GB, 50 when omitted), e.g. [{"name":"application-pool","machine_series":"e2","spot":true,"cpu_limit":16}]. A GKE pool by its machine type is still taken — `name`, `machine_type` and `max_node_count`, with optional `min_node_count`, `initial_node_count`, `disk_size_gb`, `disk_type` and `spot` — e.g. [{"name":"application-pool","machine_type":"e2-standard-4","min_node_count":1,"max_node_count":3}]. The platform's system and monitoring pools are added for you — do not list them. On an AWS cloud account a pool is a Karpenter NodePool instead: `name`, `spot` (Spot or on-demand), `instance_cpus` (any of 2, 4, 8, 16), `instance_families` (any of c, m, r, t), `cpu_limit` (the pool's total vCPU) and an optional `disk_size_gb` (each node's disk, 20 to 500 GiB, 50 when omitted), e.g. [{"name":"application-pool","spot":true,"instance_cpus":[2,4],"instance_families":["c","m"],"cpu_limit":16}]; machine types and node counts do not apply there.

params.name: primary_cidr
params.description: Subnet range for the nodes, e.g. "10.1.0.0/20". Must not overlap any network the user already has. Ask before defaulting.

params.name: pod_cidr
params.description: Secondary range for pod IPs, e.g. "10.1.16.0/20". Sized against the node pools' maximum node counts — too small and provisioning is refused. Ask before defaulting.

params.name: service_cidr
params.description: Secondary range for Kubernetes service IPs, e.g. "10.1.32.0/20". Must not overlap the other two or an existing network.

capabilities.name: query_logs
capabilities.summary: Run your own LogQL against an infrastructure, for what get_logs cannot reach.
capabilities.description:
For an application's logs use get_logs first: it resolves names the way the console does. Use this for the rest — platform components (namespaces istio-ingress, kube-system, cert-manager, the CI build pods), several namespaces at once, one pod, or a query get_logs cannot say.

`query` is LogQL, run on the infrastructure's own Loki: a stream selector with filters — `{namespace="istio-ingress"}` or `{namespace="shop", pod=~"api-.*"} |~ "error|panic"` (labels: namespace, pod, container) — or a metric query, e.g. `sum by (pod) (rate({namespace="shop"} |= "error" [5m]))`, which answers like Prometheus. Lines come back newest first, with namespace, pod and container.

Kubernetes events are here too, kept for the logs' retention where the cluster forgets them after an hour — why a pod was not scheduled (FailedScheduling), backed off, failed a probe (Unhealthy), could not mount or pull, was evicted or preempted, or a node went NotReady: `{namespace="shop", job="kubernetes-events"}`, one stream a namespace (a Node's and other cluster-wide objects' under `{job="kubernetes-events"}` alone). Each line is logfmt naming the object and what happened — `name=`, `kind=`, `reason=`, `type=`, `count=`, `msg=` — so narrow with `| logfmt | kind="Pod", name=~"api-.*"` or `|= "reason=BackOff"`.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure whose logs to query. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: query
params.description: LogQL: a stream selector with filters, or a metric query.

params.name: minutes
params.description: How far back to look, in minutes. Default 60, up to 10080 (7 days). With `around`, how far either side of it: default 10.

params.name: around
params.description: Optional moment, RFC 3339 (e.g. "2026-11-11T10:04:05.123Z"): read the `minutes` either side of it (10 by default) in place of the last `minutes`. The newest `limit` lines of that window come back; narrow `minutes` or raise `limit` to reach those before it.

params.name: limit
params.description: Maximum lines or rows to return. Default 100, maximum 1000.

capabilities.name: query_loki_logs
capabilities.summary: Run a log query against Loki and return its response verbatim.
capabilities.description:
Accepts an application name — with a service or one version of it, and the infrastructure the page shows, which must be the application's — and resolves the namespace, container and cluster server-side, as get_logs does; or a raw LogQL selector against the named infrastructure. `level` narrows to one level across the whole window.

Console only. Agents use get_logs, which takes the same names, applies the line filter and returns readable lines instead of Loki's stream envelope.

params.name: query
params.description: Raw LogQL stream selector, e.g. {namespace="x"}. Omit if passing `application` instead.

params.name: application
params.description: Application name to resolve a selector from, instead of `query`.

params.name: service
params.description: Optional service name, narrowing `application` to one service's containers.

params.name: version
params.description: Optional version, e.g. "api-v7": that version's container alone.

params.name: level
params.description: Optional level: error, warn, info or debug. A pre-filter Loki applies to every line of the window; each line's own level is read by the caller.

params.name: start
params.description: Window start, as Loki accepts it (unix seconds or nanoseconds).

params.name: end
params.description: Window end, as Loki accepts it (unix seconds or nanoseconds).

params.name: limit
params.description: Maximum log lines to return. Defaults to 100.

params.name: direction
params.description: "backward" (default) for the window's newest lines first, or "forward" for its oldest first — how a live tail reads on from where it left off without skipping a burst over the limit.

params.name: infra_id
params.description: Infrastructure whose Loki to query. With `application`, the application's own, or the read is refused; with a raw `query`, omit for the latest one.

capabilities.name: query_metrics
capabilities.summary: Run your own PromQL against an infrastructure's metrics, for what get_metric's catalog does not cover.
capabilities.description:
For an application's CPU, memory, requests or latency use get_metric first: it builds the query the console's charts use and knows Knative's naming. Use this when the catalog cannot answer — platform components (namespaces istio-ingress, kube-system, cert-manager), nodes, the cluster as a whole, your own aggregation or ratio.

It runs on the infrastructure's own Prometheus, which holds this cluster only, and it keeps only the names below: every scrape job drops the rest as it scrapes, so a name not listed has no series — do not guess one. Requests are counted at the Istio ingress (job="monitoring/inframan-ingress-gateway") on an infrastructure without zero trust, and at each service's sidecar (namespace!="istio-ingress") on a zero-trust one. What is there, by job: cAdvisor (the kubelet) (job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics/cadvisor"): container_cpu_usage_seconds_total, container_cpu_cfs_periods_total, container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total, container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total, container_spec_cpu_quota, container_spec_cpu_period, container_memory_working_set_bytes, container_memory_rss, container_memory_max_usage_bytes, container_spec_memory_limit_bytes, container_oom_events_total, container_start_time_seconds, container_fs_usage_bytes, container_fs_limit_bytes, container_fs_reads_bytes_total, container_fs_writes_bytes_total, container_network_receive_bytes_total, container_network_transmit_bytes_total, container_network_receive_packets_dropped_total, container_network_transmit_packets_dropped_total, container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total, container_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total, container_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total. the kubelet (job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics"): kubelet_volume_stats_*, kubelet_evictions, kubelet_running_pods, kubelet_running_containers, kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total. the kubelet's probes (job="kubelet", metrics_path="/metrics/probes"): prober_probe_total. kube-state-metrics (job="kube-state-metrics"): kube_pod_container_status_*, kube_pod_container_info, kube_pod_container_resource_requests, kube_pod_container_resource_limits, kube_pod_info, kube_pod_owner, kube_pod_created, kube_pod_status_phase, kube_pod_status_ready, kube_pod_status_reason, kube_pod_status_scheduled, kube_pod_status_unschedulable, kube_replicaset_owner, kube_node_*, kube_deployment_*, kube_statefulset_replicas, kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready, kube_daemonset_status_desired_number_scheduled, kube_daemonset_status_number_unavailable, kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_*, kube_job_status_*, kube_job_owner, kube_cronjob_status_last_schedule_time, kube_persistentvolumeclaim_status_phase, kube_persistentvolumeclaim_created, kube_persistentvolumeclaim_resource_requests_storage_bytes. node-exporter (job="node-exporter"): node_cpu_seconds_total, node_load1, node_load5, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes, node_memory_MemTotal_bytes, node_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total, node_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total, node_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total, node_vmstat_oom_kill, node_boot_time_seconds, node_filesystem_avail_bytes, node_filesystem_size_bytes, node_filesystem_files_free, node_filesystem_files, node_disk_io_time_seconds_total, node_network_receive_drop_total, node_network_transmit_drop_total, node_network_receive_errs_total, node_network_transmit_errs_total. Alertmanager (job="prometheus-operator-kube-p-alertmanager"): alertmanager_notifications_total, alertmanager_notifications_failed_total, alertmanager_alerts. the Prometheus operator (job="prometheus-operator-kube-p-operator"): prometheus_operator_reconcile_errors_total. Loki (job="loki"): loki_distributor_bytes_received_total, loki_distributor_lines_received_total, loki_discarded_samples_total. Tempo (job="tempo"): tempo_distributor_spans_received_total, tempo_discarded_spans_total, tempo_ingester_live_traces, tempodb_compaction_errors_total. istiod (job="istiod"): pilot_xds_pushes, pilot_total_xds_rejects, pilot_proxy_convergence_time_bucket. cert-manager (job="cert-manager"): certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds, certmanager_certificate_ready_status. KEDA's operator (job="keda/keda-operator"): keda_*. Kept whole: the Istio sidecars and ingress gateway (istio_requests_total, istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket), Knative (kn_*), the Postgres (cnpg_*; cnpg_pg_settings_setting only for name in max_connections, shared_buffers, work_mem, max_wal_size) and Redis (redis_*) exporters, and every series of a customer's own monitors. Anything else is not scraped: a name not listed here has no series. To list what a namespace has, ask `group by (__name__) ({namespace="istio-ingress"})`.

Omit `minutes` for an instant query — the value now. Set it for a range over the last N minutes, about 60 points per series. Prefer an aggregation (sum by, topk) to raw series: large answers are cut to the first series.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure whose metrics to query. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: query
params.description: PromQL, e.g. `sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[5m]))`.

params.name: minutes
params.description: Range over the last N minutes, up to 10080 (7 days). Omit for an instant query.

params.name: step
params.description: Seconds between points of a range. Default: the range divided into about 60.

capabilities.name: query_prometheus_instant
capabilities.summary: Run a raw PromQL instant query and return Prometheus's response verbatim.
capabilities.description: The console's single-value path — gauges and stat tiles. Console only; agents use get_metric, which resolves the query from a metric name.

params.name: query
params.description: PromQL expression to evaluate at the current instant.

params.name: infra_id
params.description: Infrastructure whose Prometheus to query. Omit for the latest one.

capabilities.name: query_prometheus_range
capabilities.summary: Run a raw PromQL range query and return Prometheus's response verbatim.
capabilities.description: The console's charting path: it composes PromQL in the browser and renders the matrix response directly. Console only — agents use get_metric, which takes a metric NAME and the application, and returns points rather than an envelope.

params.name: query
params.description: PromQL expression to evaluate over the window.

params.name: start
params.description: Window start: unix seconds or RFC3339, as Prometheus accepts.

params.name: end
params.description: Window end: unix seconds or RFC3339, as Prometheus accepts.

params.name: step
params.description: Resolution step, e.g. "60" or "1m".

params.name: infra_id
params.description: Infrastructure whose Prometheus to query. Omit for the latest one.

capabilities.name: reactivate_application
capabilities.summary: Bring a deactivated application back: release it again and mark it active.
capabilities.description:
The undo for deactivate_application. The application comes back through a release — the same machinery as a deploy, so everything its services need is made again: the namespace, env, secrets from the secret manager, connections, the workload identity's account — and the record is marked active only once that release serves. It shows as a new revision.

By default (source=last_image) the release runs the images, and the inframan.yaml configuration, of the revision that last served; nothing is built. Pushes that arrive while an application is inactive are not released; each one that would have released it is kept on its activity feed, and get_application shows the newest as unreleased_push, with how many arrived. source=latest_push releases that push instead, exactly as its webhook would have, building what changed. Either way a release that fails leaves the application inactive, with the failure on its activity feed. Ask the user which they want when there is an unreleased_push.

Only for an INACTIVE application. One that is already active is reported as such rather than redeployed — use restart_application to restart a serving one. One none of whose revisions ever served has nothing to bring back; deploy it instead. Refused while the traffic mode is fixed or split, under which a new revision does not serve.

THIS RETURNS BEFORE THE APPLICATION IS SERVING. It starts a workflow that runs the release — minutes, not seconds — so a successful reply means the reactivation STARTED. Confirm with list_applications or get_application: the status is active only once the services are actually back.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The inactive application to bring back. From list_applications, which includes inactive applications by default.

params.name: source
params.description: "last_image" (the default) releases the images and configuration of the revision that last served; "latest_push" releases the application's unreleased_push instead, and is refused when it has none.

capabilities.name: reconcile_infrastructure_ca
capabilities.summary: Create an infrastructure's certificate authority, which Redis external access needs, by reconciling its gateway.
capabilities.description:
Redis external access serves an install's hostname with a certificate signed by the infrastructure's certificate authority, which the gateway app's infrastructure-ca component keeps: the CA in the cloud account's secret manager, made once and never replaced, and the Issuer that signs with it. The gateway leaves it out on an infrastructure that needs none for monitoring, and opening Redis access there is refused until it exists.
