This reconciles that one component, even where the gateway would leave it out, and nothing else on the gateway changes, so nothing serving traffic restarts; the gateway keeps the CA from then on. It returns once the reconcile starts; the gateway reads updating until it ends, and access can be opened then. Refused with 409 while another change to the gateway runs. Creating the CA acts in the cloud account's secret manager, so it needs the infrastructure's Secret Manager: refused with code `secret_manager_off` while it is off, and with `cloud_account_not_ready`, naming the grants, until the account's setup is re-run and verified for them.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: From list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: refresh_infrastructure_quotas
capabilities.summary: Read an infrastructure's quotas again now, and wake what they held once they have room.
capabilities.description: Reads the infrastructure's cloud quotas fresh and asks its holds workflow to look at once: the owner of every held resource whose quotas now have room is woken to make it (the node class passes, a component is reconciled). Returns what get_infrastructure_quotas does, read fresh, with fitting: the holds whose needs fit now. Use it after a quota was raised; changes nothing in the cloud account.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: register_cloud_account
capabilities.summary: Start adding a GCP project or an AWS account as a cloud account: records it and returns the setup commands to run.
capabilities.description:
Named register, not create, because the platform creates nothing in GCP. Inframan does not create service accounts and does not grant IAM in a customer's project — it hands over the exact gcloud commands and then verifies the result.

This is step 1 of 3. It writes a PENDING row, derives every account name from that row's id, and returns `setup`: an ordered list of steps (each a command with the reason for it) and one pasteable script. Step 2 is the USER running them, in Cloud Shell or any authenticated terminal — you cannot run them and must not claim to have. Step 3 is verify_cloud_account, which checks the result by acting as the account.

Creating an infrastructure against an unverified account is REFUSED, with the reason. So the order is not advisory: register, hand over the script, wait for the user to say they have run it, verify, then provision.

For AWS (cloud "aws", only where this instance runs an AWS worker) the setup is an AWS CLI script for CloudShell in that account: it creates the role Inframan acts as, trusting only this instance's own identity, the roles EKS and its nodes run as, and the service-linked roles EKS needs. No AWS key is ever created.

params.name: name
params.description: Display name for the account, e.g. "production". Free text, shown in the console.

params.name: cloud
params.description: "gcp" (the default) or "aws". AWS is refused on an instance that runs no AWS worker.

params.name: gcp_project_id
params.description: For GCP: the project id infrastructure will be provisioned into, e.g. "acme-prod-4821". The setup commands run against this project.

params.name: aws_account_id
params.description: For AWS: the 12-digit account id infrastructure will be provisioned into. The setup script refuses to run in any other account.

capabilities.name: remove_agent_connection
capabilities.summary: Remove one of an infrastructure's model connections.
capabilities.description: Refused (409) while an agent's release calls through the connection, naming the agents: point each at another connection in its inframan.yaml and release it first. Refused for the default connection while the infrastructure has others: make another the default first. Removing an API key connection reconciles the Agents app, which takes the key out of the gateway's Secret; the infrastructure secret itself is left as it is.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: name
params.description: The connection's name, from get_agent_connections.

capabilities.name: remove_chart_resource_types
capabilities.summary: Remove the resource types a deactivated operator chart brought, and every object of each in the cluster.
capabilities.description: People only, an admin of the instance, once the application is deactivated so its operator is gone. Each resource type named — every one it brought where none is named — is deleted, and with it every object of it in the cluster. Refused for a type another chart application brings or uses, or another manager has a hand in; every type is checked before any is deleted, so a refusal removes none. `confirm` must be true. The outcome, with what was removed, is on the application's feed.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The deactivated chart application.

params.name: names
params.description: Comma-separated CRD names, from get_chart_resource_types; empty for all.

params.name: confirm
params.description: true: every object of each type is deleted.

capabilities.name: remove_console_domain
capabilities.summary: Stop serving this Inframan console on a hostname, removing it from the VM's Caddy config.
capabilities.description:
Takes an address AWAY FROM THE CONSOLE. Nothing deployed is affected — a service's own domain is detached by the application-domain tooling, not here.

The Caddyfile is regenerated without the hostname and hot-reloaded, so the console stops answering on it within seconds. REMOVING THE ADDRESS PEOPLE ARE CURRENTLY USING LOCKS THEM OUT OF THE CONSOLE, and re-adding it means waiting for a fresh certificate. Check which hostname the user is on before removing anything, and leave the default `*.console.inframan.cloud` address in place — it is the way back in when a custom domain's DNS or certificate fails.

Removing the default domain also deletes its DNS record.

params.name: domain
params.description: The exact console hostname to stop serving, as returned by list_console_domains.

capabilities.name: renew_license
capabilities.summary: Check this instance's license again now, instead of waiting for the next cycle.
capabilities.description: Forces one license renewal for this instance and returns the fresh state (the same fields as get_license, plus `renew_error` if the renewal itself failed). Use it after a lapsed or suspended license has been set right, so the instance picks it up at once rather than at its next scheduled check. It changes no entitlement — that is set in the console or by Inframan — it only re-reads and records what the instance holds.

capabilities.name: replay_release
capabilities.summary: Release a failed release's commit again: every service of the application, as a fresh release.
capabilities.description:
For a release that failed on something since put right — a domain added, a secret set, an infrastructure fixed, a flaky build — run again without pushing a new commit. It starts a new release of the SAME commit, through the same path a push takes: every service is built (or reuses the commit's image) and deployed, and the release takes traffic like any push would.

WHICH RELEASE. Name `deployment_id` (any run of it, from list_deployments or list_application_deployments) or `commit` (full or short; the newest release of that commit is used). The replay is built on the branch the release was pushed on.

REFUSED while the application has a release running (wait for it, or stop_release first), for a release that shipped (its revision is active or retired — there is nothing to replay), and for a release that recorded no commit.

THIS RETURNS AS SOON AS THE RELEASE STARTS — minutes, not seconds, before it serves. Follow it with list_application_deployments.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose release to replay. From list_applications.

params.name: deployment_id
params.description: Any run of the failed release, from list_deployments.

params.name: commit
params.description: The failed release's commit, full or short. The other way to name it.

capabilities.name: rescan_images
capabilities.summary: Check an infrastructure's images in use again now, or an application's or a service's.
capabilities.description:
Each infrastructure checks its images in use again once a day (get_infrastructure_vulnerabilities). This asks for that look now: what the cluster runs is read again — an image replaced since the last look leaves the list, a new one is inventoried — and what the ask covers is matched again against the Trivy server's database whatever it was last matched against: every image in use, or with `application_id` or `service_id` that application's or service's serving release, its image and its repository.

It returns at once: the look runs in the infrastructure (a few minutes; match Jobs in its cluster). get_image_rescan says whether it is `looking`; once it is not, the vulnerability tools read what it found. `waiting` says why it cannot look now — the infrastructure asleep, waking or not ready — and the look runs when it can. `known` false means the loop runs code from before asks, which answers at its next daily look.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: application_id
params.description: Match again only this application's services' images, of an application on the infrastructure.

params.name: service_id
params.description: Match again only this service's image and repository, of a service on the infrastructure.

capabilities.name: reset_infrastructure_status
capabilities.summary: Force an infrastructure record back to NEVER_PROVISIONED, abandoning whatever was built.
capabilities.description:
A DATABASE WRITE ONLY, and the most misleading operation in this group. Nothing is destroyed, nothing is reconciled, no workflow is cancelled — the record is relabelled as though the environment had never been provisioned.

Everything the failed or half-finished run already created stays exactly where it is: the VPC and its Cloud NAT, the GKE cluster and its node pools, the load balancer, the Artifact Registry, the Terraform state bucket. They keep running and keep being billed, and the record that named them is now gone, so nothing on this platform can find them again. Cleaning them up becomes a manual job in the GCP console.

That is what it is for: unsticking a record whose real state the platform can no longer reason about, so an operator who has decided to start over can. It is not a cleanup and it is not an undo.

To recover a failed run, use retry_infrastructure_provisioning — it reuses the same resources instead of orphaning them.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure whose status to reset, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: restart_application
capabilities.summary: Restart the services of one serving revision, keeping the same version.
capabilities.description:
Bounces the running pods. The deployed image and configuration are unchanged — this is the one to reach for when a service is wedged rather than wrong.

IT RESTARTS A REVISION, NOT "THE APPLICATION". With one revision serving that is the same thing and revision_id is unnecessary. Under a SPLIT it is not: every revision carrying traffic would be bounced, including the stable side you were deliberately not touching, so the call is REFUSED until you name one. The error lists what is serving with its percentage — pick from that rather than guessing, and if the user has not said which, ask.

Configuration is not re-read. The stored manifest is reapplied with a restart annotation, so a change made since that release will NOT take effect — push it and let the release carry it.

NO DOWNTIME. The replacement pods are brought up and waited on first, and only then does the route move to them — the revision that was serving keeps serving until that point. If the replacement never becomes ready the route is never moved, so a restart that fails leaves users exactly where they were.

A service with min_replicas: 0 is a different matter: it has nothing running to replace, and the next visitor after any idle period pays the usual cold start. That is scale-to-zero, not the restart.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to restart. From list_applications.

params.name: revision_id
params.description: Which serving revision to bounce, from list_application_revisions. Optional when exactly one revision serves; REQUIRED when more than one does. A revision with no traffic is rejected — it has no pods to restart.

capabilities.name: restore_activity_event
capabilities.summary: Put a dismissed activity event back into the default feed view.
capabilities.description:
The exact inverse of dismiss_activity_event: the event becomes visible again without asking for dismissed ones. Nothing else changes.

Find a dismissed event by calling list_application_activity with include_dismissed=true.

params.name: event_id
params.description: Id of the dismissed activity event to restore.

capabilities.name: retry_addon_install
capabilities.summary: Retry a failed Redis or Postgres install, in place.
capabilities.description:
Re-runs an install that ended in `failed`, reusing everything it was originally given — name, tier, memory. Takes only the installed_app_id, so it cannot create anything new: no name to mistype, no size to re-specify.

Only `failed` installs. A ready one has nothing to retry; a pending or installing one already has a workflow running and re-kicking it would race two reconciles against the same node pool state. Both are refused with the current status.

Read the failure before retrying. `get_installed_app` carries the reason in `error_message`, and most of them do not fix themselves — a CPUS_ALL_REGIONS quota error means the project has no room for the node, so retrying without freeing capacity or raising the quota fails identically. Retry is for transient failures and for after you have fixed the cause.

Takes MINUTES and returns as soon as the workflow starts; poll get_installed_app for the outcome.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The failed install, from list_platform_apps or get_installed_app. Not a catalog app id and not an instance name.

capabilities.name: retry_domain
capabilities.summary: Re-run certificate issuance for a domain whose HTTPS setup failed.
capabilities.description:
For a `failed` domain only — a pending or active one is refused, because retrying one that is already working would replace a live certificate for no reason.

Fix the cause FIRST. The cause is almost always the DNS A record: missing, not yet propagated, or pointing at a different infrastructure's load-balancer IP (read the right one from list_domains). This call re-verifies DNS before it does anything, so retrying against an unchanged record just fails the same way.

Nothing is destroyed and nothing is duplicated: the same domain record goes back to `pending` and the ACME challenge runs again. Poll get_domain_status afterwards. Do not add the domain again instead — it is still registered and a second add is rejected.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the domain belongs to, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: domain_id
params.description: UUID of the failed domain, from list_domains.

capabilities.name: retry_infrastructure_provisioning
capabilities.summary: Re-run provisioning for an infrastructure that failed, using the configuration it already has.
capabilities.description:
For a FAILED or NEVER_PROVISIONED infrastructure only — anything else is refused, so this cannot disturb a cluster that is working or a run that is still going.

Takes no configuration. The region, CIDRs, node pools and platform app set are read back from the record written when it was first requested, so this re-runs what a human already approved. Terraform reconciles whatever the failed run left behind rather than building a second copy of it.

FIX THE CAUSE FIRST. Read `status_message` from get_infrastructure_status. Several of the common failures cannot be fixed by retrying at all — a pod or subnet CIDR that overlaps an existing network, an exhausted quota, a missing IAM permission on the cloud account. Retrying those spends another ten to twenty minutes reaching the same error. A retry is worth it when the failure was transient: a lease that expired, an API that was slow, a worker that died mid-run.

Real cloud resources are created again, and the record goes back to PROVISIONING. Poll get_infrastructure_status afterwards.

If a previous run is somehow still executing, it is terminated and replaced rather than racing this one.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the failed infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: reveal_addon_password
capabilities.summary: Show a Redis or PostgreSQL install's password while its external access is open, or Grafana's admin, LikeC4's or pgweb's sign-in password.
capabilities.description: The password is kept in the cloud account's own secret manager. The cloud's reader reads it as the account and returns it here over gRPC — never through Temporal — and nothing stores it. For Redis and PostgreSQL only while the install's external access is open; for Grafana it is the `admin` user's password, for LikeC4 the `likec4` user's and for pgweb the `pgweb` user's, whatever their address. Who was shown it, and when, is recorded on the install and as an activity event.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The install, from get_installed_app.

capabilities.name: rotate_agent_webhook
capabilities.summary: Make an on-demand agent's webhook URL, or a new one; the URL is shown once.
capabilities.description: For an agent whose file has a webhook trigger: makes its URL, or replaces it, and returns it once. Only a hash of its token is kept, so it cannot be read again; the URL before it stops working at once. A POST to the URL starts a run with the request's body (at most 256 KiB) as the run's payload and answers 202 with the run's ID; at most sixty a minute.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the agent: the ID of its service, from list_agents.

capabilities.name: run_agent
capabilities.summary: Start a run of an on-demand agent now, with an optional input.
capabilities.description: An on-demand agent (`mode` `on_demand` in list_agents) runs as a Job in its cluster: a model with the agent's instructions, knowledge and tools, in a workspace that holds its application's repository where its file asks for it, until it ends with a summary. `input` is what this run should do, in your words (at most 16,000 characters); without it the agent does what its instructions say. A run started so needs none of its triggers, nor a trigger's phrase. Returns the `run` as it was recorded, `queued`: at most the agent's `limits.concurrency` runs run at once (1 by default) and the rest wait their turn. Read it with get_agent_run until its `status` is one it ends with. Refused for an always-on agent (400); while its infrastructure sleeps (409, code `infrastructure_asleep`: wake it first); while the agent is not released or its infrastructure has no model connection (409, `agents_not_ready`); and while ten runs of it already wait (429, `queue_full`). A run spends on the infrastructure's model connection, up to the agent's per-run budget.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the agent: the ID of its service, from list_agents.

params.name: input
params.description: What this run should do, in plain words. Optional.

capabilities.name: run_maintenance_pass
capabilities.summary: Apply every finding of the optimizer on an infrastructure now.
capabilities.description: Runs a maintenance pass now, whatever the optimizer's mode: the decisions preview_maintenance shows, made. Each lowered request is sent to its component's actor, which lowers it on the running pods in place and declares it; where the pods will not take it live it is declared for the component's next rollout, and nothing is restarted. Each raise is reported to its actor, which raises it to what the container uses now, rolling the workload out where the pods will not take it live. Read get_maintenance_pass for what each actor did. One pass at a time on an infrastructure.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: save_application_manifest
capabilities.summary: Keep a new version of an image or chart application's manifest and release it.
capabilities.description:
Replaces the whole document: read it with get_application_manifest, change it, send it back. It is validated as inframan.yaml is — `application:` and `namespace` cannot change, every service of an image application must be an `image:`, no service may be named as another application's service in the namespace (SERVICE_NAME_TAKEN), and every alert group its `notify:` names — the application's, beside `services:`, and each alert's — must be one of the instance's (ALERT_GROUP_NOT_FOUND; list_alert_groups); a chart application's manifest names none, since it has no alerts to send (CHART_APPLICATION_NOTIFY). A manifest can add, never remove: one that no longer declares a service or agent the deployment runs is refused (RELEASE_WOULD_DELETE) unless an approved deletion names it: deleting is its own operation, which keeps the version without them. A refused manifest keeps nothing. A kept one is the next version and releases at once, resolving every tag to its digest again.

For a chart application, check the change with preview_chart_application first. The saved version is installed as an upgrade; one that fails is rolled back to the last good version, which keeps running (get_chart_release says what happened). To go back to an older version, save its document again: it changes the chart's version and settings, not the data the app has stored.

To move one service to a new tag, deploy_service_image is the smaller change. For a repository's application this is refused: its configuration is the repository's inframan.yaml.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The image application. From list_applications.

params.name: manifest
params.description: The whole manifest, as get_application_manifest returned it, changed.

params.name: note
params.description: One line saying what changed, shown in the version list and the feed.

capabilities.name: search_traces
capabilities.summary: List recent distributed traces, newest first, optionally for one service.
capabilities.description:
Traces are the request-level view: one entry per traced request, with the service it entered through, the operation and how long it took. Use this to find a SLOW or FAILING request, then get_trace with the id to see where the time went.

WHERE TRACES COME FROM: only from services whose own code is instrumented with OpenTelemetry and exports its spans over OTLP to the infrastructure's collector, Alloy (alloy.monitoring.svc.cluster.local, port 4317 for gRPC or 4318 for HTTP), which forwards them to Tempo. The service mesh records NONE — Istio has no tracing configured, so a request that crossed the mesh leaves no trace by itself. A service that does not export spans has no traces at all: an empty result for it is the expected answer, not a fault, and the fix is instrumenting the service, not the platform. `traces: {}` on the service in inframan.yaml points its OpenTelemetry SDK at the collector (OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, the endpoint, a sampler: every trace on nonprod, one in ten on prod), from its next release; its code must still make the spans.

`service` matches the service name as the code reports it (OTEL_SERVICE_NAME); a Knative revision suffix (api-v7) is tolerated, so pass "api". An alternation works too: "api|web".

Returns only the summary of each trace — id, entry service, operation, start and duration. Sort by duration_ms yourself to find the slow ones; the window defaults to the last hour, which is usually where a complaint lives.

Empty result from a service you know exports spans? Check get_monitoring_status — Tempo is a separate component and can be missing while metrics work fine.

params.name: service
params.description: Optional service name, e.g. "backend". Omit for every service.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure to search, from list_infrastructures. Omit for the instance's most recent one.

params.name: minutes
params.description: How far back to search, in minutes. Default 60.

params.name: limit
params.description: Maximum traces to return. Default 20, maximum 100.

capabilities.name: set_addon_external_access
capabilities.summary: Open, extend or close a Redis or PostgreSQL install's access from outside the cluster.
capabilities.description:
Makes one install reachable from the internet at its own hostname — <instance>-<engine>.<infrastructure>.<domain> — through the infrastructure's ingress load balancer, on port 5432 for PostgreSQL and 6379 for Redis, over TLS. The database's own password is what lets a client in.

`permanent` stays open until closed. `temporary` closes itself after `duration_minutes` (5 minutes to 30 days), counted from when it opens; sending `temporary` again while open restarts the window. `off` closes it.

The hosting must have a domain (get_workload_domain), and the load balancer must carry the database ports first (open_database_ports). Redis also needs the infrastructure's certificate authority, which signs the certificate its hostname is served with: without one, opening is refused with 409 and code `infrastructure_ca_missing`, and reconcile_infrastructure_ca creates it.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The install, from get_installed_app.

params.name: mode
params.description: off, permanent or temporary.

params.name: duration_minutes
params.description: How long temporary access lasts. Required for temporary, refused otherwise.

capabilities.name: set_agent_connection
capabilities.summary: Add a model connection to an infrastructure, or change the one of that name.
capabilities.description: `name` is what an agent's file writes before its model (`<name>/<model>`): lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. Without one the connection takes its provider's own name (`anthropic`, `openai`, `azure`, `endpoint`, `gemini`, `vertex`), and a connection of that name is changed in place. With provider `anthropic_federation`, the four identifiers Anthropic's console gave (get_agent_connections says what to enter there first); with `anthropic_api_key`, `openai` or `gemini`, the name of the infrastructure secret that holds the key; with `azure_openai`, that and the resource's `base_url` and a deployment as the model its test calls; with `openai_compatible`, the endpoint's `base_url`, a model it serves for its test, a key's secret where it takes one, and its `prices` unless Inframan's list prices its models; with `vertex_ai` (a Google Cloud infrastructure), the `region` (a Vertex AI location, global by default) and, once, the setup get_agent_connections gives as `cloud_setup`, which the user runs in the project; with `bedrock` (an AWS infrastructure), the `region` (the infrastructure's own where left out) and, once, that setup run in the account. Through a cloud, an alias (opus, sonnet, haiku, fable) is called as that cloud writes Anthropic's model (Vertex AI: claude-opus-5-5; Bedrock: anthropic.claude-opus-5-5), and any other model by the ID the agent's file writes, such as Bedrock's inference profile global.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5. The infrastructure's first connection is its default; `default` makes this one the default. `default_model` is what an agent whose file names no model is given while this is the default connection. An infrastructure keeps eight connections at most. No credential is passed here. A federation connection reaches the gateway within half a minute; an API key one reconciles the Agents app, which writes the gateway's Secret again.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: name
params.description: The connection's name, as an agent's file writes it before its model. Its provider's own (`anthropic`) where left out.

params.name: provider
params.description: How the gateway reaches the model provider: anthropic_federation, anthropic_api_key, openai, azure_openai, openai_compatible, gemini, vertex_ai on a Google Cloud infrastructure, or bedrock on an AWS one.

params.name: organization_id
params.description: Federation: the Anthropic organization's ID, a UUID.

params.name: federation_rule_id
params.description: Federation: the federation rule's ID, beginning fdrl_.

params.name: service_account_id
params.description: Federation: the Anthropic service account's ID, beginning svac_.

params.name: workspace_id
params.description: Federation: the workspace's ID, beginning wrkspc_; needed when the rule spans several workspaces.

params.name: api_key_secret
params.description: API key: the NAME of the infrastructure secret holding the provider's API key (Anthropic's, OpenAI's, an Azure resource's, an endpoint's, the Gemini API's), never the key.

params.name: default_model
params.description: The model an agent whose file names none is given while this is the default connection: an alias (opus, sonnet, haiku, fable) or a model ID. Optional.

params.name: default
params.description: Make this the infrastructure's default connection. The first connection is the default whatever this says.

params.name: region
params.description: vertex_ai: the Vertex AI location the model is called in, such as global (the default), us, eu or us-central1. bedrock: the AWS region, the infrastructure's own where left out.

params.name: project_id
params.description: vertex_ai: the Google Cloud project, which is the infrastructure's own whatever is given. Leave it out.

params.name: test_model
params.description: The model a test of the connection calls, as its provider names it: an Azure OpenAI deployment's name, or a model an OpenAI-compatible endpoint serves (required for both). OpenAI's is gpt-5-nano, the Gemini API's and Vertex AI's gemini-3.5-flash-lite where left out.

params.name: base_url
params.description: azure_openai: the resource's endpoint, https://<resource>.openai.azure.com (its /openai/v1 is added). openai_compatible: the endpoint's API, https://<host>/v1 on a public name, or http://<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:<port>/v1 for a model server in this cluster. Never an address.

params.name: api
params.description: openai_compatible: which of OpenAI's APIs the endpoint speaks, chat_completions (the default) or responses.

params.name: prices
params.description: The connection's own prices, as a JSON list: [{"model":"llama-3.3-70b","input":0.6,"cached_input":0.3,"output":0.8}], in dollars a million tokens; a model ending in * prices every model that begins so. They come before the list prices Inframan ships, and a model not of Anthropic's that neither prices refuses the agent's release. Left out, the connection's prices are kept; "[]" clears them.

capabilities.name: set_business_hours
capabilities.summary: Schedule the hours an infrastructure stays up, sleeping it the rest of the week.
capabilities.description:
Sets when this cluster's workloads stay running: the days, a start and a stop time, in a timezone. Inside those hours the workloads run; outside them the platform stops everything. The clock is the whole decision — whether anyone is using the cluster at the stop time does not change it. A build or deploy that is running, or finished within the last hour, holds the cluster up past its stop.

The default is around the clock: no schedule, which is the same as every day from 00:00 to 24:00. A stop of "24:00" is midnight at the end of the day, so whole days work — weekdays "1,2,3,4,5" from 00:00 to 24:00 keeps the cluster up all week and asleep all weekend.

WHAT SLEEPING ACTUALLY DOES: everything in the cluster stops — the customer's services of every kind (web, worker, Knative), the databases, the monitoring stack, CI/CD, the Knative control plane and the ingress gateway with its load balancer — and every node is released, the system pool's too. On AWS the NAT gateways are deleted, and on GCP a hub spoke is detached. Nothing answers until the cluster wakes: at the schedule's next start, when someone wakes it, or when a release starts — a request does not. Nothing is lost: disks, the load balancer's and the NAT's addresses, secrets and every Kubernetes object survive, so DNS records and allow-lists hold. What stops being billed is the nodes, the load balancer, the NAT gateways and a spoke; the control plane, disks and reserved addresses keep costing regardless.

CONFIRM WITH THE USER BEFORE CALLING THIS, and confirm two things specifically: which environment it is, and that they accept everything on it — its web applications included — being down outside those hours until the schedule or a wake brings it back. This is a cost feature for development and staging clusters. Setting it on anything serving real traffic changes that traffic's behaviour on a timer, and the platform deliberately does not refuse to do so — plenty of clusters tagged prod are demo and internal environments — so the judgement is yours and the user's, not the platform's.

TIMES ARE LOCAL TO THE TIMEZONE YOU PASS. "9 to 6" is a statement about a working day, so pass the user's IANA zone ("Asia/Kolkata", "Europe/Berlin", "America/New_York") rather than converting to UTC yourself — the schedule then follows daylight saving on its own.

A window that crosses midnight is refused: pick the days you mean and keep start before stop, with 24:00 for a day that runs to midnight. Pass enabled=false to switch the schedule off; a cluster asleep at that moment is woken by the next scheduler tick rather than left down.

This replaces the whole schedule rather than patching it: send every field you want kept.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether this cluster sleeps outside the window. Defaults to true. Pass false to switch the schedule off and leave the cluster running around the clock; the other arguments are then ignored.

params.name: weekdays
params.description: The days the cluster is up, as numbers 0-6 separated by commas, where 0 is Sunday and 6 is Saturday. "1,2,3,4,5" is the working week and is where most of the saving comes from — two weekend days are 28% of a week. A day that is not listed is a day the cluster sleeps through entirely.

params.name: start
params.description: When the cluster's workloads come back, as 24-hour local time, e.g. "09:00", or "00:00" for a day that starts at midnight. A wake re-applies every app from its declared configuration and waits for the rollouts, so allow a few minutes: pick a start a little before people actually arrive.

params.name: stop
params.description: When the cluster sleeps, as 24-hour local time, e.g. "19:00", or "24:00" for a day that runs to midnight. Must be after start.

params.name: timezone
params.description: IANA timezone name for start and stop, e.g. "Asia/Kolkata". Defaults to UTC, which is almost never what a user means by business hours — ask for their zone rather than defaulting.

capabilities.name: set_cicd_type
capabilities.summary: Switch where an infrastructure builds its images: on Inframan's builder machines, or inside the infrastructure on its own node pool.
capabilities.description: Changes the CI/CD type of a running infrastructure. `in-cluster`: every build runs as a Job on a dedicated, network-isolated node pool of the infrastructure (ci-pool, scale-to-zero, Spot on nonprod), in the customer's project — the switch creates the pool, the firewall fence around it and the build account, which is minutes of Terraform. `builder-vm`: builds run on Inframan's pool of builder machines (Spot unless the build-server settings say on-demand), the servers kept warm start at once, and the switch removes the pool, the fence and the account; toward in-cluster the builder machines go as their builds end. Nothing running is touched either way; a build in flight keeps the type it started with. In-cluster builds are Dockerfile builds only (a service with build.method buildpack is refused at its next build). Returns as soon as the reconcile starts; poll get_infrastructure_features for `builds.type` and `builds.status` to read `ready`. On an AWS infrastructure builds always run in-cluster — builder machines are GCP's — and the switch is refused.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to switch. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: type
params.description: "in-cluster" or "builder-vm".

capabilities.name: set_cloud_account_secret_manager
capabilities.summary: Put Secret Manager's grants in a cloud account's role list, or take them out.
capabilities.description:
A cloud account's role list — what its setup asks for and its verification checks — holds Secret Manager's grants (its API and the inframanSecretWriter role on GCP, the Secrets statement on AWS) while `secret_manager` is true. It follows the account's infrastructures by itself: an infrastructure created with Secret Manager, or turning it on, puts the grants in, and once none of the account's live infrastructures has it on — the last turning it off, or the first created without it — they come out. This sets it directly.

ON is allowed at any time; the account then reads needs_update for the grants it adds until the user reruns its setup and verifies it. OFF is refused with 409 and code `secret_manager_in_use`, listing in `in_use` the account's infrastructures that have Secret Manager on, while any does: turn it off on them first. Answers with the account: `id`, `name`, `secret_manager`, `effective_status`, `missing`, and a `message`.

params.name: cloud_account_id
params.description: UUID of the cloud account, from list_cloud_accounts.

params.name: enabled
params.description: true to put Secret Manager's grants in the account's role list, false to take them out.

capabilities.name: set_connection_env_var
capabilities.summary: Connect a service to a sibling service or an installed database.
capabilities.description:
Stores a LINK, not a value — the platform resolves the address at deploy time, so nothing sensitive passes through this call. That is why this is available where setting a secret is not.

Give either target_service_id (a service in the SAME application) or target_installed_app_id (a Redis, Postgres or Storage from list_platform_apps). The key is the environment variable the service reads: a Redis or Postgres connection puts the connection URL there, a Storage connection the bucket's name.

A STORAGE connection is refused until two ceremonies are done, neither of which Inframan can do for the user: the service's Workload Identity (enable_wif, the user runs the commands, verify_wif), and then the grant on the bucket (get_storage_access_setup, the user runs the two gcloud commands, verify_storage_access). The platform never grants a bucket to an account.

Both targets are checked for reachability, not just existence: an installed app must be READY and on the same infrastructure, and a sibling service must be in the same application. A link that fails those resolves to an address the workload cannot reach, and it would fail at runtime rather than here.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service that needs the connection. From list_services.

params.name: key
params.description: Environment variable name the service reads, e.g. "REDIS_URL", "API_URL" or "UPLOADS_BUCKET".

params.name: target_service_id
params.description: A sibling service in the same application. From list_services.

params.name: target_installed_app_id
params.description: An installed Redis, Postgres or Storage. From list_platform_apps. Must be READY.

capabilities.name: set_default_agent_connection
capabilities.summary: Make one of an infrastructure's model connections its default.
capabilities.description: The default connection is what an agent whose file names no connection is called through (an alias or a claude-… ID written alone, or no model at all). An agent takes the new default at its next release; agents already released keep the connection their release chose. Nothing is reconciled.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: name
params.description: The connection's name, from get_agent_connections.

capabilities.name: set_domain_iap
capabilities.summary: Set a domain's Identity-Aware Proxy block: who may reach it, through Google sign-in.
capabilities.description: `iap` is `{enabled, members: ["user:…", "group:…", "domain:…", "serviceAccount:…"], oauth_client_id, oauth_client_secret}` — the secret is the NAME of an infrastructure secret; without a client, IAP signs in with Google's managed one, which admits the project's organisation's accounts only — or null to unset the level. Needs the cloud account's IAP grants. Refused where a service it would protect is also reachable at an l4 domain or its automatic address. IAP is a WHOLE block at three levels — the infrastructure (every l7 domain), the domain, the service (inframan.yaml `network.iap`, an environment's block replacing the service's) — and the most specific level that sets a block is the whole of it there: nothing above it is read. `{enabled: false}` turns IAP off for that scope. It applies only on l7 domains. Cloud Armor is not available.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: domain_id
params.description: UUID of the domain, from list_domains.

params.name: iap
params.description: The block, a JSON object; null to unset.

capabilities.name: set_domain_type
capabilities.summary: Move a custom domain between the network (l4) and the application (l7) load balancer.
capabilities.description: A migration, not a cut: both load balancers serve the domain until a request through the new one is seen to reach the gateway, its record points at `point_at` (get_domain_edge), and resolvers' old answers have expired — or a person finishes it (finish_domain_switch). To l7 is refused until the infrastructure's application load balancer is on and ready (get_edge `ready`), and past its domain limit (200 on Google Cloud, 25 on AWS); back to l4 while any path of the domain is behind IAP, and wherever a service on it would be left behind IAP while reachable at an l4 domain or its automatic address. Leaving l7 never takes the load balancer down: only turning it off does.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: domain_id
params.description: UUID of the domain, from list_domains.

params.name: type
params.description: `l4` (network load balancer) or `l7` (application load balancer).

capabilities.name: set_edge_iap
capabilities.summary: Set the infrastructure's Identity-Aware Proxy block: who may reach it, through Google sign-in.
capabilities.description: `iap` is `{enabled, members: ["user:…", "group:…", "domain:…", "serviceAccount:…"], oauth_client_id, oauth_client_secret}` — the secret is the NAME of an infrastructure secret; without a client, IAP signs in with Google's managed one, which admits the project's organisation's accounts only — or null to unset the level. Needs the cloud account's IAP grants. Refused where a service it would protect is also reachable at an l4 domain or its automatic address. IAP is a WHOLE block at three levels — the infrastructure (every l7 domain), the domain, the service (inframan.yaml `network.iap`, an environment's block replacing the service's) — and the most specific level that sets a block is the whole of it there: nothing above it is read. `{enabled: false}` turns IAP off for that scope. It applies only on l7 domains. Cloud Armor is not available.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: iap
params.description: The block, a JSON object; null to unset.

capabilities.name: set_edge_load_balancer
capabilities.summary: Turn an infrastructure's application load balancer on or off.
capabilities.description: On, the application load balancer is made with no domain on it — on Google Cloud a global address, the Gateway Google builds it from, its firewall rule and TLS policy; on AWS an Application Load Balancer — in five to ten minutes, and billed by the cloud while it exists. Once get_edge reads `ready`, its `application_address` is where a domain added as l7 points, and an l4 domain can move onto it. Off takes it down and releases its address; refused while any domain is l7 or moving (get_edge `on_it`). Turning it on needs the cloud account's certificate-store grants.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: enabled
params.description: true to make the application load balancer, false to take it down.

capabilities.name: set_edge_request_logs
capabilities.summary: Turn the application load balancer's request logs on or off for an infrastructure.
capabilities.description: Off by default: the cloud bills what it keeps. On Google Cloud `sample_percent` (1 to 100, 100 by default) is the share of requests sent to Cloud Logging; on AWS every request is written to a bucket of the infrastructure's own, kept 30 days, and the share is not read.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether to log requests.

params.name: sample_percent
params.description: Google Cloud: the percent of requests logged, 1 to 100.

capabilities.name: set_env_var
capabilities.summary: Set a plain environment variable on a service.
capabilities.description:
Upsert by key: this replaces that one variable and leaves every other one alone.

For VALUES ONLY. Secrets cannot be set here and the call is refused if you try — a secret sent through a tool call ends up in the conversation and in the client's logs, so it belongs in the console, which writes it to Secret Manager without it passing through anything else. To link a service to another service or to an installed database, use the connections: block in inframan.yaml.

Takes effect on the next deploy. rebuild.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service to set it on. From list_services.

params.name: key
params.description: Variable name, e.g. "LOG_LEVEL".

params.name: value
params.description: The value. Not for secrets — use the console for those.

params.name: is_build_arg
params.description: Also pass this to the Docker build as a build arg. Default false.

capabilities.name: set_github_personal_access_token
capabilities.summary: Store the calling user's GitHub Personal Access Token, encrypted.
capabilities.description:
The LEGACY credential, kept for accounts that predate the GitHub App. It authenticates repository browsing for that one user and nothing else: builds clone with an App installation token, and push webhooks are verified against the App's webhook secret, so storing a token here does not make anything deploy.

For deployments, connect a GitHub App instead — get_github_app_status says whether one is connected.

params.name: token
params.description: A GitHub Personal Access Token with repo scope. Stored encrypted against the calling user.

capabilities.name: set_investigator_settings
capabilities.summary: Set what an infrastructure's investigations call and may spend.
capabilities.description: `model` is the model investigations call, as an agent's file writes one (`<connection>/<model>`, or a model alias alone); empty for the default connection's default model. `budget` is one investigation's ($0.10 to $100, $1.00 by default) and `month_budget` the month's across the infrastructure's investigations ($1 to $10,000, $50 by default), written as "$1.00"; empty keeps what is set. An investigation running keeps what it was started with. Answers the infrastructure's readiness as get_investigation_status says it.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure.

params.name: model
params.description: The model, or empty for the default.

params.name: budget
params.description: One investigation's budget, as "$1.00".

params.name: month_budget
params.description: The month's budget, as "$50".

capabilities.name: set_maintenance_window
capabilities.summary: Set when maintenance may restart an infrastructure's platform components.
capabilities.description:
Sets an infrastructure's maintenance window: the days, a start time, a length of 1 to 12 hours, and a timezone. The window may cross midnight. Pass enabled=false to remove it.

A window that falls while the business hours have the cluster up — every window, for a cluster up around the clock — is refused (409, MAINTENANCE_IN_BUSINESS_HOURS, with the overlap in words) unless acknowledge_business_hours is true: platform components may restart in it while the cluster serves traffic. The person confirms that; the console asks them in a dialog. A window that falls while the cluster sleeps wakes it for the window and puts it back to sleep after.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether the infrastructure has a window. Defaults to true; false removes it.

params.name: weekdays
params.description: The days the window opens, as numbers 0-6 separated by commas, 0 Sunday. Required unless enabled is false.

params.name: start
params.description: When it opens, as 24-hour local time, e.g. "02:00".

params.name: hours
params.description: How long it stays open, 1 to 12 hours.

params.name: timezone
params.description: IANA timezone of the start, e.g. "Asia/Kolkata". Defaults to the business hours' timezone, else UTC.

params.name: acknowledge_business_hours
params.description: Saves a window that falls while the cluster serves traffic: the person confirmed that platform components may restart then.

capabilities.name: set_monitoring_retention
capabilities.summary: Set how long an infrastructure keeps its logs, traces or metrics, in days.
capabilities.description: Each given retention is held to its store's bounds (get_monitoring_retention) and refused outside them, with why. The stores that change are reconciled now, as a change to the Monitoring app's configuration is; Prometheus is also told to keep to 85% of its disk. A shorter retention deletes what is older at the store's next compaction.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: logs_days
params.description: Days of logs to keep.

params.name: traces_days
params.description: Days of traces to keep.

params.name: metrics_days
params.description: Days of metrics to keep.

capabilities.name: set_postgres_client
capabilities.summary: Switch a PostgreSQL install's client on or off: whether pgweb, the infrastructure's database client (DbGate), connects to it.
capabilities.description:
pgweb is one per infrastructure, served at an HTTPS address with a password or an OAuth provider, and connects only to the databases whose client switch is on — as each one's own user, TLS required, and to no database typed in by hand. While the switch is on, the database's NetworkPolicy lets pgweb's pods in; off, the default for every database, pgweb has no connection to it and the database does not let it in.

`enabled` true where pgweb is not installed needs `pgweb`: {"address": {"mode":"auto"} or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}, "auth": {"mode":"password"} or an OAuth block as install_platform_app takes it} — pgweb is installed first. Without it the call is refused with 409 and code `pgweb_not_installed`. The database must be ready (or failed).

Returns once the change is handed over: the database's NetworkPolicy is applied, then pgweb restarts once with the databases now switched on. get_installed_app shows the switch under metadata.client, and pgweb's own install lists the databases it has under metadata.databases. pgweb keeps its password in the cloud account's secret manager, so switching on needs the infrastructure's Secret Manager.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The PostgreSQL install, from get_installed_app.

params.name: enabled
params.description: true lets pgweb connect to the database; false takes it away.

params.name: pgweb
params.description: Only where pgweb is not installed and enabled is true: a JSON object, {"address": {…}, "auth": {…}}, how pgweb is installed first.

capabilities.name: set_secret_manager
capabilities.summary: Turn an infrastructure's Secret Manager on or off: whether it keeps secrets in its cloud account's secret manager.
capabilities.description:
Secret Manager is an infrastructure feature, on for every new infrastructure. While it is on, the infrastructure keeps its secrets in the cloud account's secret manager — infrastructure secrets, secret env-group variables, the passwords of Redis, PostgreSQL, Grafana, LikeC4 and pgweb, its certificate authority, the wildcard certificate's key — and the account's setup asks for Secret Manager's grants.

ON adds those grants to the cloud account's role list. An account not verified for them reads needs_update, naming them, until the user reruns its setup (get_cloud_account_setup) and verifies it (verify_cloud_account); meanwhile only what needs Secret Manager on the infrastructure is refused, and its automatic HTTPS addresses wait. The answer's message says so, with the Cloud accounts page's link.

OFF is refused with 409 and code `secret_manager_in_use`, listing in `in_use` what reads it, while anything does — and on an infrastructure whose monitoring is read through its gateway the certificate authority always does, so only a zero-trust infrastructure read across the instance's hub can turn it off. Off on the account's last infrastructure that had it, the grants leave the account's setup. While it is off, what needs it is refused with code `secret_manager_off`. Nothing in the cloud or the cluster changes either way: it is the infrastructure's record, and what the account is asked for follows it.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: enabled
params.description: true to turn Secret Manager on, false to turn it off.

capabilities.name: set_zero_trust
capabilities.summary: Switch an infrastructure's zero-trust posture on or off at runtime. Not available in this release.
capabilities.description: NOT AVAILABLE IN THIS RELEASE: the call is refused; zero trust is chosen when the infrastructure is provisioned. What it will do — zero trust is Network Policy on the cluster, a sidecar in every service pod with a PERMISSIVE mTLS policy and an allow policy per service, and injection plus a NetworkPolicy per Redis/Postgres install. This switches all of it in either direction on a running infrastructure: every application is re-rendered and rolled through its own revision deploy (the image comes from the build cache — no rebuild), every datastore is re-reconciled, and Google's Network Policy enforcement is switched on the cluster. Enforcement recreates node pools; for its duration every service and the ingress edge run at least two replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget and the pools are surged, so nothing user-facing drops (a Basic-tier datastore is one pod and restarts once). Takes tens of minutes; poll get_infrastructure_features for `zero_trust_transition` to return to empty. One switch at a time per infrastructure.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure to switch. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: enabled
params.description: true to enable the zero-trust posture, false to disable it.

capabilities.name: sleep_infrastructure
capabilities.summary: Send a cluster to sleep now, before its window closes.
capabilities.description: Stops everything in the cluster immediately — the customer's services of every kind, the databases, the monitoring stack, CI/CD, the Knative control plane and the ingress gateway with its load balancer — releases every node, and takes down the network's billed parts. Only the control plane and the reserved addresses stay; nothing answers until the schedule's next start time, wake_infrastructure or a release. Nothing is lost. get_sleep_run shows it step by step.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: start_investigation
capabilities.summary: Start the platform's investigator on an issue: it finds the root cause and reports it, changing nothing.
capabilities.description: The investigator is the platform's own agent, part of the Agents app: it reads the logs, metrics, releases, activity and, where the issue names an application with a repository, its code at the commit the issue names (else the one that serves), and ends with a report: the root cause, the evidence, what to change and what it could not determine. It reads and reports; it changes nothing, opens no pull request, and runs no command. Name the issue by `subject`, its key — An issue's key: `platform_alert:<alert id>` (list_platform_alerts' `id`), `event:<event id>` (a failure or a warning of list_application_activity), a cluster alert's `subject_key` from list_firing_cluster_alerts, or a log line's `log:…` key, which get_investigation_status answers for a line named in `log_lines`. — or a log line by `log_line`: A log line is named by where it is and what it says, as a JSON object: a line of the infrastructure's logs by `infrastructure_id`, `namespace`, `container`, `ts` (Loki's timestamp of the line in nanoseconds, a line's `ts` in get_logs and query_logs) and `text`; a line of a release's step by `deployment_id`, `step` (the step's ID from get_deployment_pipeline, or `system` for the run's own log) and `text`; a line of a sleep's or a wake's step by `sleep_run_id`, `step` (the step's key from get_sleep_run) and `text`. `text` is the line as it was read, its first 2,048 characters. Every line of every level can be investigated. Two lines that say the same thing — another number, request ID, time, address, duration or quoted value, another pod or release of the service — are one issue: `log:<infrastructure>:<namespace>:<service>:<fingerprint>`, or `log:deployment:<id>:<step>:<fingerprint>`, `log:sleep_run:<id>:<step>:<fingerprint>`. A log line is read again from where it is kept (the infrastructure's logs at its stream and timestamp, or its step) before anything starts, and is refused if it is not there (409 `subject_gone`); a line of the infrastructure's logs named by its key alone starts only where an earlier investigation of it was handed the line (else 400 `log_line_needed`), while a release's or a sleep's line is found by its key in its step. Returns the `investigation`, `queued`: at most three run at once on an infrastructure, the rest wait their turn. Read it with get_investigation until its `status` is one it ends with (succeeded, failed, timed_out, budget_reached, cancelled, skipped); its `summary` is the report. One investigation of an issue is queued or running at a time: a start while one is is refused 409 `investigation_running`, with that one as `investigation` — open it instead. Also refused: while the infrastructure's Agents app is not installed or has no model connection (409 `agents_not_ready`, with `link` to set it up); while the infrastructure sleeps (409 `infrastructure_asleep`); once the month's investigation budget is spent (409 `budget_reached`); a cluster alert no longer firing (409 `subject_gone`); an event that is neither a failure nor a warning (400 `not_an_issue`); ten already waiting (429 `queue_full`). An agent cannot start one: a person does, from the issue's button. An investigation spends on the infrastructure's model connection, up to its budget ($1 by default) — get_investigation_status says the budget, the month's and what is spent.

params.name: subject
params.description: An issue's key: `platform_alert:<alert id>` (list_platform_alerts' `id`), `event:<event id>` (a failure or a warning of list_application_activity), a cluster alert's `subject_key` from list_firing_cluster_alerts, or a log line's `log:…` key, which get_investigation_status answers for a line named in `log_lines`. Or `log_line` in its place.

params.name: log_line
params.description: A log line, in place of `subject`: A log line is named by where it is and what it says, as a JSON object: a line of the infrastructure's logs by `infrastructure_id`, `namespace`, `container`, `ts` (Loki's timestamp of the line in nanoseconds, a line's `ts` in get_logs and query_logs) and `text`; a line of a release's step by `deployment_id`, `step` (the step's ID from get_deployment_pipeline, or `system` for the run's own log) and `text`; a line of a sleep's or a wake's step by `sleep_run_id`, `step` (the step's key from get_sleep_run) and `text`. `text` is the line as it was read, its first 2,048 characters. Every line of every level can be investigated. Two lines that say the same thing — another number, request ID, time, address, duration or quoted value, another pod or release of the service — are one issue: `log:<infrastructure>:<namespace>:<service>:<fingerprint>`, or `log:deployment:<id>:<step>:<fingerprint>`, `log:sleep_run:<id>:<step>:<fingerprint>`.

capabilities.name: stop_agent_run
capabilities.summary: Stop a run of an agent that waits or runs.
capabilities.description: The run's Job is deleted, its agent told to stop, and the run ends `cancelled` within moments; a run that still waited for its turn never starts. What the agent had already done stays done. A run that has ended already is refused with a 409.

params.name: service_id
params.description: UUID of the agent: the ID of its service, from list_agents.

params.name: run_id
params.description: The run's ID, from list_agent_runs.

capabilities.name: stop_release
capabilities.summary: Stop a release that is still running. Nothing it has not deployed is deployed, and traffic does not move.
capabilities.description:
For a release that should not have started — a merge that should have carried [skip ci], a push to the wrong branch, a build of the wrong commit. It cancels the release: every build still running is stopped and its build Job deleted, every run that had not finished is marked CANCELLED, the revision is recorded as `cancelled`, and NO TRAFFIC MOVES — whatever was serving before is still serving after.

THIS IS NOT A ROLLBACK, and the difference is the whole choice. A stop only reaches a release that is still running; it cannot take back one that already shipped, and it is refused with that said once the revision has taken traffic. To go back to an earlier version use update_revision_setting with mode="fixed" — that is rollback.

A service that had already deployed inside the stopped release keeps its deployed workload: the stop does not tear down what is running, because removing a healthy version is not what someone asking to stop a build wants. The one exception is a `recreate` rollout, which stops the old version before starting the new one: there the previous revision is brought back, the same restore a failed recreate gets.

WHICH RELEASE. With nothing named it stops the application's one release in flight, which is the usual case. Name `commit` (the commit the release is building, full or short) or `deployment_id` (any run of it, from list_deployments) when more than one is running — it refuses and lists them rather than picking. A release that has already finished is refused with its state named.

It returns as soon as the cancellation is accepted; the runs settle to CANCELLED within seconds and the stop appears in list_application_activity as `release_stopped`. No release-failed alert is raised — a stop is a decision, not a failure.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application whose release to stop. From list_applications.

params.name: commit
params.description: The commit the release is building, full or short. Use it when the application has more than one release running.

params.name: deployment_id
params.description: Any run of the release to stop, from list_deployments. The other way to name one release when several are in flight.

capabilities.name: test_agent_connection
capabilities.summary: Test one of an infrastructure's model connections: one exchange and one tiny call through its gateway.
capabilities.description: Asks the infrastructure's agent gateway, inside its cluster, to use a connection once (`name`; the default connection where left out): for federation it exchanges a fresh cluster token with Anthropic, for Vertex AI or Bedrock it takes its cloud identity afresh, then makes one call of a single output token (a fraction of a cent, on the connection's account). Returns `ok`, or the `stage` that failed — `gateway` (it could not be asked), `connection` (none set, or the gateway has not read it), `exchange` (Anthropic refused the cluster's token, or the cloud gave the gateway no identity: its setup has not been run, or the connection not saved since) or `call` — with the provider's `status` and `message` and a `hint` saying where to look: for a refused exchange, Anthropic's authentication history, which names the reason (a wrong issuer, subject or audience in the rule); for a cloud's refused call, the role or policy the identity lacks, or the model to enable. The answer holds no credential. It is kept as the connection's `last_test` (get_agent_connections). Takes up to a minute.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: name
params.description: The connection to test, by its name from get_agent_connections. The default connection where left out.

capabilities.name: test_alert_group
capabilities.summary: Send each of an alert group's channels a test message now, as the group's messages come, and say what each answered.
capabilities.description: The same send a message takes, to every channel of the group — one that is off too — of a message that says it is a test of the group. Answers `ok` (every channel took it) and each channel's `answer` in `channels`. Admins only.

params.name: group_id
params.description: The group's ID, from list_alert_groups.

capabilities.name: test_notification_channel
capabilities.summary: Send a notification channel a test message now, and say what it answered.
capabilities.description: The same send a message takes — the address checked, TLS verified, the secret decrypted for it alone — of a message that says it is a test. Answers `ok` and the channel's `answer`: an SMTP server's refusal of the user name or password, a Slack webhook's no_service, a host that is not public. A channel that is off is tested too. To test what a group's messages look like on each of its channels, use test_alert_group. Admins only.

params.name: channel_id
params.description: The channel's ID, from list_notification_channels.

capabilities.name: uninstall_platform_app
capabilities.summary: Uninstall Knative, KEDA, Grafana, LikeC4 or pgweb from an infrastructure, removing it from the cluster.
capabilities.description:
For single-instance store apps — today, Knative, KEDA, Grafana, LikeC4 and pgweb. The platform's own apps (gateway, monitoring, cicd) are REFUSED: they are what an infrastructure is and go with it. Knative is REFUSED while any service on the infrastructure has scaling.type: concurrency, and KEDA while any has scaling.type: event — the reply names them; set scaling.type: hpa on each and deploy before uninstalling.

Grafana REQUIRES `keep_data`: true keeps its bucket (its database: dashboards, users, alert rules) and the stored admin password in the customer's cloud account, so installing Grafana on this infrastructure again restores everything; false deletes them with it. Ask which — it is the customer's data. LikeC4 keeps nothing: the applications' models stay in their repositories, and its stored password goes with it. pgweb keeps nothing either, and is REFUSED while any database has its client switched on — the reply names them; switch each off with set_postgres_client first.

Returns as soon as the teardown workflow starts; the cluster catches up over minutes. Watch list_platform_apps for the app to disappear.

For a named Redis or Postgres install, this is the wrong tool — use delete_installed_app, which takes the installed_app_id.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure to uninstall from. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: app_id
params.description: Catalog app id from list_platform_apps.

params.name: keep_data
params.description: Grafana only, and required for it: keep its bucket and stored admin password for a reinstall (true), or delete them (false).

capabilities.name: unlink_pipeline
capabilities.summary: Detach a pipeline from an application without deleting it.
capabilities.description: Stops the pipeline running for this application. The definition survives and stays linked to any other application — this is the reversible way to stop a pipeline. Deleting the definition outright is a console operation.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to detach it from. From list_applications.

params.name: pipeline_id
params.description: The pipeline to detach.

capabilities.name: update_alert_group
capabilities.summary: Change an alert group: its description, channels, whether it sends resolves, or whether it is on.
capabilities.description: A field not sent keeps what is set; `channel_ids` replaces the group's channels whole. Its name does not change — files name it: make a group of the new name, point the files at it, then delete this one. Turning it off silences it: nothing is sent by it until it is on again. Admins only.

params.name: group_id
params.description: The group's ID, from list_alert_groups.

params.name: name
params.description: Refused unless it is the group's own name: a name is fixed once made.

params.name: description
params.description: What the group is for, at most 300 characters.

params.name: channel_ids
params.description: The channels it sends to, by their IDs from list_notification_channels: 1 to 10, in order, as a JSON array.

params.name: send_resolved
params.description: Whether a message also goes when an alert resolves; true for a new group.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether it sends at all; true for a new group.

capabilities.name: update_application
capabilities.summary: Change an application's default branch, for it and all its services: what a release no push started builds, and where its pull requests merge.
capabilities.description:
Writes the branch on the application and on every one of its services. It decides what a release that no push started builds — one a person starts by hand, or one a changed secret or env group starts — and the base branch of the pull requests Inframan opens on the application when none is chosen: a config pull request, an optimization, a vulnerability fix, an agent's. It does NOT decide which pushes release: a push releases when the trigger branch of one of the application's pipelines matches the branch pushed to (list_linked_pipelines shows them), and that release builds the branch pushed, whatever this says. Changing it releases nothing.

Only an application with a repository has a branch. An application of published images, an agent deployment and a chart application keep their configuration as versions of a manifest in Inframan, and are refused (NO_REPOSITORY): a change to one is a new version of its manifest (save_application_manifest), released or installed as it is saved.

The branch is the only updatable field, and that is deliberate. The application NAME is immutable platform-wide: it seeds the Kubernetes namespace, the application: field in the repo's inframan.yaml, and every deployed resource's identity. CI validates the yaml against the database on every push, so a rename here would leave the repo disagreeing with the platform and every subsequent push rejected as drift. Renaming needs a migration, not a field write — do not offer it as an option.

To change how a service RUNS without changing its code, edit inframan.yaml and push. The build is skipped when the commit already has an image, so the existing image is redeployed with the new configuration as a new revision.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to update, one with a repository. From list_applications.

params.name: branch
params.description: The default branch, e.g. "main" — one the repository has (list_github_branches): a release no push started builds it.

capabilities.name: update_application_pools
capabilities.summary: Change an infrastructure's application pools: Karpenter's pools on AWS, its classes on nonprod GKE.
capabilities.description:
Replaces the APPLICATION pools of a ready infrastructure — the pools its services run on — with the list given, in the shape provisioning takes.

On AWS each is a Karpenter NodePool: `name`, `spot`, `instance_cpus` (any of 2, 4, 8, 16), `instance_families` (any of c, m, r, t), `cpu_limit` and, optionally, `disk_size_gb` (each node's disk, 20 to 500 GiB; 50 when omitted). A changed pool is re-applied and Karpenter replaces its nodes one at a time; a new pool costs nothing until a pod needs it.

On a nonprod GKE infrastructure each is a class of Inframan's Karpenter: `name`, `machine_series` (e2 or n2d), `spot`, `cpu_limit` (its vCPU in total) and, optionally, `disk_size_gb` (20 to 500 GB, 50 when omitted). Everything but a class's name may change, as an EKS pool's: give each class as it should be, starting from what get_application_classes says (an omitted `spot` is on-demand; `disk_size_gb` 0 or omitted keeps its disk). A new `machine_series`, `spot` or `disk_size_gb` replaces the class's nodes as Karpenter's drift does: nodes of the new shape come up first, then the old ones are drained onto them one at a time, and a service with one replica restarts once. `cpu_limit` (a multiple of its machine type's vCPU) holds the nodes it may add: lowered, it removes no running node. A new class costs nothing until a service needs a node. A prod GKE infrastructure keeps the pools it was created with, and the call is refused there.

On both a pool left out is deleted and its nodes drained — refused while any service runs on it (move the service's node_pool first). The platform's own pools (system, monitoring, ci) are not part of the list and are kept as they are. Waits for the cluster to take the change and says so; the infrastructure's record changes only once it has.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure whose application pools change. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: node_pools
params.description: JSON array of every application pool as it should be, e.g. on AWS [{"name":"application-pool","spot":true,"instance_cpus":[2],"instance_families":["c","m"],"cpu_limit":8,"disk_size_gb":50}], on GKE [{"name":"application-pool","machine_series":"e2","spot":true,"cpu_limit":16,"disk_size_gb":50}].

capabilities.name: update_cloud_account
capabilities.summary: Change the name or service-account emails on an existing cloud account link.
capabilities.description:
A partial update: omitted fields are left as they are, so pass only what the user actually asked to change. The GCP project id can be changed but almost never should be — infrastructures already provisioned through this link keep pointing at it, and repointing the row does not move anything that was built in the old project.

Renaming is safe. Editing an sa_email is not: the new address must be a service account that exists and holds the platform's roles, which only `inframan cloud add` creates. A wrong value here saves cleanly and breaks the NEXT provision, not this call. If the intent is to repair a broken cloud account, the fix is to re-run the CLI bootstrap rather than to edit these fields.

params.name: cloud_account_id
params.description: UUID of the cloud account to update, from list_cloud_accounts.

params.name: name
params.description: New display name. Omit to leave unchanged.

params.name: gcp_project_id
params.description: New GCP project id. Omit to leave unchanged — changing it does not migrate anything already provisioned.

params.name: sa_email
params.description: New managed service-account email, from a CLI bootstrap. Omit to leave unchanged.

params.name: cluster_sa_email
params.description: New GKE node service-account email. Omit to leave unchanged.

params.name: builder_sa_email
params.description: New CI builder service-account email. Omit to leave unchanged.

capabilities.name: update_env_group_vars
capabilities.summary: Set variables in an environment group, upserting by key.
capabilities.description:
UPSERT BY KEY, not a replace: a key you send is created or overwritten, and a key you leave out is left exactly as it was. Nothing here deletes — the console is the only way a variable leaves a group. (Do not confuse this with the envGroups: block in inframan.yaml, which IS a replace: that one detaches every group you omit.)

`is_secret` and `is_build_arg` are not yours to choose. They are forced from the group's type: everything in a `secret` group is a secret AND a build arg, everything in an `env` group is neither.

In a `secret` group, sending an empty value for an existing key KEEPS its current Secret Manager reference — that is how a form that cannot display secrets is saved without wiping them. In an `env` group an empty value is stored as an empty value.

A `secret` group's values are kept in the cloud account's secret manager, so writing them needs the infrastructure's Secret Manager: refused with code `secret_manager_off` while it is off, and with `cloud_account_not_ready`, naming the grants, while the account is not yet verified for them. An `env` group needs neither.

Takes effect on the next deploy of each attached service.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure the group belongs to, from list_infrastructures.

params.name: group_id
params.description: UUID of the group to write into, from list_env_groups.

params.name: variables
params.description: The variables to upsert: a JSON array of {"key":"NAME","value":"..."} objects. Only the keys you send are touched.

capabilities.name: update_grafana_settings
capabilities.summary: Change where an infrastructure's Grafana is served, or how people sign in to it.
capabilities.description: `address`: {"mode":"auto"}, the hosting's automatic HTTPS address, or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}, one of the infrastructure's active domains no service routes on. `auth`: {"mode":"login"} or an OAuth block, as install_platform_app takes it; its `client_secret` is the NAME of an infrastructure secret. A field left out keeps its value. Checked against the infrastructure before anything changes, then Grafana is reconciled and restarts once; its data is untouched. OAuth reads its client secret from the cloud account's secret manager, so it is refused with `secret_manager_off` while the infrastructure has Secret Manager off.

params.name: infrastructure_id
