params.description: Infrastructure Grafana is installed on. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: address
params.description: A JSON object, {"mode":"auto"} or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}.

params.name: auth
params.description: A JSON object, {"mode":"login"} or {"mode":"oauth", …}.

capabilities.name: update_installed_app_config
capabilities.summary: Change the settings of one installed Redis or Postgres instance.
capabilities.description:
Applies to a NAMED install (a Redis or Postgres instance), not to the platform's own components. Settings are resolved through the app's own rules — some keys are passed through to the engine's config, some are translated into pod resources, and some are refused outright with the reason — and then a partial reconcile pushes the result to the cluster over the next minute or two.

`redis_config` is authoritative: whatever you send REPLACES the freeform config, so send the full set you want, not just the key you are changing.

The install must be on a READY infrastructure and not already updating.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: UUID of the install, from list_platform_apps or get_installed_app.

params.name: redis_config
params.description: The engine's own settings as a JSON object of string values, e.g. {"maxmemory-policy":"allkeys-lru"}. Replaces the current set entirely.

params.name: tier_overrides
params.description: Explicit size overrides as a JSON object of string values, e.g. {"memory":"2gb"}. Merged into what is already set.

capabilities.name: update_likec4_settings
capabilities.summary: Change where an infrastructure's LikeC4 is served, or how people sign in to it.
capabilities.description: `address`: {"mode":"auto"}, the hosting's automatic HTTPS address, or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}, one of the infrastructure's active domains no service routes on. `auth`: {"mode":"password"} or an OAuth block, as install_platform_app takes it for LikeC4; its `client_secret` is the NAME of an infrastructure secret. A field left out keeps its value. Checked against the infrastructure before anything changes, then LikeC4 is reconciled, restarts once and rebuilds its site from the applications' models. OAuth reads its client secret from the cloud account's secret manager, so it is refused with `secret_manager_off` while the infrastructure has Secret Manager off.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure LikeC4 is installed on. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: address
params.description: A JSON object, {"mode":"auto"} or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}.

params.name: auth
params.description: A JSON object, {"mode":"password"} or {"mode":"oauth", …}.

capabilities.name: update_notification_channel
capabilities.summary: Change a notification channel: its settings, whether it is on, or its secret.
capabilities.description: A field not sent keeps what is set; `secret` empty keeps the secret kept, a new one replaces it. A channel's type does not change, and it has no rules: a request that sends `rules` is refused, since what it is sent is the alert groups' it is in (update_alert_group). A channel that is off is sent nothing by any group. Admins only.

params.name: channel_id
params.description: The channel's ID, from list_notification_channels.

params.name: name
params.description: What the channel is called, one line of at most 60 characters.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether it gets messages.

params.name: smtp_host
params.description: Email: the SMTP server's host, a public name.

params.name: smtp_port
params.description: Email: its port, 587 by default (465 for TLS).

params.name: smtp_security
params.description: Email: starttls, or tls (implicit, usually 465); by the port where not given.

params.name: smtp_username
params.description: Email: the user name it signs in with; empty for a server that takes mail without one.

params.name: from_address
params.description: Email: the address messages come from.

params.name: from_name
params.description: Email: the name they come from, Inframan where not given.

params.name: recipients
params.description: Email: the addresses it writes to, comma-separated, at most 50.

params.name: webhook_url
params.description: Webhook: its https:// address, on a public host.

params.name: secret
params.description: The channel's secret: the SMTP password, the Slack, Google Chat or Teams webhook's address, or the webhook's signing secret (16 to 256 characters). Empty keeps the one kept.

params.name: rules
params.description: Not taken: a channel has no rules. A request that sends rules is refused; what a channel is sent is its alert groups' (create_alert_group).

capabilities.name: update_pgweb_settings
capabilities.summary: Change where an infrastructure's database client (pgweb, running DbGate) is served, or how people sign in to it.
capabilities.description: `address`: {"mode":"auto"}, the hosting's automatic HTTPS address, or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}, one of the infrastructure's active domains no service routes on. `auth`: {"mode":"password"} or an OAuth block, as install_platform_app takes it for pgweb; its `client_secret` is the NAME of an infrastructure secret. A field left out keeps its value. Checked against the infrastructure before anything changes, then pgweb is reconciled and restarts once, ending the sessions open in it. OAuth reads its client secret from the cloud account's secret manager, so it is refused with `secret_manager_off` while the infrastructure has Secret Manager off.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure pgweb is installed on. From list_infrastructures.

params.name: address
params.description: A JSON object, {"mode":"auto"} or {"mode":"domain","domain":"…"}.

params.name: auth
params.description: A JSON object, {"mode":"password"} or {"mode":"oauth", …}.

capabilities.name: update_pipeline
capabilities.summary: Replace a pipeline's definition with new YAML.
capabilities.description:
Read the current definition first with export_pipeline_yaml, edit it, and send it back.

Fields absent from the YAML are left as they are, so this is a merge rather than a replace — sending only a trigger change will not blank the steps.

Takes effect on the next push that matches the trigger; it does not re-run anything already deployed. A `webhooks:` or `release_stages:` list, when present, replaces the pipeline's webhooks or stages whole, and a step list written out — `post_deploy: []` included — replaces that phase's steps. A description written out empty clears it.

A pipeline is written in any of three formats, all the same pipeline: `inframan` (Inframan YAML, the default: the shape export_pipeline_yaml returns), `github` (GitHub Actions workflow syntax: a step is a job, its commands the job's run: steps, the phases where jobs sit around two fixed jobs `build` and `deploy` — `uses: inframan/build@v1` and `uses: inframan/deploy@v1` — and what GitHub has no word for under an `inframan:` key; any workflow written for GitHub's runners converts too: checkout, caches, docker build/push, cloud sign-ins and deploys are Inframan's own and replaced, setup-node/python/go/java choose the step's image, a matrix is expanded, a notify step or stage is a job of one `uses: inframan/notify@v1` step with its settings under `with:` (a stage's job carries `inframan: {stage: true}`), a job's `${{ secrets.X }}` becomes the step's secret X (an infrastructure secret of that name) and its `services:` the pre-build step's sidecars, and what a pipeline cannot hold — environment:, unknown actions, a second trigger — is reported unsupported, never dropped unsaid) and `json` (the console's Visual form, the API's field names). A step's `secrets:` maps a variable to the NAME of an infrastructure secret (list_infra_secrets), never a value: the step gets it as that variable, masked in its log. A pre-build step's `sidecars:` ({name, image, env, command, ready}) are containers beside it — a database for its tests — reached at their name or localhost, `ready` a command run in one until it succeeds. list_repository_workflows reads a repository's .github/workflows to import, and convert_pipeline shows what a document becomes before anything is saved.

Webhooks (`webhooks:` list) are notifications. Each: `name` (unique in the pipeline), `url` (https:// only; the certificate is verified and redirects are not followed), `method` (POST default; PUT, PATCH, GET), `headers` (map), `events` — `deploy_success` (per service, once its version is ready) and/or `release_success` (once per release, after its traffic has moved; POST only; body {event, delivery_id, application, infrastructure_id, revision, images: {service: image}}), `vulnerabilities_found` (per service, when its release's image scan finds anything at or above the service's security.fail_on — high where it has no policy) and/or `scan_blocked` (per service, when its security policy refuses the release); both carry {event, delivery_id, application, infrastructure_id, service, deployment_id, image, digest, critical, high, medium, low, fixable, secrets, blocked, code, message, findings: [IDs]}. Optional: `secret` — the NAME of an infrastructure secret (list_infra_secrets), never a value; it is read at send time and sent in `secret_header` (default Authorization) after `secret_prefix` (default "Bearer " in Authorization, otherwise none); `retries` (0-10, default 3, attempts after the first, from 10s doubling to 5m; 5xx, 408, 429 and network errors are retried); `success_codes` (default any 2xx); `timeout_seconds` (1-60, default 10); `exclude_services` (left out of release_success's images). There is no copy_images_to: copying images is a promote_images release stage. Deliveries are on the application's activity feed as webhook_delivered / webhook_failed; a webhook never fails a release.

Release stages (`release_stages:` list) run in order once per release, after its traffic has moved (never for a superseded, failed or fixed-traffic release), and never fail the release. Each: `id` ([a-z][a-z0-9_], at most 32, unique), `name`, `type`, `continue_on_failure` (default false: a failed stage skips the ones after it). Types: `promote_images` — `registry` (a path such as asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/project/repo; GCP infrastructures only), optional `services` and `exclude_services`; copies each image to <registry>/<last repository segment>:<tag> as the infrastructure's cloud account (it needs roles/artifactregistry.writer there), digest kept; outputs `images` {service: copy}. `webhook` — the webhook keys above but `events`, plus optional `body`, a Go text/template over .release {application, infrastructure_id, revision, images, delivery_id} and .stages.<earlier id> {status, outputs}, with functions `json` and `default` (empty body = that data as JSON; a JSON body that does not render valid JSON fails the stage); sent with X-Inframan-Event: release_success and X-Inframan-Delivery equal to .release.delivery_id; outputs `status_code`, `response`. Example body: {"images": {{ json .stages.promote.outputs.images }}, "revision": {{ .release.revision }}}. `notify` — a message through the instance's notifications (below). `wait` — `duration_seconds` (1-86400). `manual_judgment` — `prompt`, `timeout_minutes` (1-10080, default 1440); a person approves or rejects it in the console (an agent cannot); reject or timeout fails it. `publish_files` — `service` (the service whose image holds the files: one built FROM scratch with them, never run — scaling off, min_replicas 0), `bucket` (a Cloud Storage bucket name, no gs://; GCP infrastructures only), optional `prefix` (where the files go; `{version}` in it is replaced by the content of `version_file`, a file in the image, which it then requires) and `overwrite` (default false: a file the bucket already has is left as it is, so a published version never changes); uploads every regular file of the release's image of the service as the infrastructure's cloud account (it needs roles/storage.objectCreator on the bucket, objectAdmin to overwrite); outputs `version`, `bucket`, `prefix`, `files`, `published`, `already_there`. list_release_stages reads how a release's stages ran.

A notify step sends a message through the instance's notifications (list_alert_groups, list_notification_channels). In any phase's steps it is a step with `name` and `notify: {group | channels, when, message}` in place of image and commands; as a release stage it is `type: notify` with `group` or `channels`, `when` and `message`. Exactly one of `group` (an alert group's name) and `channels` (1-10 channel names) — a save refuses a group the instance does not have (ALERT_GROUP_NOT_FOUND) or a channel (CHANNEL_NOT_FOUND). `when`: `success` (the default: the run, or the release, got this far), `failure` (it failed before this step, or the release failed) or `always`. A failed run still sends its later failure and always steps, and a failed release its failure and always stages; a stopped one sends nothing. `message` is optional, a Go text/template of at most 2000 characters over .application, .infrastructure, .revision, .commit, .commit_message, .branch, .started_by, .service, .build, .phase, .step, .status, .reason, .link (a stage also .stages.<earlier id> {status, outputs}), built-in functions only; one that fails to render sends the default with a note. A notify step takes no image, commands, env, secrets, sidecars, shell, working_directory, watch_paths or force, and never fails a release: what it sent, or why nothing, is on the step's record. A notify step or stage is the only way a release's outcome reaches a channel: a failed release is on the bell and the feed, and no alert group is sent it by itself, so a release stage with `when: failure` or `always` is how people hear of one. An alert group or a channel a pipeline names cannot be deleted.

params.name: pipeline_id
params.description: The pipeline to update. From list_pipelines.

params.name: yaml
params.description: The updated pipeline definition, in `format`: by default Inframan YAML, in the same shape the export returns.

params.name: format
params.description: The document's format: inframan (default), github (a GitHub Actions workflow) or json.

params.name: drop_unsupported
params.description: Save a GitHub workflow without the parts the pipeline cannot hold. Without it such a workflow is refused, each part named, so it can be taken out of the document first.

capabilities.name: update_preferences
capabilities.summary: Set the instance's display timezone, instance-wide.
capabilities.description:
Changes how every timestamp is rendered FOR EVERYONE on this instance, not just for the caller — there is no per-user setting behind this. Ask the user which zone they want rather than inferring one from a machine clock or a locale.

The value must be an IANA name such as "Asia/Kolkata", "Europe/London" or "UTC". Anything the platform cannot load is refused outright, because a zone that silently fails to load would degrade every timestamp on the instance to UTC and look identical to the setting not working.

Takes effect immediately and is undone by setting it back; nothing is stored against the old value.

params.name: timezone
params.description: IANA timezone name, e.g. "Asia/Kolkata", "Europe/London" or "UTC". Not an abbreviation such as "IST" and not a UTC offset.

capabilities.name: update_revision_setting
capabilities.summary: Choose which revision serves an application: latest, a fixed one, or a split. THIS IS HOW YOU ROLL BACK.
capabilities.description:
Decides which REVISION users reach. A revision is an immutable version of the whole application — every service together — so this moves people between versions of the application, never between services.

THIS IS ROLLBACK. There is no separate rollback tool and no snapshot to restore: going back means pointing traffic at an earlier revision with mode="fixed". Read the revision list, take the id of the last one that was good, and send it. Its Knative services are redeployed from the manifest that release stored, traffic moves to it, and every revision left with no traffic has its Knative services removed — traffic FIRST, so nothing is torn down while it is still serving.

Going forward again is the same call: mode="latest", or fixed on a newer id. Nothing was destroyed on the way back, which is why this is safe to do while you are still working out what broke.

Three modes, and picking the right one is the whole job:
• `latest` — the newest deployed revision serves everything, and keeps serving as new ones land. The normal state.
• `fixed` — one named revision serves everything and STAYS there even when newer ones deploy. Use it to hold a known-good version while something is investigated.
• `split` — weighted across two or more revisions, for a canary. Refused for an application whose services keep a disk (storage:): one disk holds one revision's version at a time.

`revision_id` is required for `fixed`. `splits` is required for `split`, as `revision_id=percent` comma separated and summing to exactly 100 — e.g. `a1b2c3d4-...=90,e5f6a7b8-...=10`. Neither is needed for `latest`: it resolves the newest deployed revision itself, so do not try to find the id yourself.

Get ids from list_application_revisions, newest first. A revision that failed to deploy cannot take traffic, and one belonging to another application is rejected.

IT RETURNS BEFORE THE CLUSTER HAS CAUGHT UP. The setting is queued for the application's deploy queue, which changes the application one request at a time: after a release that is deploying, never beside another change. In its turn it stores the weights, brings back a revision's workload if it has to, moves the routes, and deletes what no longer serves once the gateway routes by them — seconds, or minutes behind a release or when pods wait on cluster capacity. Do NOT send the setting again to check — that queues a second change. Watch list_application_activity instead: `deploy_plan` is the change starting, with what it will do, and `traffic_settled` is the cluster having caught up. Everything the platform does lands there, so it is the one place to look rather than polling the revision list and comparing fields yourself.

This moves real users immediately. It is reversible: send another setting and nothing has been overwritten — the revision you left is still a revision.

Internal service-to-service calls are unaffected: they address a pinned version directly and deliberately bypass this.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application to change. From list_applications.

params.name: mode
params.description: Which of the three modes to use. Declared as a closed set, so choose one rather than composing it: "latest", "fixed" or "split".

params.name: revision_id
params.description: Required for mode="fixed": the revision that serves all traffic. Ignored otherwise.

params.name: splits
params.description: Required for mode="split": weights as revision_id=percent, comma separated, summing to 100. At least two revisions — use mode="fixed" to send everything to one.

capabilities.name: update_service_env_groups
capabilities.summary: Replace the environment groups attached to a service.
capabilities.description:
A REPLACE, not a merge: the set you send becomes the set attached, and anything absent is detached. Read the current set with get_service_env_groups first and send it back with your change, or you will silently remove groups the service depends on.

Takes effect on the next deploy.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service to update. From list_services.

params.name: env_group_ids
params.description: Comma-separated env group ids — the COMPLETE desired set. Send an empty string to detach all.

capabilities.name: validate_route
capabilities.summary: Check whether a domain and path prefix are free before assigning them to a service.
capabilities.description:
A read: it looks for a collision and writes nothing. Nothing is reserved, so a route reported free is only free until someone deploys onto it.

Call it for each domain and path before writing them into a service's `domains:` in inframan.yaml. One domain can serve several services at different paths (`/api` and `/` are two routes; the longest path is matched first), but two services on the same domain+path cannot both be served, and the release of the second is refused (ROUTE_TAKEN). A domain where Grafana, LikeC4 or pgweb is served is never free.

`available: false` comes with the service (and application) already holding the route, so the answer to give the user is which service to change, not that the platform refused something.

This checks the ROUTE only. It says nothing about whether the domain is attached or its certificate is issued — get_domain_status is what answers that, and a free route on a domain that is not active still cannot serve traffic.

params.name: domain
params.description: The hostname to check, e.g. "api.example.com". No scheme and no path.

params.name: path_prefix
params.description: Path prefix on that hostname, e.g. "/api". Defaults to "/": every path of the domain no longer path claims.

capabilities.name: verify_application_identities
capabilities.summary: Verify every service of an application that is waiting for its cloud identity, at once.
capabilities.description: verify_wif for each service waiting for its identity (PENDING_BINDING), after the user ran the ceremony get_application_identities or enable_application_identities returned. Each verification proves its own binding from inside the cluster and records its verdict on its service: read get_application_identities for them, which also says which are still running.

params.name: application_id
params.description: The application. From list_applications.

capabilities.name: verify_builder_identity
capabilities.summary: Verify an in-cluster infrastructure's build identity by reading the builder account's IAM policy, after the user has run the ceremony.
capabilities.description: Applies the ci-builder Kubernetes service account in inframan-ci, then reads the builder service account's IAM policy as the cloud account for the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser binding to it. Only that binding marks the identity verified; a failure names the missing grant. Returns as soon as the read starts; poll get_builder_identity_setup for the verdict, which takes seconds — a grant made moments ago may not be in the policy yet. Safe to call more than once.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure. From list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: verify_cloud_account
capabilities.summary: Check that a cloud account's setup was run, by acting as the account.
capabilities.description:
Step 3. Starts a check that impersonates the account through the platform's own controller identity and calls the APIs a provision would call: the impersonation grant, the project roles, the enabled APIs, the custom roles and their permissions, the node account and who may attach it, and — for an instance with its own GCP project — the network hub. The builder account and each app's grants are not part of it: they are asked for once per infrastructure, right after GKE (get_provisioning_setup).

Returns as soon as the check STARTS. The account moves to verifying and then to verified, or — when something is missing — to failed if it has never passed, and to needs_update if it passed before; read it back with get_cloud_account or get_cloud_account_setup. IAM takes up to a minute to propagate, so the check retries for about two minutes before it calls a missing grant missing.

A failure names the first thing that is wrong and the step to rerun. Report that sentence to the user rather than a summary of it: it is the difference between rerunning one command and rerunning the ceremony.

params.name: cloud_account_id
params.description: UUID of the cloud account, from list_cloud_accounts.

capabilities.name: verify_cloud_identity
capabilities.summary: Check an add-on's cloud identity is set up, by reading its IAM policy as the cloud account.
capabilities.description:
On an AWS infrastructure it reads the tier's IAM role back as the account's role instead, and judges its trust: EKS Pod Identity, this cluster, the tier's namespace. Each install is handed the role as it is created.

Applies the add-on's namespace and Kubernetes service account in the cluster, then reads the tier's GCP service account as the cloud account: it must exist, grant roles/iam.serviceAccountUser to the cloud account and roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser to the tier's pods, and hold any project role the app declares. Call it after the user tells you they have run the commands from get_cloud_identity_setup.

WHY A READ. The cloud account's own ceremony grants it a small IAM reader role, so Inframan can act as it and read exactly what the ceremony set, in seconds, and name the grant that is missing. It reads the policy rather than obtaining a token through it, so a grant made moments ago can be in the policy and still be settling.

WHAT A PASS PROVES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It proves the account exists and carries the bindings the ceremony makes, so every install of this tier runs under them. It does NOT prove the identity can read or write anything else, and it says nothing about any other tier. Do not report it as "backups are working"; report it as "the identity is established". The response and get_cloud_identity_setup both carry a `proves` field saying this; prefer its wording to your own.

Returns as soon as the read starts. It takes seconds — re-read get_cloud_identity_setup for the verdict, where a failure arrives as `last_error` naming the missing grant. A failure is almost always that the commands have not actually been run yet; show the user `last_error` rather than guessing.

Safe to call more than once, and safe to call before the user has done anything — the worst case is a failed probe that tells them so. It creates nothing billable: a namespace the app is going to need anyway, the tier's service account, and a Job that deletes itself.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: Infrastructure whose cluster the probe runs on. It must be READY — there is no cluster to run a pod on before that.

params.name: app_id
params.description: Catalog app id for the add-on, from list_platform_apps.

params.name: tier
params.description: Which tier's identity to verify. Defaults to "basic". Verifying one tier says nothing about another.

capabilities.name: verify_provisioning_setup
capabilities.summary: Verify provisioning's setup after the user has run its script; a pass resumes provisioning.
capabilities.description: Reads every grant the provisioning setup's script makes back as the cloud account (and, for in-cluster builds, applies the ci-builder Kubernetes account first). Returns as soon as the check starts; poll get_provisioning_setup for the verdict, which takes seconds — a grant made moments ago may not be in the policy yet, so a failure right after the script is worth one more try. A pass resumes provisioning on its own. Only while status is pending or failed.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: The infrastructure. From list_infrastructures.

capabilities.name: verify_storage_access
capabilities.summary: Verify a service's grant on a Storage bucket by reading the bucket's IAM policy, after the user ran the grant commands.
capabilities.description:
Reads the bucket's IAM policy as the cloud account for roles/storage.objectAdmin and roles/storage.legacyBucketReader granted to the service's Google account. Only both mark the grant verified; a failure names the missing role in `last_error` — show it to the user rather than guessing.

Call it after the user says they ran the commands from get_storage_access_setup. Returns as soon as the read starts; poll get_storage_access_setup for the verdict, which takes seconds — a grant made moments ago may not be in the policy yet. Safe to call more than once.

On AWS it simulates the service's role against the bucket as the account's role instead (s3:ListBucket on the bucket; s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject on its objects); a failure names the action the role may not take.

params.name: installed_app_id
params.description: The Storage instance, from list_platform_apps.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service whose grant to verify. From list_services.

capabilities.name: verify_wif
capabilities.summary: Prove a service's Workload Identity binding works, after the ceremony was run.
capabilities.description:
Creates the service's Kubernetes service account in the cluster, then reads the Google account's IAM policy as the cloud account for the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser binding to it. Only that binding marks the service BOUND; any other outcome is written on the service as last_error, naming the missing grant, so you can say what to fix.

Call it after the user has run the commands from enable_wif. It returns as soon as the verification starts; poll get_service_wif_info for the verdict, which takes seconds — a grant made moments ago may not be in the policy yet. On success the application is redeployed so its pods pick up the identity.

On an AWS infrastructure it reads the role's trust as the account's role instead: it must admit only EKS Pod Identity from this cluster for this service's namespace and Kubernetes account. Then it makes the Pod Identity association that hands the role to that account.

params.name: service_id
params.description: The service whose binding to verify. From list_services.

capabilities.name: wake_infrastructure
capabilities.summary: Bring a sleeping cluster back now, without waiting for its start time.
capabilities.description:
Brings a sleeping cluster back immediately: its network, its node pools, the gateway with its load balancer on the same address, its databases, every app re-applied from its declared configuration, and every service back to the replicas it had. Use it when someone needs a sleeping environment outside its hours — an engineer working late, a demo, an application that does not answer. Nothing on a sleeping cluster wakes on its own request; this, the schedule or a release is what brings it back.

Returns as soon as the transition starts. The wake itself takes a few minutes; get_sleep_run follows it step by step, and names anything that did not come back.

A WAKE OUTSIDE BUSINESS HOURS IS A SESSION, NOT A PERMANENT OVERRIDE. The cluster stays up for four hours and then the schedule takes over again. That is deliberate: an open-ended wake on a Friday night would keep the cluster up all weekend. Call it again to extend. Waking a cluster that is already inside its business hours has no expiry, because the schedule is keeping it up anyway.

Safe to call on a cluster that is already awake — it is a no-op the platform reports as unchanged rather than an error.

params.name: infrastructure_id
params.description: UUID of the infrastructure, from list_infrastructures.
